papers.paper_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat properties such as pressure, temperature, boiling point, structure of an atom, and electron configuration as if they are not consistently categorized; the paper notes opposite answers for similar items, indicating confusion about which are macroscopic versus sub-microscopic.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Macroscopic properties are bulk, observable properties; sub-microscopic properties concern particles and their structure/configuration.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should ask whether the property describes the bulk sample that can be directly observed/measured (macroscopic) or the particles/particles' arrangement and electron structure (sub-microscopic).
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "About a half of the students tested had difficulty in answering Question 1 correctly"
misconceptions.prevalence: About half of students (average performance in Question 1: 58% correct; 40–64% correct by item)
misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students (n=148 total; 46 first year, 55 second year, 47 third year)
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that a statement like 'copper metal conducts electricity because all metals conduct electricity' is an explanation rather than just a description or classification.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: An explanation must give the mechanism at the particle level, not merely cite a general rule.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish a general descriptive statement from a mechanism-based explanation by asking whether the statement says why at the particle level; for metal conduction, the explanation should refer to electron flow in metals.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "two-thirds of the students thought erroneously that 'copper metal conducts electricity because all metals conduct electricity' was an explanatory statement."
misconceptions.prevalence: Two-thirds of students (Question 2(d))
misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not know that liquid water consists of H2O molecules; some may not represent liquid water at the molecular level correctly.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Liquid water is made of H2O molecules as the stable particles present.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the substance and recall its stable molecular particles; for liquid water, the particles are intact H2O molecules, not separate atoms or ions.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "more than 60 % of the students tested did not know that the particles that exist in liquid water (Question 3(c)) ... are H2O molecules."
misconceptions.prevalence: More than 60% incorrect
misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that water vapour contains particles other than intact H2O molecules, including H2 and O2 molecules or H atoms and O atoms, or that H2O decomposes on boiling.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Water vapour consists of H2O molecules; boiling is a phase change, not decomposition.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that a phase change changes only particle spacing/arrangement, not chemical identity; therefore molecules remain H2O in the vapour.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The main error in Question 4 was due to students thinking that H2O molecules in liquid water decompose into H2 and H2 0 molecules when it is boiled."
misconceptions.prevalence: More than 60% incorrect on related item(s); Question 4 average 24% correct
misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students consider only the solute particles in aqueous solutions and do not recognize that water molecules are also present in aqueous sodium chloride and glucose solutions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Aqueous solutions contain H2O molecules along with the dissolved solute particles.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that 'aqueous' means the solvent is water, so water molecules remain in the solution as part of the particle mixture.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the main source of error was due to students not recognizing that aqueous solutions always contain H2O molecules: they considered only the solute particles."
misconceptions.prevalence: Described as the main source of error; Question 3(f) and 3(g) were very poorly answered (overall average for Question 3: 19% correct)
misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think molecules are distributed uniformly between the liquid and vapour phases in a closed vessel at equilibrium.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: At liquid-vapour equilibrium, the same substance is present in both phases, but particle density is much higher in the liquid than in the vapour; the distribution is not uniform across phases.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from phase density: particles are closely packed in the liquid and much more dispersed in the vapour, even though exchange balances at equilibrium.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The majority thought, surprisingly, that the molecules are distributed uniformly in the liquid and vapour phases (response (e))."
misconceptions.prevalence: Majority of students chose the incorrect uniform-distribution option; only about a quarter correct on Question 5
misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the main reason a gas expands on heating at constant pressure is simply the increase in temperature or the increase in molecular speed.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Heating increases molecular speed, which leads to greater spacing between molecules; the increase in volume is due to increased space between molecules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect higher temperature to faster molecular motion, then infer that faster motion at constant pressure requires a larger average separation, increasing gas volume.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The majority of students thought erroneously that response (e) was correct. Increase in temperature cannot, however, be considered to be the reason for the increase in gas volume when it is heated: it is an experimental fact. Similarly, increase in the speed of the molecules (response (c)) is not the main reason for the increase in volume."
misconceptions.prevalence: Only about 15% correct on Question 10
misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the bonds that break when ice melts are covalent O-H bonds within H2O molecules.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Melting breaks intermolecular forces between water molecules, not the covalent bonds inside each molecule.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular bonds, which hold atoms together within a molecule, from intermolecular bonds, which hold molecules together; melting disrupts the latter only.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "More than half of the students tested had difficulty and they thought that the bonds that break when ice melts are covalent O-H bonds within the molecules."
misconceptions.prevalence: More than half incorrect; Question 11 average 42% correct
misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students write reaction equations in molecular form (e.g. HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O) when the question asks for the particles actually involved, i.e. ions/electrons.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: For ionic reactions, equations should be written using the reacting ions and relevant particles only, such as H+ and OH- for acid-base neutralization.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the species actually present and changing in solution, omit spectator ions, and write the balanced ionic equation based on particles involved.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Most students wrote the equations correctly in terms of molecules. For example, about 70 % of them wrote correctly the equation for the reaction between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide using molecules (HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O)."
misconceptions.prevalence: About 70% gave the molecular equation instead of the requested particle-level equation for Question 12(d)
misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not write reactions in terms of bonds broken and formed, missing that chemical change involves breaking and making specific covalent bonds.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Chemical reactions can be represented by counting bonds broken in reactants and bonds formed in products.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should translate each molecule into its bond structure, then count bonds broken and formed while conserving atoms.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The very poor performance was due to students not writing the given balanced equations in terms of the bonds in the reactant and product molecules."
misconceptions.prevalence: Less than 10% correct on Question 13
misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot write the half-equation for removal of two electrons from a copper atom.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Removing two electrons from copper is Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e-.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that electron loss produces a positively charged ion and balance charge and electrons on both sides.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it was surprising that they could not write the simple equation for the removal of two electrons from a copper atom (Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-)."
misconceptions.prevalence: About 30% could not answer part 12(a)
misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe solid NaCl conducts electricity simply because it contains Na+ and Cl- ions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Solid NaCl does not conduct electricity because its ions are not mobile; conductivity requires mobile ions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish the presence of ions from their mobility: in a solid lattice the ions are fixed, so current cannot flow.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "(b) Solid NaCl consists of Na+ ions and Cl– ions and hence will conduct electricity"
misconceptions.prevalence: About 54% correct, so about 46% held the misconception
misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not correctly relate molecular mass to molecular speed, or cannot order gases by speed and density using mass reasoning.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: At the same temperature, lighter gas molecules move faster than heavier ones; gas density at fixed temperature and pressure increases with molecular mass.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare relative molecular masses: lower mass means higher average speed and lower density under the same T and P.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Student performance in the next question, which tests explanation of molecular speed and gas density in terms of the mass of the molecules, was very poor."
misconceptions.prevalence: Only about 20% correct on Question 15
misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students struggle to connect molecular shape and intermolecular forces to density and melting point in packed hydrocarbon solids.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular shape affects packing efficiency and intermolecular interactions, which in turn affect density and melting point.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare linear vs branched molecules: better packing usually gives higher density and, depending on packing/intermolecular contacts, affects melting point.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Though Question 16 appears to be more difficult than Question 15, because its solution needs the correlation of density/melting point with some properties of molecules and intermolecular forces, student performance was much better."
misconceptions.prevalence: About half correct; about half incorrect on Question 16
misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

papers.paper_title: University Students' Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Comparison of First & Third-Year Students

misconceptions.target_misconception: Some first-year students do not recognize that a functional group can affect a molecule's boiling point, implying they think compounds with the same carbon atoms should have the same boiling point or that functional group differences are not important.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Functional groups can change the type and strength of intermolecular forces, which changes boiling point; alcohols boil higher than ethers because alcohols can form hydrogen bonds while ethers cannot.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the functional groups, identify whether hydrogen bonding is possible, and then infer that stronger intermolecular forces lead to a higher boiling point.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Some first-year students seem unaware that a functional group can affect a molecule's boiling point."
misconceptions.prevalence: 50% of first-year students answered correctly; 100% of third-year students answered correctly
misconceptions.population: First-year (2023) and third-year (2021) chemistry education students; 10 students in each cohort
misconceptions.concept_category: boiling point factors / functional group effects
misconceptions.source_title: University Students' Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Comparison of First & Third-Year Students

misconceptions.target_misconception: Several first-year students believe that the most volatile compounds are the ones with the highest boiling points and molar masses, and that higher molar mass means lower boiling point because the intermolecular bonds are weaker in larger nonpolar hydrocarbon molecules.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Higher molar mass and greater polarizability generally strengthen London dispersion forces, which can raise boiling point; nonpolar molecules still experience van der Waals (dispersion) forces.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should relate molecular size and electron cloud polarizability to dispersion forces, then predict that stronger dispersion forces usually increase boiling point rather than decrease it.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Several first-year students assume that the most volatile compounds are the compounds with the highest boiling points and molar masses."
misconceptions.prevalence: 50% of first-year students answered correctly; 100% of third-year students answered correctly
misconceptions.population: First-year (2023) and third-year (2021) chemistry education students; 10 students in each cohort
misconceptions.concept_category: boiling point factors / molar mass and dispersion
misconceptions.source_title: University Students' Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Comparison of First & Third-Year Students

misconceptions.subtopic: Polarizability, atomic size, and steric effects
misconceptions.target_misconception: Some students failed to connect larger atomic size with easier polarization, suggesting they do not reason that a larger iodine atom is more polarizable than bromine because its valence electrons are less tightly held by the nucleus.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A larger atom with more weakly held valence electrons is more easily polarized, which strengthens London dispersion forces and can affect boiling point.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare atomic size, infer electron-cloud polarizability, and then connect greater polarizability to stronger dispersion forces and higher boiling point.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "They failed to realize that the size of the iodine atom is greater than the bromine atom, so the valence electron in the iodine atom is weakly bound by the nucleus more than the bromine atom."
misconceptions.prevalence: 70% of third-year students answered correctly; 20% of first-year students answered correctly
misconceptions.population: First-year (2023) and third-year (2021) chemistry education students; 10 students in each cohort
misconceptions.source_title: University Students' Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Comparison of First & Third-Year Students

misconceptions.target_misconception: Some first-year students appear to think that the higher the hydrocarbon compound's molar mass, the lower its boiling point because of weaker bonds between hydrocarbon molecules and their nonpolar character, rather than recognizing that nonpolar molecules still interact through van der Waals forces.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nonpolar molecules do experience London dispersion forces; as molar mass and polarizability increase, these forces generally become stronger and can increase boiling point.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the molecule as nonpolar, then apply London dispersion forces rather than dismissing intermolecular interactions altogether.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "They failed to recognize that the van der Waals forces exist in non-polar molecules."
misconceptions.prevalence: 50% of first-year students answered correctly
misconceptions.population: First-year (2023) chemistry education students; 10 students in the cohort
misconceptions.concept_category: nonpolar molecules / van der Waals forces
misconceptions.source_title: University Students' Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Comparison of First & Third-Year Students

misconceptions.target_misconception: Some students did not identify London dispersion forces as the interaction between methane molecules, implying they may think nonpolar molecules have no intermolecular forces or choose stronger polar interactions instead.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Methane is nonpolar, so the dominant intermolecular force between methane molecules is London dispersion force.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine that methane is nonpolar, then select London dispersion forces as the appropriate intermolecular interaction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the interaction between the methane molecules is London dispersion forces because methane is a nonpolar molecule."
misconceptions.prevalence: 20% of first-year students answered correctly; 50% of third-year students answered correctly
misconceptions.population: First-year (2023) and third-year (2021) chemistry education students; 10 students in each cohort
misconceptions.source_title: University Students' Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Comparison of First & Third-Year Students

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may incorrectly think hydrogen bonding occurs whenever a molecule contains hydrogen atoms, rather than only when hydrogen is covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom and interacts with a lone pair on another electronegative atom.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires H covalently bonded to N, O, or F and attraction to a lone pair on another electronegative atom.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should inspect the bonding environment of hydrogen and verify whether the donor atom is sufficiently electronegative before concluding that hydrogen bonding is possible.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students assume hydrogen bonds involve hydrogen atoms, occurring when a C atom binds to an H atom in the molecule."
misconceptions.population: Students discussed in cited prior research (Cooper et al., 2015; related studies mentioned in the paper)
misconceptions.source_title: University Students' Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Comparison of First & Third-Year Students

papers.paper_title: 2.2 Research instruments

misconceptions.subtopic: Phase change and bond breaking in water
misconceptions.target_misconception: Heating water breaks the covalent bond between the O and H atoms in the water molecule.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Phase changes such as heating, melting, or evaporation do not break intramolecular covalent O–H bonds in water; they overcome intermolecular attractions between molecules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular bonds from intermolecular forces: heating supplies energy to separate water molecules from each other during a phase change, but the O–H covalent bonds within each molecule remain intact unless a chemical reaction occurs.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "there was a covalent bond break between the O and H atoms in the water molecule due to heating"
misconceptions.prevalence: 24.6% of 69 students
misconceptions.population: Grade XI high school students (n=69 for the IFDI misconception table; overall class XI sample n=101)
misconceptions.source_title: 2.2 Research instruments

misconceptions.subtopic: Comparison of intermolecular and intramolecular forces
misconceptions.target_misconception: Intermolecular forces are stronger than intramolecular forces.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intramolecular bonds are stronger than intermolecular forces; intermolecular forces are weaker attractions between molecules compared with covalent/ionic bonds within molecules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the kinds of interactions: bonds holding atoms together inside a molecule require more energy to break than the attractions between separate molecules, so intermolecular forces cannot be stronger than intramolecular bonds.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Intermolecular force is stronger than intramolecular force"
misconceptions.prevalence: 23.1% of 69 students
misconceptions.population: Grade XI high school students (n=69 for the IFDI misconception table; overall class XI sample n=101)
misconceptions.source_title: 2.2 Research instruments

misconceptions.target_misconception: The concave shape of a liquid surface is caused by dipole–dipole intermolecular force.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The shape of a liquid surface (e.g., meniscus) is determined by the balance of adhesive and cohesive forces with the container surface, not simply by dipole–dipole attraction alone.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from the interactions between the liquid and the container: if adhesion and cohesion differ, the liquid surface curves accordingly; the shape is not directly explained by naming one type of intermolecular force without considering the solid–liquid interactions and relative strengths.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the surface shape of concave fluids is influenced by dipole–dipole intermolecular force"
misconceptions.prevalence: 29.2% of 69 students
misconceptions.population: Grade XI high school students (n=69 for the IFDI misconception table; overall class XI sample n=101)
misconceptions.source_title: 2.2 Research instruments

misconceptions.target_misconception: During melting and freezing, the volumes of ice and water are the same.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ice and liquid water have different volumes for the same mass because water expands on freezing and contracts on melting; density changes accompany the phase change.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare densities of the two phases: because the arrangement of water molecules in ice is more open than in liquid water, a given mass occupies a larger volume as ice than as liquid water.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "in the smelting and freezing process, the volume of ice and water is the same"
misconceptions.prevalence: 27.7% of 69 students
misconceptions.population: Grade XI high school students (n=69 for the IFDI misconception table; overall class XI sample n=101)
misconceptions.source_title: 2.2 Research instruments

misconceptions.subtopic: Vapor pressure and intermolecular force strength
misconceptions.target_misconception: Substances with strong intermolecular forces have large vapor pressures.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Stronger intermolecular forces lead to lower vapor pressure because molecules are less able to escape from the liquid into the gas phase.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect vapor pressure to molecular escape from the liquid surface: if attractions between molecules are strong, fewer molecules leave the liquid, so vapor pressure is lower, not higher.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "substances that have strong intermolecular forces have large vapor pressures"
misconceptions.prevalence: 26.2% of 69 students
misconceptions.population: Grade XI high school students (n=69 for the IFDI misconception table; overall class XI sample n=101)
misconceptions.source_title: 2.2 Research instruments

papers.paper_title: Investigating the impact of three-dimensional learning interventions on student understanding of structure-property relationships

misconceptions.topic: Boiling point trends and intermolecular forces
misconceptions.subtopic: Hydrogen bonding as evidence for higher boiling point
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that a substance's higher boiling point can be explained without linking it to stronger intermolecular forces and the extra energy required to overcome them, or they give only a surface-level mention of hydrogen bonding with no causal mechanism.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A higher boiling point is caused by stronger intermolecular forces; molecules with stronger attractions require more energy to separate before boiling occurs.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the compound with stronger intermolecular forces, explain that these stronger attractions make molecules harder to separate, and state that more energy is needed to overcome those interactions, leading to a higher boiling point.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students may be able to easily make a claim, they can struggle with identifying appropriate evidence or being able to clearly link evidence to the claim through reasoning"
misconceptions.prevalence: 40% of Cohort 1 provided no explanation or non-normative responses; 50% of Cohort 4 gave the most sophisticated reasoning including energy
misconceptions.population: General chemistry students across four cohorts (Cohort 1 N=119; Cohort 2 N=106; Cohort 3 N=86; Cohort 4 N=70)
misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of three-dimensional learning interventions on student understanding of structure-property relationships

misconceptions.topic: Boiling point trends and intermolecular forces
misconceptions.subtopic: Correct boiling point ranking for ethanol vs dimethyl ether
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students incorrectly choose dimethyl ether or cannot predict the higher-boiling compound when comparing ethanol and dimethyl ether.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ethanol has the higher boiling point than dimethyl ether because ethanol can form hydrogen bonds in addition to dipole-dipole interactions and London dispersion forces.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the intermolecular forces present in each compound, recognize that ethanol has hydrogen bonding while dimethyl ether does not, and conclude that ethanol’s stronger overall intermolecular attraction gives it the higher boiling point.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The majority of students in the control group incorrectly identified the claim"
misconceptions.prevalence: In Cohort 1, 35% selected ethanol as the correct claim before intervention; this increased to 52% in Cohort 2 and 80% in Cohort 3
misconceptions.population: General chemistry students in the structure-property assessment at the end of GC2
misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of three-dimensional learning interventions on student understanding of structure-property relationships

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students draw hydrogen bonding within a molecule as if it were a covalent bond between H and O rather than as an intermolecular, non-covalent attraction between separate molecules.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is a non-covalent interaction between different molecules, not a bond within one molecule.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify donor and acceptor sites, then draw the hydrogen bond between molecules with a dashed or dotted line to show an intermolecular attraction rather than a covalent bond inside the ethanol molecule.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students have difficulty differentiating between bonding and intermolecular forces"
misconceptions.prevalence: Less than 20% of Cohort 1 correctly represented hydrogen bonding as between molecules; 52% of Cohort 2; 57% of Cohort 3; 79% of Cohort 4
misconceptions.population: General chemistry students drawing hydrogen bonding for three ethanol molecules
misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of three-dimensional learning interventions on student understanding of structure-property relationships

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think covalent bonds are broken during the boiling process.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling separates molecules by overcoming intermolecular forces; covalent bonds within molecules are not broken when a liquid boils.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular covalent bonds from intermolecular attractions and reason that heat supplied during boiling is used to overcome intermolecular forces between molecules, not to break covalent bonds inside molecules.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "along with the misunderstanding that covalent bonds are broken during the boiling process"
misconceptions.population: Students answering questions on hydrogen bonding and boiling point explanations
misconceptions.concept_category: phase change / bonding vs intermolecular forces
misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of three-dimensional learning interventions on student understanding of structure-property relationships

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students omit or fail to use the idea that stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to overcome, or they do not connect energy to the boiling point difference.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to overcome, which leads to a higher boiling point.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare interaction strengths, state that stronger attractions are harder to overcome, and infer that more energy is needed to boil the substance with stronger intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students were more likely than Cohorts 1-3 to also include the ideas of energy needed to overcome stronger forces for a more sophisticated explanation"
misconceptions.prevalence: 17-33% for Cohorts 1-3 versus 50% for Cohort 4
misconceptions.population: Students responding to Question 6 on the structure-property assessment
misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of three-dimensional learning interventions on student understanding of structure-property relationships

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students explain boiling point by saying one substance has 'more bonds' that must be broken to boil.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point depends on intermolecular force strength, not on having more covalent bonds to break.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should not count bonds in the molecule; instead, they should focus on the strength and type of intermolecular forces between molecules and the energy required to overcome them.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Because ethanol will have more bonds than dimethyl ether, therefore have more bonds to break to reach a boiling point"
misconceptions.population: Students coded as giving non-normative reasoning in Question 6
misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of three-dimensional learning interventions on student understanding of structure-property relationships

papers.paper_title: Gamifying intermolecular forces: Improving student performance outcomes for college freshman-level intermolecular forces

misconceptions.subtopic: London dispersion forces and molecular size
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the relative boiling point can always be predicted only by the simple rule that a molecule with hydrogen bonding must boil higher than one with only London dispersion forces, and they do not apply this to exceptions where a larger molecule with stronger LDFs can boil higher than a smaller molecule with weak H-bonding.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point depends on the overall balance of intermolecular forces; a larger, more polarizable molecule can have stronger London dispersion forces and a higher boiling point than a smaller molecule even if the smaller one can hydrogen bond weakly.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Compare the size/polarizability and the types of intermolecular forces in both molecules, then weigh which set of attractions is stronger overall rather than relying on a single surface rule.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “they are often unable to reason that a large molecule with high LDFs may have a higher boiling point than a small molecule with weak H-bonding.”
misconceptions.population: college freshman-level chemistry students
misconceptions.concept_category: boiling point trends / LDF vs hydrogen bonding
misconceptions.source_title: Gamifying intermolecular forces: Improving student performance outcomes for college freshman-level intermolecular forces

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may fail to recognize that a molecule can be capable of hydrogen bonding even when it is not a typical alcohol or common textbook example.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding occurs when a molecule has H bonded to N, O, or F and a suitable lone-pair acceptor; uncommon or unstable molecules can still be hydrogen-bond donors/acceptors if they meet the structural criteria.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Inspect the functional groups and Lewis structure for N–H, O–H, or F–H bonds and lone pairs on N/O/F, then decide whether hydrogen bonding is possible regardless of whether the molecule is a familiar example.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students were not significantly better or worse at recognizing that methylimine is ‘capable’ of hydrogen bonding as a cause for its higher boiling point compared to ethene.”
misconceptions.prevalence: Pre-activity correct responses: 60.6%; post-activity correct responses: 61.9%
misconceptions.population: students in the freshman-level IMF activity (matched n = 236 responses)
misconceptions.source_title: Gamifying intermolecular forces: Improving student performance outcomes for college freshman-level intermolecular forces

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not correctly determine how molecular geometry affects polarity, leading them to miss that a cis isomer can have stronger dipole-dipole interactions than the trans isomer.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular geometry determines whether bond dipoles cancel; a cis isomer may be polar while the trans isomer is nonpolar or less polar, so the cis isomer can have stronger dipole-dipole interactions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Draw or interpret the molecular geometry, add bond dipoles as vectors, and decide whether a net dipole remains; if the cis isomer has a net dipole and the trans does not, the cis isomer has stronger dipole-dipole forces.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students were not significantly better or worse at recognizing that the cis- isomer of dichloro-difluroxenon has stronger dipole-dipole interactions than the trans- isomer.”
misconceptions.prevalence: Pre-activity correct responses: 63.1%; post-activity correct responses: 67.4%
misconceptions.population: students in the freshman-level IMF activity (matched n = 236 responses)
misconceptions.source_title: Gamifying intermolecular forces: Improving student performance outcomes for college freshman-level intermolecular forces

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may fail to recognize that cis and trans alkene isomers can differ in polarity and dipole-dipole forces.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The cis isomer of dichloroethene has a net dipole and therefore stronger dipole-dipole interactions than the trans isomer, whose dipoles cancel more effectively.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Use the molecular geometry to assess whether the bond dipoles cancel; then compare the strength of dipole-dipole interactions based on the net molecular dipole.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students were significantly better at recognizing that the cis- isomer of dichloro-ethene has stronger dipole-dipole interactions than the trans- isomer”
misconceptions.prevalence: Pre-activity correct responses: 55.1%; post-activity correct responses: 66.1%
misconceptions.population: students in the freshman-level IMF activity (matched n = 236 responses)
misconceptions.source_title: Gamifying intermolecular forces: Improving student performance outcomes for college freshman-level intermolecular forces

misconceptions.subtopic: Hydrogen bonding and boiling point comparison
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may incorrectly think that a substance with fewer hydrogen-bonding opportunities can still have the higher boiling point, rather than connecting more hydrogen bonding to stronger intermolecular attraction and higher boiling point.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: More hydrogen bonding generally increases intermolecular attraction and raises boiling point; glycerol has more hydrogen bonding than pentanol, so glycerol boils higher.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Count the hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors available, compare the extent of hydrogen bonding in each molecule, and infer that more extensive hydrogen bonding usually raises boiling point.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students are significantly better at recognising that glycerol has more hydrogen bonding than pentanol as a cause for glycerol having the higher boiling point.”
misconceptions.prevalence: Pre-activity correct responses: 69.1%; post-activity correct responses: 76.3%
misconceptions.population: students in the freshman-level IMF activity (matched n = 236 responses)
misconceptions.source_title: Gamifying intermolecular forces: Improving student performance outcomes for college freshman-level intermolecular forces

misconceptions.subtopic: Comparing LDFs and dipole-dipole interactions in sulfur oxides
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think sulfur trioxide should have dipole-dipole interactions like sulfur dioxide, or may not understand that the stronger LDFs of the larger molecule can outweigh sulfur dioxide's dipole-dipole interactions in boiling point comparison.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Sulfur trioxide is nonpolar and has no dipole-dipole interactions; its larger electron cloud gives stronger London dispersion forces than sulfur dioxide, contributing to the higher boiling point.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Determine whether the molecule has a net dipole. If not, rule out dipole-dipole forces, then compare size/polarizability to judge London dispersion strength and its effect on boiling point.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students are significantly better at recognising that sulfur trioxide does not have dipole-dipole interactions, but has significantly stronger LDFs when compared to sulfur dioxide's weaker LDFs and dipole-dipole interaction, as a cause for sulfur trioxide having the higher boiling point.”
misconceptions.prevalence: Pre-activity correct responses: 30.9%; post-activity correct responses: 41.5%
misconceptions.population: students in the freshman-level IMF activity (matched n = 236 responses)
misconceptions.concept_category: polarity / LDF vs dipole-dipole interactions / boiling point trends
misconceptions.source_title: Gamifying intermolecular forces: Improving student performance outcomes for college freshman-level intermolecular forces

papers.paper_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Dipole-dipole interactions occur within a single molecule, not between two molecules.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interactions are intermolecular forces that occur between separate molecules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify that the interaction is between the partial positive end of one polar molecule and the partial negative end of another polar molecule, not between atoms within the same molecule.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “a large portion of the students believed that intermolecular forces were within a single molecule rather than between”
misconceptions.population: students in general chemistry; discussion references prior work
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Any molecule containing nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine can hydrogen bond.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires a hydrogen atom bonded to N, O, or F and interaction with a lone pair on N, O, or F; the presence of N, O, or F alone is not sufficient.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check both the donor and acceptor conditions for hydrogen bonding, rather than assuming that the presence of N, O, or F automatically makes a molecule hydrogen-bonding capable.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students often generalize principles associated with intermolecular forces such that any molecule with either nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine carries the ability to hydrogen bond”
misconceptions.population: students in general chemistry; prior literature summarized in the paper
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Lone pairs or open electron sites are places that should bond with another atom, so the dipole-dipole interaction is treated like a covalent bond formation site.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interactions are attractions between partial charges on different molecules; lone pairs may influence polarity and molecular shape but are not themselves bonding sites for intermolecular force formation.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use molecular polarity and partial charges to locate the attraction between molecules, not infer that a lone pair is an available bonding site that must be filled.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the lone pairs represent sites that are free to bond with other atoms.”
misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in 5 students in Version 1 (Sawyer, Sasha, Sadie, Sabrina, Sebastian) when discussing Lewis dot structures; also discussed as a broader pattern in the Discussion
misconceptions.population: Version 1 students in second semester general chemistry (n=9 in Version 1; 18 total interviewed)
misconceptions.concept_category: bonding availability / intermolecular vs intramolecular forces
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: If a representation shows no explicit lone pairs or bonds, the atom has an 'open spot' that needs to be filled by an intermolecular interaction to satisfy the octet.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Missing dots or bonds in a representation do not mean an atom needs an additional bond; dipole-dipole interactions depend on partial charges between molecules, not octet completion in the displayed model.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should interpret the representation in terms of electron distribution and polarity, and recognize that intermolecular attractions do not add bonds to complete octets.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students considered the space around each atom as the location where dipole-dipole interactions could occur”
misconceptions.population: students in both protocol versions; especially Version 1 space-filling and chemical formula tasks
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Molecular geometry is explicitly shown in Lewis dot structures, so a Lewis structure can be read as linear unless lone pairs are added mentally afterward.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lewis structures encode connectivity and lone pairs, and molecular geometry must be inferred using electron-domain considerations; lone pairs change shape and therefore polarity.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should examine the presence and arrangement of lone pairs to infer the true molecular geometry, then determine whether the molecule is polar and where dipole-dipole attraction can occur.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students carried the assumption that molecular geometry was explicit in Lewis dot structures”
misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in 3 students in Version 2 (Regan, Rachel, Rebecca) before correction
misconceptions.population: Version 2 second semester general chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

misconceptions.subtopic: Linear and nonpolar assumption for SeO2
misconceptions.target_misconception: Selenium dioxide is linear and nonpolar when first viewed in Lewis dot form because lone pairs are not initially considered.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Selenium dioxide is bent because lone pairs on selenium affect bond angle, making the molecule polar.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should count electron domains and include lone pairs in VSEPR reasoning; the bent geometry creates a net dipole that allows dipole-dipole interactions.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “designated the molecule as linear and non-polar, without taking into account the influence of lone pairs”
misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in 3 students in Version 2 before they corrected themselves
misconceptions.population: Version 2 students working on Lewis dot structures
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: The larger atom in a ball-and-stick or space-filling model is the preferred location for dipole-dipole interaction because larger size means stronger attraction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interaction location is determined by molecular polarity and partial charges, not by atomic size; size in these models is not itself a proxy for dipole-dipole strength.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use electronegativity and molecular geometry to identify partial positive and negative regions, then place the interaction between opposite partial charges on different molecules.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the bigger the two atoms that are bonding are, the weaker the forces are.”
misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in multiple Version 1 students; 3 students (Sandeep, Spencer, Sebastian) explicitly began to use size in ball-and-stick tasks, and 1 student (Sandeep) stayed with size in space-filling
misconceptions.population: Version 1 second semester general chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: In space-filling models, larger atom size directly corresponds to higher electronegativity and therefore identifies the interaction site.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atom size in a space-filling model is a graphical convention and is not equivalent to electronegativity; the interaction site should be inferred from polarity and partial charge, not from visual size alone.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish the representational cue of atomic size from chemical properties such as electronegativity, and use electron distribution to determine the dipole-dipole interaction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “I think it's just because seeing how one ball can be bigger than the other throws you off easily.”
misconceptions.population: Version 1 students; discussed in relation to space-filling representations
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Atoms in the molecules carry fixed valence charges or ionic charges that can be used to predict dipole-dipole attraction by pairing opposite charges.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interactions arise from partial charges in polar covalent molecules; atoms do not need to be treated as ionic species with fixed charges from the periodic table.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use electronegativity differences and molecular geometry to identify partial positive and partial negative ends, then connect those ends between molecules.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “began assigning charges to each of the atoms in the molecules”
misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in 4 students in Version 2 (Ria, Rachel, Rebecca, Richard) in the space-filling task
misconceptions.population: Version 2 second semester general chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: A central atom cannot participate in or be used to locate dipole-dipole interactions because it is already in the middle of the molecule and is not available to connect.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The relevant interaction site is the region of partial charge in the molecule, which may involve a central atom’s bonded environment; being central does not by itself prevent intermolecular attraction.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate the molecule’s polarity from electronegativity and geometry, rather than excluding atoms solely because of their position in the structure.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “I don't know about this one because chlorine is the central... and I don't really know how it's going to connect to the hydrogen.”
misconceptions.population: Version 2 chemical formula task; reported for Rachel and also discussed for Ranger and Richard
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: A triple bond or greater number of bonds directly means a stronger dipole-dipole interaction or stronger intermolecular attraction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond order affects intramolecular bonding, but dipole-dipole interactions depend on molecular polarity and the magnitude/direction of partial charges between molecules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should not infer intermolecular force strength from the number of covalent bonds; instead they should analyze electronegativity differences and geometry to locate the partial charges that attract between molecules.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the number of bonds signifies the strength of dipole-dipole interactions in the molecule.”
misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in Version 2 ball-and-stick task; explicitly noted for Ria, and Rebecca linked affinity to number of bonds
misconceptions.population: Version 2 second semester general chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

papers.paper_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

misconceptions.target_misconception: Dipole-dipole forces occur within a single molecule at polar bonds rather than only between molecules.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole forces are intermolecular attractions between separate molecules, not bonds within one molecule.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first determine the molecular dipole for each molecule from bonded-atom electronegativity differences, then identify that the attractive interaction occurs between the positive end of one molecule and the negative end of another molecule.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "identify the pair(s) of atoms where the strongest intermolecular force would occur?"
misconceptions.prevalence: 11 of 18 participants consistently showed dipole-dipole as an intramolecular force; 61% in prior work drew dipole-dipole within a molecule.
misconceptions.population: Second semester general chemistry students (18 interview participants); prior cited study of students drawing ethanol molecules.
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

misconceptions.target_misconception: Any positive and negative partial charges or dipoles anywhere in a molecule pair can be directly connected as the location of dipole-dipole interaction, including when the charges were inferred from unbonded atoms or different molecules without first establishing molecular dipoles correctly.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole attraction should be based on the interaction between the positive end of one molecular dipole and the negative end of another molecular dipole, derived from correct bonded-atom polarity analysis.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare electronegativities only for bonded atoms to identify bond dipoles, combine bond dipoles to determine each molecule's polarity, and then use the positive and negative molecular ends to locate the intermolecular attraction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "In this case, since F would have the more negative partial charge in the iodine monofluoride and then Se would have the positive dipole on the selenium dioxide. It makes sense that they're connected."
misconceptions.prevalence: 10 of 18 participants used opposite charges attract as a basis; some varied in how they determined molecular dipoles.
misconceptions.population: Second semester general chemistry interview participants
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

misconceptions.target_misconception: Electronegativity should be compared between atoms on different molecules to decide where dipole-dipole attraction occurs, rather than only between bonded atoms within a molecule.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electronegativity is used first between bonded atoms to determine bond polarity; intermolecular dipole-dipole location is then inferred from the resulting molecular dipoles.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify bonded atoms, subtract electronegativity values only for those bonded pairs, decide which bonds are polar, determine each molecule's dipole, and then place the intermolecular force between opposite molecular ends.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I think the sulfur [in SCl2] and the nitrogen [in NH3] might be able to, just because the electronegativity difference is 0.5."
misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in approach 1B and 2A/2B; e.g., one participant in approach 1B and three participants in approach 2A compared atoms on different molecules.
misconceptions.population: Second semester general chemistry interview participants
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

misconceptions.target_misconception: Electronegativity can be compared between unbonded atoms within the same molecule to decide where dipole-dipole attraction is located.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electronegativity comparisons for bond polarity must be made only between atoms that share a chemical bond.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should restrict electronegativity differences to bonded atoms, use those bond polarities to infer molecular polarity, and then locate dipole-dipole attraction between molecules.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the chlorine [in CH3Cl] does have a stronger electronegativity than the hydrogen atoms [in CH3Cl]. So that tells me that the chlorine is found to be partially negative."
misconceptions.prevalence: Documented for Lam in approach 1C; Lam compared unbonded atoms within one molecule in one prompt.
misconceptions.population: One second semester general chemistry interview participant (Lam)
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

misconceptions.target_misconception: Any atom pair whose electronegativity difference is greater than 0.5 is the site of dipole-dipole interaction, even if the pair is within a molecule and not a bond site for intermolecular attraction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A difference greater than 0.5 is used to classify a bond as polar covalent, not to directly locate an intermolecular dipole-dipole force.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the 0.5 threshold only to decide bond polarity for bonded atoms, then use the set of bond dipoles to determine molecular polarity and the intermolecular attraction between molecules.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "bonds between S and chloride [in SCl2], and N and hydrogen [in NH3] are all polar bonds because the difference between electronegativity of S and Cl is 0.5."
misconceptions.prevalence: 4 participants consistently used bonded-atom EN differences above 0.5 to assign dipole-dipole location within a molecule; additional students used this idea inconsistently.
misconceptions.population: Second semester general chemistry interview participants
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

misconceptions.target_misconception: The atom pair with the largest electronegativity difference is automatically where dipole-dipole force occurs.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Largest electronegativity difference does not by itself determine the location of dipole-dipole force; bond polarity and molecular dipoles must be considered.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare bonded atoms only, determine which bonds are polar, build each molecular dipole, and then identify the positive-to-negative attraction between molecules rather than simply choosing the maximum EN difference.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I feel like the more [EN] difference there is between the two, the more that they're going to interact."
misconceptions.prevalence: 4 participants (Ethan, Feng, Kavita, Mason) used the largest EN difference approach.
misconceptions.population: Second semester general chemistry interview participants
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

misconceptions.target_misconception: The atom with the biggest electronegativity value is the one that attracts the other molecule most strongly and therefore marks the dipole-dipole location.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electronegativity is used comparatively to create bond dipoles; the larger raw value alone is not the site of intermolecular attraction.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use electronegativity differences between bonded atoms to establish polarity, then use the resulting molecular dipole directions to locate the intermolecular force.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it's [N in NH3] more electronegative, so connect that to chlorine because that's [Cl in SCl2] also the most electronegative."
misconceptions.prevalence: 3 participants (Ethan, Lam, Quinn) focused on the biggest EN values; Quinn used it consistently across all four prompts.
misconceptions.population: Second semester general chemistry interview participants
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

misconceptions.target_misconception: The largest atoms in the two molecules are the ones that will experience dipole-dipole attraction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole attraction depends on molecular polarity arising from bond polarity and molecular shape, not on atomic size.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should ignore atom size as the basis of intermolecular attraction, determine bond polarities from electronegativity differences, identify molecular dipoles, and then place the dipole-dipole interaction between opposite molecular ends.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the I [in IF] is significantly bigger than the F [in IF]...It makes me feel that the I should have more attraction to it"
misconceptions.prevalence: 1 participant (Ethan) used atomic size as the basis in the prompts where size was visually explicit.
misconceptions.population: One second semester general chemistry interview participant (Ethan)
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

misconceptions.target_misconception: Bent molecular shape itself means the bonds inside that molecule are the dipole-dipole force location.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular shape helps determine molecular polarity, but dipole-dipole forces occur between molecules, not inside the bent molecule's bonds.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use shape together with bond polarity to infer whether a molecule has a net dipole, then use the positive and negative ends of two molecules to locate the intermolecular attraction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "because dipole-dipole exists where...molecules are bent, and these [sulfur to chlorine bonds] are in a bent shape right here. So these two bonds would be dipole-dipole."
misconceptions.prevalence: 1 participant (Danh) consistently used molecular shape in all four prompts.
misconceptions.population: One second semester general chemistry interview participant (Danh)
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

misconceptions.target_misconception: If a molecule is not bent, it has no dipole and therefore cannot participate in dipole-dipole interactions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular polarity depends on the vector sum of bond dipoles and overall geometry; a molecule can have a dipole even if a student does not recognize a bent shape in the representation.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine the bond dipoles from electronegativity differences, consider the molecular geometry, and decide whether the bond dipoles cancel or produce a net molecular dipole rather than using bend/no-bend as the only criterion.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "when asked whether there was a dipole in IF, Danh replied there was not a dipole because it did not show a bent geometry."
misconceptions.prevalence: 1 participant (Danh) explicitly said IF had no dipole because it was not bent.
misconceptions.population: One second semester general chemistry interview participant (Danh)
misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

papers.paper_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

misconceptions.target_misconception: Intermolecular forces occur within a single molecule rather than between molecules.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are interactions between molecules, not intramolecular forces within one molecule.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the two separate molecules in the task and determine the strongest attractive interaction between them based on their electrostatic properties, not on bonds within one molecule.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "over half of participants held the conception that intermolecular forces occur within a single molecule rather than between molecules."
misconceptions.prevalence: over half of participants (from Cooper et al., cited in paper)
misconceptions.population: general chemistry students in prior study cited by the paper
misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

misconceptions.target_misconception: A lone pair on an atom is a direct indicator that a hydrogen can bond there in intermolecular force tasks.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding occurs between a hydrogen attached to N, O, or F and a lone pair on another electronegative atom; lone pairs alone are not simply 'bonding sites' by themselves.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the intermolecular force definition and identify complementary partial positive and partial negative regions between different molecules rather than treating any lone pair as an available bond site.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Because I have a lone pair ... the hydrogen could bond there."
misconceptions.prevalence: 5 students
misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

misconceptions.target_misconception: An atom's octet state or how 'surrounded' it is determines whether it can participate in intermolecular interactions, and an incomplete octet means it is a bonding site.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular interactions are determined by partial charges and electrostatic attraction between molecules, not by whether an atom has a full octet or appears 'surrounded'.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should look for electrostatic complementarity between molecules and connect partial positive regions to partial negative regions, rather than inferring intermolecular interaction sites from octet completeness.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it doesn't have its full like ... it's not like surrounded"
misconceptions.prevalence: 5 students
misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

misconceptions.target_misconception: An uneven distribution of electrons or extra lone pairs in a Lewis structure directly means the atom has a negative charge and is attractive for intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Partial charges arise from differences in electron density and electronegativity across the molecule, not simply from counting lone pairs or noticing an 'uneven' Lewis structure.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from electronegativity and electron density to determine where partial positive and partial negative regions exist, then infer the likely intermolecular interaction site from those partial charges.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "there's an extra lone pair on the side and that gives it a negative charge."
misconceptions.prevalence: part of the 5-student availability-for-bonding group
misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

misconceptions.target_misconception: Electronegativity values can be subtracted within a single molecule to decide which molecule has the strongest intermolecular force.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electronegativity differences within a bond help infer bond polarity and molecular polarity, but intermolecular force strength is determined by interactions between molecules, not by the molecule with the largest internal electronegativity difference.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first use electronegativity differences to infer bond polarity and then use molecular polarity and complementary partial charges to determine the strongest force between two molecules.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "participants subtracted the provided elemental electronegativity values within the same molecule and identified the one with the largest difference as having the strongest intermolecular force."
misconceptions.prevalence: 5 students
misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

misconceptions.target_misconception: A Lewis structure's drawn appearance can be taken as the actual molecular geometry; for example, a molecule that appears linear in the Lewis structure is treated as linear and nonpolar.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Actual molecular geometry must be inferred from structure and electron-domain arrangement, not from the flat Lewis drawing; molecular shape determines polarity and thus intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use VSEPR or equivalent geometry reasoning to determine the true 3D shape, then decide whether the molecule is polar and what intermolecular force is strongest.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "if it was linear for example, then you couldn't because it pulls equally in both directions, so no dipole"
misconceptions.prevalence: mentioned for Ellie
misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

misconceptions.target_misconception: The explicit lone pairs shown in a Lewis structure are the key features for determining intermolecular force strength and location, so forces are treated as if they depend on structural placeholders rather than molecule-to-molecule electrostatics.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular force location should be based on electrostatic attraction between partial charges on different molecules; explicit lone pairs are not the force itself.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should translate the structural information into polarity and partial charges, then identify where opposite charges on separate molecules attract.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the explicit lone pairs on the Lewis Dot structure as indicators of available interaction sites."
misconceptions.prevalence: 5 students
misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

misconceptions.subtopic: color interpretation in electrostatic potential maps
misconceptions.target_misconception: The colors on an electrostatic potential map indicate force strength or magnitude of intermolecular attraction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The colors on an electrostatic potential map represent relative electron density/partial charge, not intermolecular force strength itself.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should interpret the color key as electron-density information, identify partial positive and partial negative regions, and then reason about which molecules will attract each other.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "several participants carrying intramolecular force conceptions viewed the colors on the EPM as a measure of force strength/magnitude."
misconceptions.prevalence: several participants
misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

misconceptions.target_misconception: Symmetrical nonpolar molecules should lack areas of high and low electron density on an EPM because opposing dipoles cancel out.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Even symmetric molecules can show regions of different electron density on an EPM because the map displays local electron distribution; cancellation of the net dipole does not mean the map is uniform.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between overall molecular polarity and local electron-density variation, recognizing that a nonpolar molecule can still have electron-density gradients across bonds and atoms.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "several participants seemed to hold the conception that the EPM of symmetrical molecules would be devoid of areas of high and low electron density because of the opposite but equal dipole moments."
misconceptions.prevalence: several participants
misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

misconceptions.target_misconception: London dispersion forces result from random electron movement being directly visible as changing electron density on the map, so a static EPM can misrepresent dispersion as non-random or non-physical.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces arise from temporary fluctuations in electron distribution; an EPM is a static representation of electron density, not a movie of electron motion.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should understand that an EPM shows a snapshot of electron density and that dispersion forces are described by temporary induced dipoles and fluctuating electron motion, not fixed map colors alone.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the EPM presentation of electron density as a static characteristic which dissuaded students from a conception of London dispersion forces that result from random electron movement."
misconceptions.prevalence: several participants
misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

misconceptions.target_misconception: More electron density, more bonds, or a more 'balanced' electron-density pattern means a molecule is stronger and therefore has stronger intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular force type and strength depend on the nature of intermolecular electrostatic interactions between molecules, not on how hard it seems to pull a molecule apart or on the number of bonds within it.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the types of intermolecular attractions possible between two molecules and use polarity/partial charges, not internal bonding or perceived molecular stability, to judge the strongest intermolecular force.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "CCl4 has overall higher electron density, which I'm pretty sure means that it's harder to pull the atoms apart from each other in the molecule, which would mean that it's stronger."
misconceptions.prevalence: Ivy; part of intramolecular-force-conception group of 5
misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
