misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a hydrogen atom in water can form more than one covalent bond, or that oxygen can make double bonds to hydrogen to complete an octet like carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In water, each hydrogen forms only one covalent bond, and the water molecule has a bent structure with two O-H covalent bonds and two lone pairs on oxygen.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should apply valence and bonding rules: hydrogen can only have one bond, oxygen typically forms two covalent bonds in water, and lone pairs on oxygen influence molecular shape but do not create extra covalent bonds to hydrogen.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the oxygen atom formed double bonds with hydrogen atoms to complete an octet"
misconceptions.prevalence: part of 3/10 category A diagrams
misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students are unsure how lone pairs participate and may think lone pairs on oxygen collectively form one negatively charged region that attracts neighboring molecules without a clear directional lone-pair-to-hydrogen interaction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Each lone pair on oxygen can serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor site, and hydrogen bonds are directional interactions between a specific hydrogen atom and a specific lone pair on a neighboring molecule.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify individual lone pairs as distinct electron-rich sites on oxygen and match them with hydrogen atoms on adjacent molecules, showing a directional interaction rather than a diffuse attraction from an undifferentiated negative region.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the role of lone pairs of electrons in forming a hydrogen bond is unclear. The lone pairs form an electron dense region around the oxygen atom to form one or numerous hydrogen bonds"
misconceptions.prevalence: 20/60 diagrams
misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the two lone pairs on oxygen collectively form a single partially negative region that attracts multiple neighbors without directionality.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The lone pairs are separate electron domains on oxygen and hydrogen bonding involves specific donor-acceptor directions between particular sites on adjacent molecules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should represent each lone pair as a distinct accepting site and show how each site participates in a limited number of directional hydrogen bonds according to molecular geometry.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the two lone pairs of electrons collectively formed a single partially negative ( δ - ) region"
misconceptions.prevalence: about half of category B diagrams; 8/20 category B diagrams
misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a hydrogen atom in water can attract more than one neighboring oxygen, allowing one hydrogen to make multiple hydrogen bonds.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Each hydrogen atom can donate only one hydrogen bond because it has only one covalently bonded hydrogen available as the donor site.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that a single hydrogen participates in one covalent O-H bond and can serve as one hydrogen-bond donor to one acceptor at a time, constrained by water's geometry.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "each hydrogen atom of a central molecule appeared to have enough positive charge to attract more than one oxygen atom from neighbouring water molecules"
misconceptions.prevalence: reported in category B; specific count not given
misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think each individual nonbonding electron on oxygen can independently form a hydrogen bond, as if each electron is a separate bonding site.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding involves the lone pair as the acceptor site on oxygen; it is not each electron individually that forms a bond.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason in terms of lone pairs/electron domains and molecular geometry, not individual electrons; the oxygen atom offers acceptor lone-pair sites for hydrogen bonding.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "each of the four nonbonding electrons on the oxygen atom in a water molecule can individually form a hydrogen bond with a hydrogen atom in a neighbouring water molecule"
misconceptions.prevalence: 8/20 category B diagrams
misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonds are nondirectional attractions between broad positive and negative regions and can be represented in a flat 2D plane.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonds are directional intermolecular interactions between specific hydrogen atoms and lone pairs on neighboring molecules, and real water networks in snowflakes are three-dimensional.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should place molecules according to water's tetrahedral electron-domain geometry and show specific H-to-lone-pair interactions in 3D rather than a flat, undirected arrangement.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "hydrogen bonds were not covalent in nature – they are electrostatic interactions between molecules but the role of lone pairs of electrons in forming a hydrogen bond is unclear"
misconceptions.prevalence: 25/60 diagrams for 2D space; 5/60 for 3D space
misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think water molecules in snowflakes interact only in a flat plane rather than in three dimensions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In snowflakes, water molecules form a 3D tetrahedral hydrogen-bond network with four hydrogen bonds per water molecule.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should infer from water's molecular geometry that hydrogen bonding extends in three dimensions, with two donor and two acceptor sites arranged tetrahedrally.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the interactions among water molecules were represented in 2D space"
misconceptions.prevalence: 25/60 diagrams
misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a water molecule can form only two hydrogen bonds because only the lone pairs on oxygen participate, or otherwise fail to recognize the four-bond maximum in snowflakes.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Each water molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds: two as donor through its hydrogens and two as acceptor through its lone pairs.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should count both donor and acceptor sites on water and use the tetrahedral arrangement to explain why the maximum number is four.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "one water molecule in a snowflake could form a maximum of two hydrogen bonds with neighbouring molecules in 2D"
misconceptions.prevalence: present in some category C diagrams; specific count not given
misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a water molecule can form more than four hydrogen bonds because molecules can approach too closely in a 2D representation.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A water molecule has only four hydrogen-bonding sites in total, so it cannot exceed four hydrogen bonds in the snowflake network.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the two hydrogens and two lone pairs as the limit on hydrogen-bond formation and recognize that geometry prevents more than four total hydrogen bonds per molecule.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "water molecules could approach each other so closely that a hydrogen atom in one water molecule could form more than one hydrogen bond and a water molecule could form more than four hydrogen bonds with neighbouring molecules"
misconceptions.prevalence: in one category C example (Albert); not quantified for all students
misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think two oxygen atoms from different molecules can share a common hydrogen atom as part of hydrogen bonding.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A hydrogen bond is not a shared covalent hydrogen between two oxygens; it is an attraction between a hydrogen bonded to one oxygen and a lone pair on another oxygen.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish covalent O-H bonds within a molecule from hydrogen-bond attractions between molecules and avoid depicting a hydrogen atom as being jointly shared by two oxygens.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "two oxygen atoms of different molecules sharing a common hydrogen atom between them"
misconceptions.prevalence: listed among alternative conceptions in the conclusion; specific count not given
misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

papers.paper_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think dipole-dipole interactions occur within a single molecule rather than between two molecules.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interactions are intermolecular forces that occur between separate molecules, not within one molecule.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the partial positive region of one polar molecule and the partial negative region of another polar molecule, then connect the interacting atoms across the two molecules.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “a large portion of the students believed that intermolecular forces were within a single molecule rather than between”
misconceptions.prevalence: a large portion of the students (no exact count given)
misconceptions.population: students in a study of intermolecular forces cited in the paper
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat lone pairs as bonding sites that should be shared or filled by forming a new bond between molecules.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lone pairs are nonbonding electron pairs; they do not become shared covalent bonds in a dipole-dipole interaction task.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use lone pairs to infer molecular polarity or geometry when appropriate, but should still locate dipole-dipole attraction between partial charges on separate molecules, not create a new covalent bond.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “participants carried a conception that these interactions could be thought of in a similar fashion to covalent bonding.”
misconceptions.population: participants in this study
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think lone pairs are ‘available’ or ‘free to bond’ with other atoms, so they identify the lone pair itself as the interaction site.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lone pairs are electron pairs on an atom; they can influence polarity and geometry, but the intermolecular attraction is between molecular dipoles, not a lone pair bonding with another atom.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that lone pairs contribute to electron density and molecular shape, then use the resulting dipole orientation to determine where the attraction between molecules occurs.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the lone pairs represent sites that are free to bond with other atoms”
misconceptions.prevalence: 5 students in Version 1 (Sawyer, Sasha, Sadie, Sabrina, Sebastian)
misconceptions.population: Version 1 students working with the Lewis dot representation
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a molecule has an ‘open spot’ or incomplete octet that must be filled, and use that as the dipole-dipole interaction site.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interactions are not determined by filling an octet; they depend on the alignment of partial charges in polar molecules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate electronegativity and molecular geometry to locate partial positive and negative ends, rather than searching for empty bonding sites.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students considered the space around each atom as the location where dipole-dipole interactions could occur”
misconceptions.prevalence: observed in Version 1 and discussed as recurring across participants; exact count not given
misconceptions.population: students in Version 1 and in the discussion of the study overall
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assume molecular geometry is explicit in Lewis dot structures and can be read directly without considering lone pairs.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lewis dot structures do not explicitly show 3D geometry; geometry must be inferred from electron domains and lone pairs.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should count bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central atom to infer shape, then use that shape to determine polarity and the dipole-dipole interaction site.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “three students carried the assumption that molecular geometry was explicit in Lewis dot structures”
misconceptions.prevalence: 3 students in Version 2 (Regan, Rachel, Rebecca)
misconceptions.population: Version 2 students working with the Lewis dot representation
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think selenium dioxide is linear and nonpolar when lone pairs are ignored.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SeO2 has lone pairs on selenium that create a bent molecular geometry, making the molecule polar.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should include selenium’s lone pairs in the electron-domain arrangement, infer a bent shape, and then recognize that the dipoles do not cancel.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “designated the molecule as linear and non-polar, without taking into account the influence of lone pairs”
misconceptions.prevalence: 3 students in Version 2 initially (Regan, Rachel, Rebecca)
misconceptions.population: Version 2 students in the Lewis dot structure task for selenium dioxide
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think bigger atoms produce stronger dipole-dipole interactions, or that size itself determines the interaction site.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atom size in these models is not the basis for dipole-dipole attraction; the interaction depends on molecular polarity and partial charges.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use electronegativity and molecular geometry to determine the dipole direction, and treat size as a representational feature not directly tied to interaction strength.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “The bigger the two atoms that are bonding are, the weaker the forces are.”
misconceptions.prevalence: 3 students in Version 1 (Sandeep, Sebastian, Spencer) used size in the ball-and-stick task; Sandeep remained consistent with size in space-filling
misconceptions.population: Version 1 students working with ball-and-stick and space-filling representations
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the number of bonds indicates the strength of dipole-dipole interactions or that more bonds mean a stronger intermolecular force.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond order describes intramolecular bonding; dipole-dipole strength is determined by molecular polarity and the arrangement of partial charges between molecules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate intramolecular bond order from intermolecular force strength, then compare electronegativity differences and geometry to locate the dipole-dipole interaction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the number of bonds signifies the strength of dipole-dipole interactions in the molecule”
misconceptions.prevalence: observed in Version 2 ball-and-stick task; exact count not given
misconceptions.population: Version 2 students in the ball-and-stick representation
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assign ionic or valence charges to atoms and use opposite charges as the basis for dipole-dipole attraction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interactions arise from partial charges in polar covalent molecules, not from assigning full ionic charges to atoms.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should infer partial positive and partial negative regions from electronegativity and molecular geometry, rather than treating atoms as ions with fixed charges.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students began assigning charges to each of the atoms in the molecules”
misconceptions.prevalence: 4 students in Version 2 (Ria, Rachel, Rebecca, Richard)
misconceptions.population: Version 2 students working with the space-filling representation
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think dipole-dipole interaction could cause atoms to rearrange into new products, as if the molecules were undergoing a reaction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interaction is an intermolecular attraction in the present molecules; it does not imply atom rearrangement or product formation.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should locate the most positive and negative ends of the two molecules and draw an attraction between them without changing the molecules’ connectivity.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “I guess you could rearrange the atoms so that it would make each-- HCl would be a product.”
misconceptions.population: Richard in Version 2
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a central atom cannot participate in dipole-dipole interactions because it is central or less accessible.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The central atom can still contribute to molecular polarity and can be part of the dipole orientation; being central does not prevent intermolecular attraction.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate the full molecular dipole from electronegativity and geometry, including the central atom’s role in bond polarity.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “chlorine is the central… and I don't really know how it's going to connect to the hydrogen”
misconceptions.prevalence: observed in Version 2 chemical formula task; exact count not given
misconceptions.population: Rachel and also Ranger/Richard with central carbon in Version 2
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think any bent geometry automatically means a molecule has dipole moments or that geometry alone determines polarity.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bent geometry can contribute to polarity, but polarity must be evaluated by considering bond polarity and whether dipoles cancel.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify molecular shape from lone pairs and then determine whether the vector sum of bond dipoles is nonzero.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “molecules with bent geometry always have dipole moments”
misconceptions.prevalence: 1 student explicitly: Roger in Version 2
misconceptions.population: Version 2 ball-and-stick task
misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

papers.paper_title: Development and Assessment of a Molecular Structure and Properties Learning Progression

misconceptions.target_misconception: Atoms form bonds because they "want" an octet.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms form bonds because the bonded system is more stable than the unbonded system, i.e. bonding lowers the system's energy.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that bonding occurs when atom-atom interactions decrease potential energy and produce a more stable arrangement; the octet rule is a guideline for drawing Lewis structures, not the causal explanation for bond formation.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: One common misconception that students hold is that atoms form bonds because they "want" an octet, rather than because bonded atoms are more stable than unbonded ones.
misconceptions.population: students
misconceptions.source_title: Development and Assessment of a Molecular Structure and Properties Learning Progression

misconceptions.target_misconception: Lewis structures are the same as the actual three-dimensional molecular structure, rather than simplified representations of it.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lewis structures are two-dimensional representations ("cartoons") that encode information about underlying three-dimensional molecular structure.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should understand that a Lewis structure is a symbolic, simplified model; they should translate between 2D drawings and 3D geometry rather than treating the drawing as the molecule itself.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: we stress the fact that Lewis structures are merely a convenient way to represent something more complex.
misconceptions.population: students
misconceptions.source_title: Development and Assessment of a Molecular Structure and Properties Learning Progression

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students can read only explicit structural information from Lewis structures and do not recognize that they also encode information needed to infer physical and chemical properties.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lewis structures can be used, together with molecular shape, electronegativity, and intermolecular forces, to infer properties such as boiling point, melting point, acidity/basicity, and reactivity.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the structural features in the Lewis structure, infer 3D shape and bond polarity, determine intermolecular forces, and then use those forces to predict macroscopic properties.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: the information that can be determined from a Lewis structure
misconceptions.prevalence: End of Fall: physical properties 13% control vs 38% treatment; reactivity 13% control vs 40% treatment; acidity/basicity 14% control vs 19% treatment. End of Spring: physical properties 27% control vs 54% treatment; reactivity 37% control vs 63% treatment; acidity/basicity 38% control vs 70% treatment.
misconceptions.population: general chemistry students in control and CLUE treatment cohorts
misconceptions.source_title: Development and Assessment of a Molecular Structure and Properties Learning Progression

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat boiling point and melting point as isolated facts to rank, but do not generalize to the broader category of physical properties.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: From molecular structure, students should infer broader physical properties, not only specific ranking tasks such as boiling point or melting point.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should move from structure to intermolecular forces and then to a wider class of physical properties, recognizing that boiling/melting point are examples rather than the whole category.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: some students from the control group chose melting and boiling points, but not physical properties.
misconceptions.prevalence: End of Fall: relative boiling points 20% control vs 56% treatment; relative melting points 18% control vs 50% treatment; physical properties 13% control vs 38% treatment. End of Spring: relative boiling points 46% control vs 54% treatment; relative melting points 38% control vs 48% treatment; physical properties 27% control vs 54% treatment.
misconceptions.population: general chemistry students in control and CLUE treatment cohorts
misconceptions.source_title: Development and Assessment of a Molecular Structure and Properties Learning Progression

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not recognize that a molecular structure can indicate acidic or basic behavior.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Functional groups and local structure can signal whether a substance may have acidic and/or basic properties.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should inspect the structure for proton-donating or proton-accepting sites and reason from those functional groups to acidity/basicity.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: CLUE students appear to have a better understanding of the uses of and information that is encoded into a Lewis structure.
misconceptions.prevalence: End of Fall: 14% control vs 19% treatment. End of Spring: 38% control vs 70% treatment; alanine prediction: 51% CLUE vs 23% control recognized acidic/basic properties.
misconceptions.population: general chemistry students in control and CLUE treatment cohorts
misconceptions.source_title: Development and Assessment of a Molecular Structure and Properties Learning Progression

papers.paper_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

misconceptions.topic: Dissolution of ionic and molecular compounds
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat gaseous HCl as an ionic compound made of H+ and Cl− ions, or think it breaks apart into ions like NaCl when dissolved in water.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: HCl(g) is a molecular compound; it first dissolves as HCl(aq), and only then reacts with water to form hydronium and chloride ions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish a molecular gas from an ionic solid: HCl has covalent bonding in the gas phase, so dissolution should be represented as HCl(g) -> HCl(aq), followed by the acid reaction with water if describing the aqueous acid equilibrium.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the most common representations displayed HCl gas as an ionic compound that breaks up into H+ and Cl- ions”
misconceptions.prevalence: Teachers: 54% used HCl(g) -> H+(aq) + Cl−(aq); 46% used HCl(g) + H2O(l) -> H3O+(aq) + Cl−(aq). Students: 2/13 wrote HCl dissociating into ions initially; 3/13 drew ions forming.
misconceptions.population: High school chemistry teachers (N=13) and first-semester general chemistry students (N=13)
misconceptions.source_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

misconceptions.topic: Dissolution of ionic and molecular compounds
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the dissolution of HCl is simply HCl -> H+ + Cl−, with no separate solvation step, as if HCl were an ionic solute.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The correct process is first solvation/dissolution of the molecular gas into aqueous HCl, then acid ionization in water; the molecular compound itself is not initially ionic.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that a molecular solute can dissolve without immediately producing ions; the equation should show HCl(g) -> HCl(aq) when the focus is dissolution, and only then show reaction with water if focusing on acid behavior.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the more pressing issue was the ‘simplification’ of the dissolution, resulting in H+ and Cl- ions, effectively portraying HCl as an ionic compound.”
misconceptions.prevalence: 13/13 teachers discussed this issue; among students, 6/13 continued to describe or depict HCl as ionic despite instruction.
misconceptions.population: High school chemistry teachers and first-semester general chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

misconceptions.topic: Dissolution of ionic and molecular compounds
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students conflate dissolution and acid reaction, writing HCl(g) + H2O(l) -> H3O+(aq) + Cl−(aq) as if the dissolution and ionization happen as a single step.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dissolution of HCl gas and its acid reaction with water are distinct processes; the molecular gas first becomes HCl(aq), then can react with water to form ions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate the physical process of dissolving from the chemical reaction in water, and should not collapse both into one equation unless explicitly modeling the acid-base equilibrium in solution.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “reacting gaseous HCl as an acid without representing the solvation of HCl in addition to the acid-base reaction that occurs in solution”
misconceptions.prevalence: 5/13 teachers and 3/13 students initially used a direct reaction with water for HCl(g)
misconceptions.population: High school chemistry teachers and first-semester general chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

misconceptions.topic: Dissolution of ionic and molecular compounds
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe pure HCl(g) is already composed of H+ and F−/Cl− ions, or otherwise has ionic composition before dissolving.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Pure gaseous HCl is a molecular substance with covalent bonding, not an ionic assembly of ions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the state and bonding information: a gas-phase molecular compound consists of molecules held together by covalent bonds, not pre-existing ions.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “more than a third of students answered that pure gaseous HF is in some way composed of H+ and F- ions despite being explicitly told in the prompt that HF is a molecular compound.”
misconceptions.prevalence: HF question on summative assessment: 22% selected ‘is made up of H+ and F− ions’; 15% selected both that and ‘is held together by a sigma bond’; total >33% endorsed ionic composition.
misconceptions.population: First-semester general chemistry students (N=686)
misconceptions.source_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

misconceptions.topic: Dissolution of ionic and molecular compounds
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think NaCl remains intact in water and should be written as NaCl(aq).
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: NaCl is an ionic compound that dissociates into hydrated Na+(aq) and Cl−(aq) ions in water.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that ionic lattices separate into ions upon dissolution, and the aqueous notation should represent separated hydrated ions rather than intact NaCl molecules.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students relied on inaccurate alternative conceptions of ionic compounds remaining intact upon dissolving—i.e., NaCl(aq).”
misconceptions.prevalence: 4 students represented NaCl remaining intact in solution; 30% of students relied on NaCl(aq).
misconceptions.population: First-semester general chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

misconceptions.topic: Dissolution of ionic and molecular compounds
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students interpret HCl as a strong acid that simply ‘splits’ or ‘breaks apart’ into H+ and Cl− because the bond breaks when it dissolves.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Acid behavior in solution must be distinguished from the molecular nature of HCl(g); dissolution and ion formation are not the same as an ionic compound simply breaking apart.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first identify that HCl is molecular, then distinguish dissolution into water from acid ionization; strong acid behavior does not mean the pure gas is ionic.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “Yes, it's a strong acid, so it will split, the bond will break, and it will go into H plus ions, and Cl minus.”
misconceptions.prevalence: Quoted student response; 6/13 students overall still described/drew HCl as ionic after instruction.
misconceptions.population: First-semester general chemistry student
misconceptions.source_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

misconceptions.topic: Dissolution of ionic and molecular compounds
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that once HCl is described as molecular, nothing further happens in solution; they stop at HCl(aq) and deny subsequent acidic reaction with water.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: HCl(aq) can further react with water to produce H3O+(aq) and Cl−(aq); being molecular does not mean it remains unchanged in aqueous solution.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that molecular identity and acidic behavior are compatible: after dissolution, an acid can ionize in water, so the process is not complete at HCl(aq).
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “they completely disregarded its acidic nature once dissolved”
misconceptions.prevalence: Several students who wrote HCl(g) -> HCl(aq) paused; 5 students (N, U, V, X, Z) believed the process was complete, and 1 student (X) said nothing else would occur.
misconceptions.population: First-semester general chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

misconceptions.topic: Intermolecular forces in molecular hydrogen chloride
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students classify pure HCl(g) as having ion-ion interactions, implying it is made of ions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Pure gaseous HCl has London dispersion forces and dipole-dipole interactions; it is molecular, not ionic.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the compound type from bonding and state of matter, then assign intermolecular forces appropriate to polar molecules rather than ion-ion attractions.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the most common mistake was selecting ‘ion-ion’ interactions in their responses, which accounted for 27% of students describing HCl(g) as an ionic compound composed of ions.”
misconceptions.prevalence: 27% on second-semester general chemistry assessment (N=675)
misconceptions.population: Second-semester general chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

papers.paper_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

misconceptions.subtopic: Type of atoms forming covalent bonds
misconceptions.target_misconception: Covalent bonding is formed between a metal and a nonmetal atom.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Covalent bonding is typically formed between nonmetal atoms that share electrons.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the element types and compare their tendency to share rather than transfer electrons; two nonmetals form covalent bonds by sharing valence electrons, whereas metal–nonmetal pairs usually form ionic bonds by electron transfer.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "covalent bonding is formed between a metal and a nonmetal atom"
misconceptions.prevalence: Held by multiple students; Appendix-2 lists S4 and S5, and the discussion says a "great deal of students" had this misconception.
misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58); also 10 interviewed students
misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

misconceptions.subtopic: Type of atoms forming covalent bonds
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think covalent bonding is formed only when atoms 'want' or 'need' to gain electrons to achieve noble-gas configuration, as if atoms have human-like intentions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms do not 'want' anything; bonding depends on electronic structure, electronegativity, and energetic stability, not intentional desire.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain bonding in terms of valence electrons, electronegativity, and attraction between nuclei and shared electron pairs rather than anthropomorphic 'wants' or 'needs'.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "They form covalent bonding, because they want to gain electrons to resemble stable noble gases configuration."
misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in interview responses (e.g., S1); Appendix-2 notes this idea for S1 and S9.
misconceptions.population: Interviewed 11th grade students
misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

misconceptions.subtopic: Type of atoms forming covalent bonds
misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen is treated as a metal atom, so students classify H-containing covalent compounds as if they involved metal–nonmetal bonding.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen is not a metal in this context; whether a bond is covalent depends on the bonding partners and electron sharing/transfer, not on misclassifying hydrogen as a metal.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize hydrogen’s role in bonding and use periodic-table category plus electron behavior correctly; hydrogen in HCl, NH3, and H2O participates in covalent bonding with nonmetals by sharing electrons.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Because hydrogen is a metal atom and oxygen is a nonmetal atom, they bond to each other by the electron transfer"
misconceptions.prevalence: Reported for H2O in Appendix-1; also linked to HCl and NH3 misconceptions in Appendix-2.
misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58)
misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

misconceptions.target_misconception: Covalent bonds are formed by electron transfer rather than electron sharing.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Covalent bonds are formed when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons; electron transfer is characteristic of ionic bonding.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should describe covalent bond formation as mutual sharing of valence electrons and identify electron transfer as producing ions and ionic bonds, not covalent bonds.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "covalent bonding is formed by the electron transfer within hydrogen chloride and ammonia"
misconceptions.prevalence: Documented across several items and interviews; Appendix-1 and discussion indicate this was common.
misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58); also interviewed students
misconceptions.concept_category: bond formation / electron transfer vs sharing
misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

misconceptions.subtopic: Formation of covalent bonds in water
misconceptions.target_misconception: Water contains ionic bonding because hydrogen is a metal and oxygen is a nonmetal, so electrons are transferred between them.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Within H2O, the O–H bonds are covalent; oxygen and hydrogen share electrons, with oxygen attracting the bonding electrons more strongly.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify H2O as a covalent molecule and reason from electron sharing and electronegativity, not from metal/nonmetal transfer logic.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Ionic bonding is formed between oxygen and hydrogen atom within a water molecule, because hydrogen is a metal and oxygen is a nonmetal atom. They bond with each other by the electron transfer."
misconceptions.prevalence: Shown in item 3 and Appendix-1 (7% for this specific version; also 9% for ionic bonding in water).
misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58)
misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

misconceptions.subtopic: Formation of covalent bonds in water
misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonding is the bond within a water molecule, instead of covalent bonding.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The bonds within a water molecule are covalent O–H bonds; hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction between molecules, not the intramolecular bond in H2O.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular covalent bonds from intermolecular hydrogen bonds and apply the term hydrogen bonding only to attractions between molecules.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonding is formed between oxygen and hydrogen atoms in a water molecule."
misconceptions.prevalence: Item 3 and Appendix-1 report this misconception (5%); Appendix-2 lists it for interview student S9.
misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58)
misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

misconceptions.target_misconception: Polar and nonpolar covalent bonds are reversed: identical atoms are said to form polar covalent bonds and different atoms nonpolar covalent bonds.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Identical atoms generally form nonpolar covalent bonds, while different atoms with different electronegativities generally form polar covalent bonds.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use electronegativity difference to determine bond polarity and keep the definitions of polar and nonpolar bonds consistent with electron distribution.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Nonpolar covalent bonding is formed between different nonmetal atoms, while polar covalent bonding is formed between identical nonmetal atoms."
misconceptions.prevalence: Appeared in item 2 and interview 3; Appendix-1 lists several variants, e.g. 12% polar in H2 and 14% nonpolar in H2S.
misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58); also interviewed students
misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

misconceptions.target_misconception: Bond polarity is the same as molecule polarity; students use 'polar/nonpolar molecule' instead of 'polar/nonpolar bond'.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond polarity refers to unequal or equal sharing of bonding electrons in a bond; molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and molecular shape.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish the polarity of a bond from the overall polarity of a molecule and reason from electronegativity and geometry separately.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students confused 'polar and nonpolar molecule' with 'polar and nonpolar covalent bonding'"
misconceptions.prevalence: Documented in the discussion and Appendix-1 note (5).
misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58)
misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

misconceptions.target_misconception: Bonding electrons are equally distant from both atoms in all covalent molecules, regardless of electronegativity differences.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In polar covalent bonds, bonding electrons are drawn closer to the more electronegative atom; only in nonpolar bonds are electrons shared equally.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the electronegativities of the bonded atoms and place the electron pair closer to the atom that attracts electrons more strongly.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Bonding electrons place equidistantly to the bonded atoms in all covalent molecules"
misconceptions.prevalence: Appendix-1 reports 7%.
misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58)
misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

misconceptions.subtopic: Type of covalent bonding and bond formation
misconceptions.target_misconception: There is no distinction among covalent bonds; all covalent bonds are the same and are based on electron transfer.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Covalent bonds can differ, for example as polar and nonpolar covalent bonds, and they are formed by electron sharing, not transfer.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize bond types based on electronegativity differences and electron sharing patterns, not collapse all covalent bonds into one category or into ionic-like transfer.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "No, all covalent bonds are the same. Covalent bonding is formed between atoms by sharing of single electrons."
misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in interview question 3 for students S4 and S5.
misconceptions.population: Interviewed 11th grade students
misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

misconceptions.target_misconception: Van der Waals forces, dipole-dipole forces, and hydrogen bonding are types of covalent bonding.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Van der Waals forces, dipole-dipole interactions, and hydrogen bonding are intermolecular forces, not types of covalent bonds.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate intramolecular covalent bonding from intermolecular forces and classify each interaction according to whether it holds atoms within a molecule or molecules together.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Van der Waals, dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonding are the types of covalent bonding"
misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in interview student S9.
misconceptions.population: Interviewed 11th grade students
misconceptions.concept_category: intermolecular forces vs covalent bond types
misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

misconceptions.target_misconception: Graphite conducts electricity because it contains free carbon atoms that are not bonded to anything and can move through the structure.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Graphite conducts electricity because it has delocalized electrons that are free to move through its layers; carbon atoms are still covalently bonded in a network.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain conductivity in terms of mobile delocalized electrons in graphite’s structure, not free carbon atoms.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "there is a free carbon atom which was not bonded to any carbon atom. These free carbon atoms move through the structure of graphite. Graphite conducts electricity due to these free carbon atoms."
misconceptions.prevalence: Appendix-1 reports 26%.
misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58)
misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

misconceptions.target_misconception: Graphite conducts electricity because its carbon layers can slide over each other.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrical conductivity in graphite is due to delocalized electrons, not the sliding of layers.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the role of delocalized pi electrons and distinguish mechanical layering from electrical conduction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "graphite has the layers of carbon atoms which slide over each other, it conducts electricity due to these layers which could be able to move"
misconceptions.prevalence: Appendix-1 reports 17%.
misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58)
misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

misconceptions.target_misconception: Diamond is viewed as a 'unitary' structure without layers, contrasted with graphite layers, rather than as a giant covalent network.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Diamond and graphite are both giant covalent structures, but diamond is a 3D tetrahedral network and graphite is layered with delocalized electrons between layers.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should describe each allotrope with the correct extended covalent structure and connect structure to properties like conductivity.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Diamond has a unitary structure. It has no layers."
misconceptions.prevalence: Linked to item 4 responses; no exact percentage provided for this wording.
misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58)
misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

papers.paper_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that when water is heated, the molecules simply move faster without necessarily connecting that speed change to particle-level motion in the boiling process, or they describe motion only in macroscopic terms.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Heating increases the kinetic energy of water molecules, so they move faster at the molecular level.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect added heat to increased molecular kinetic energy and infer that water molecules move faster as temperature rises and during boiling.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "most students understood that as the temperature rises, the particles/molecules move faster"
misconceptions.prevalence: Mentioned as a common pattern; no exact percentage given.
misconceptions.population: 35 high school students in six Scientific Visualization classes
misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

misconceptions.subtopic: Composition of bubbles in boiling water
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the bubbles are not steam, or that bubble composition is something like air, oxygen/hydrogen, or unspecified gas rather than water vapor.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The bubbles in boiling water are steam (water vapor).
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the idea that boiling converts liquid water to gaseous water and infer that the bubbles are water vapor/steam, not air or split elements.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "What are the bubbles made of?"
misconceptions.prevalence: The paper notes that there was no change on this item across groups, but gives no exact misconception count.
misconceptions.population: Students in the 35-student analysis sample; also the full pre/posttest population of 94 originally participated.
misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think water can keep getting hotter while it is boiling, or that temperature continues to rise during boiling.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: At the boiling point, added energy goes into the phase change and the temperature remains constant until boiling is complete.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that once water reaches its boiling point, additional energy is used to overcome intermolecular attractions rather than increase temperature, so temperature plateaus.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "you cannot get hotter than boiling water. Like I thought that there was boiling and then you could still get higher."
misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in student interview responses; no percentage given.
misconceptions.population: Student T3-2 and others in the interview sample
misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students define boiling point only as a specific temperature value or as the moment water is very hot, without relating it to vapor pressure and atmospheric pressure.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid’s vapor pressure equals atmospheric pressure.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect boiling to pressure balance, recognizing that boiling occurs when vapor pressure matches external pressure and that the numerical temperature depends on pressure.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "When water reaches 212°F (100°C) –or just before it does (The temperature only)"
misconceptions.prevalence: Appears in the rubric as a low-level response category; no exact count reported.
misconceptions.population: Students responding to WISE question 6
misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think boiling bubbles rise simply because 'heat rises' or because they contain gas, rather than because of pressure differences between the vapor in the bubble and surrounding water.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Vapor bubbles rise because their internal vapor pressure is lower than the surrounding water pressure; density differences also matter.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from pressure and density: vapor bubbles form, and if internal pressure is less than surrounding pressure the bubbles rise to the surface.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I didn't know that the, um, the bubbles didn't have like as much pressure as the outside area did."
misconceptions.prevalence: Reported as a student misconception in Table 4.10; no percentage given.
misconceptions.population: Student T3-7
misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not distinguish particle spacing across phases, treating proximity as similar in solids, liquids, and gases, or failing to represent gas particles as far apart and liquid particles as close together.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Particles are closer together in liquids than in gases; gas particles have negligible interactions and are far apart.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use a particulate model in which particle arrangement changes with phase: tightly packed in condensed phases and much farther apart in gases.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "This may represent an incomplete knowledge of the actual positioning and configuration of molecules in each phase"
misconceptions.prevalence: Discussed qualitatively; rubric data show Group 1 average PROXIMITY 0.67, Group 2 0.78, Group 3 1.42, but no direct misconception percentage given.
misconceptions.population: 35 students across Groups 1-3
misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students rely on macroscopic images and do not include molecules/particles in their representations, or treat the animation as only a macroscopic boiling scene.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A scientifically accurate animation should include a particulate-level representation of water molecules and their motion during boiling, alongside macroscopic features.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the text to both macro and micro levels, adding molecular representations to show how boiling occurs at the particulate level.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "only 22.9% of students including molecules in their animations"
misconceptions.prevalence: 22.9% included molecules in their animations.
misconceptions.population: 8 of 35 analyzed students
misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

misconceptions.subtopic: Movement of particles in a liquid vs. gas
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think particles in one phase move together or all at the same speed, instead of showing random motion and different speeds across phases.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Particles move randomly, and motion varies with phase; in general gas particles move faster than liquid particles.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that thermal energy increases random molecular motion and that gaseous particles move faster and more randomly than particles in the liquid state.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Shows particles in motion but they are all moving together (coordinated movement)"
misconceptions.prevalence: Appears in the project rubric as a low-level motion category; no direct count reported.
misconceptions.population: Student animations from the 35-student sample
misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe water molecules move at the same speed in the solid, liquid, and gaseous phases.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular speed differs by phase; molecules move fastest in the gaseous phase.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare kinetic energy across phases and infer that heating increases molecular speed and that gas particles move fastest.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Water molecules move at the same speed in the solid, liquid, and gaseous phases."
misconceptions.prevalence: This was a specific incorrect option on the pre/posttest; no percentage reported.
misconceptions.population: Pre/posttest respondents
misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think matter is continuous or that there is matter between atoms/molecules in a substance.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: There is empty space between atoms and molecules, especially in liquids and gases.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that substances are particulate and that the spaces between particles are not filled with matter.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "matter is continuous and there is no vacuum or space between them"
misconceptions.prevalence: Presented as a documented misconception from prior research cited in the paper; not tied to a new count in this study.
misconceptions.population: Prior literature cited in the paper
misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think atoms are large enough to be seen under a microscope, or they confuse atom size with macroscopic objects.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms and molecules are too small to be seen directly with classroom microscopes.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize the nanoscopic scale of atoms and infer that they require indirect models and instruments rather than direct viewing.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "atoms are large enough to be seen under a microscope"
misconceptions.prevalence: Listed as a common misconception in cited literature.
misconceptions.population: Grade-12 students in Griffiths & Preston, as cited by the paper
misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

misconceptions.subtopic: Molecule and atom movement in solids
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think molecules in a solid do not move.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecules in solids do move; they vibrate in place.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should understand that solid particles have kinetic energy even though the solid maintains shape, so the particles vibrate rather than remain motionless.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Molecules in a rock are not moving"
misconceptions.prevalence: This item appears on the pre/posttest as a misconception probe; no percentage reported.
misconceptions.population: Pre/posttest respondents
misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think molecules and atoms are all the same size.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms and molecules differ in size; molecules are composed of atoms and can vary in size.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from molecular structure that different substances have different particle sizes and that molecules are built from atoms.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Molecules and atoms are all the same size"
misconceptions.prevalence: Listed as an assessment item targeting a known misconception.
misconceptions.population: Pre/posttest respondents
misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think molecules in liquids are always further apart than in solids, with no distinction based on phase-specific packing.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecules in liquids are close together but can move past one another; gases are much farther apart.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare phase structures and recognize that liquids remain relatively dense while allowing flow, unlike gases.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Molecules in liquids are always further apart than in solids"
misconceptions.prevalence: Included in the ParNoMA instrument; no study-specific percentage provided.
misconceptions.population: Pre/posttest respondents
misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

misconceptions.subtopic: Matter made of visible objects only
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think only visible things are made of molecules.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: All matter, visible or not, is made of molecules/atoms.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should infer that invisibility to the eye does not mean absence of molecules, because molecules make up all matter.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Only things you can see are made of molecules"
misconceptions.prevalence: Included in the ParNoMA instrument; no study-specific percentage provided.
misconceptions.population: Pre/posttest respondents

misconceptions.subtopic: Composition of matter in a gas
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think something other than empty space exists between molecules in a gas, such as air or atmosphere.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: There is empty space between molecules in a gas.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that gas particles are widely separated and that the space between them is not filled with matter.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "In a pure sample of oxygen gas, what exists between the oxygen molecules?"
misconceptions.prevalence: Included in the pre/posttest; no percentages reported.

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think heat causes molecules to expand or makes molecules bigger.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Heat increases particle motion and, in phase changes, can separate particles; it does not make molecules themselves expand.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate molecular size from thermal motion and understand that heating changes motion and arrangement rather than molecule size.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Heat causes molecules to expand."
misconceptions.prevalence: Included as a wrong option on the pre/posttest.

papers.paper_title: Intermolecular forces: a methodological proposal of teaching based on experimentation

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe chemical bonds and intermolecular forces are the same force.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Chemical bonds are intramolecular forces that hold atoms together within a substance, whereas intermolecular forces are attractions between particles of different molecules or ions and are distinct interactions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish where each force acts: first identify bonding within a molecule or ionic lattice, then identify weaker attractions between separate molecules or particles. Because these act at different structural levels and have different roles, they cannot be treated as synonymous.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: they presented some conceptual errors about intermolecular forces, leaving to understand that for them the chemical bonds and the intermolecular forces were the same force.
misconceptions.population: high school students; 1st year class (22 students) and two 3rd year classes (47 students)
misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular forces: a methodological proposal of teaching based on experimentation

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe intermolecular forces act only in homogeneous mixtures and do not exist in heterogeneous mixtures.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces exist between particles in all पदार्थ/mixtures where particles are present; whether a mixture is homogeneous or heterogeneous depends on miscibility and interactions among components, not on the existence of intermolecular forces itself.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that all substances have intermolecular interactions, but the strength and type of interactions can lead to complete mixing or phase separation. Heterogeneous mixtures still involve intermolecular forces between the species present, even if they are not sufficient to produce one uniform phase.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: the students demonstrated to believe that intermolecular forces act only in homogeneous mixtures, thus not existing intermolecular forces in heterogeneous mixtures.
misconceptions.population: students in the experiment classes
misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular forces: a methodological proposal of teaching based on experimentation

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think only homogeneous mixtures have interactions between components, and heterogeneous mixtures do not.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular interactions occur between components in both homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures; the difference is how completely the components mix or separate into phases.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify that particles of different substances can interact regardless of whether the final mixture looks uniform. The visible phase behavior does not mean interactions are absent; rather, the balance of attractions, polarity, and other properties determines the mixture type.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: only has interactions between compounds that form a homogeneous mixture, and in the heterogeneous mixture, there are no interactions between the components that compose it.
misconceptions.population: students discussed in the paper, as cited from classroom observations and literature context
misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular forces: a methodological proposal of teaching based on experimentation

misconceptions.target_misconception: Some students attributed the density difference as responsible for whether mixtures are homogeneous or heterogeneous.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Miscibility and mixture homogeneity are explained by intermolecular interactions, especially polarity and the relative strength of attractions between components, not simply by density differences.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the polarity and intermolecular attractions of the substances. If attractions between unlike particles are favorable, the substances mix to form a homogeneous mixture; if not, phase separation occurs. Density alone cannot explain why one pair mixes while another with different densities may still be homogeneous.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: Some of them attributed the density difference as responsible for the heterogeneity of the mixtures. But when confronted with other mixtures with liquids of different densities that resulted in a homogeneous mixture, the students could not argue about the possible causes.
misconceptions.population: students in the observed classes
misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular forces: a methodological proposal of teaching based on experimentation

misconceptions.target_misconception: Most students thought surface tension is the factor responsible for the dye floating in milk.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The behavior of the dye in milk is explained by intermolecular interactions and the effect of detergent on the milk's fat and surface properties; surface tension alone is not the complete explanation for the observed phenomenon.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the dye movement to how detergent disrupts interactions in milk, especially between fat and water, changing the local balance of forces and allowing the dye to spread. The explanation should involve particle interactions rather than naming surface tension as the sole cause.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: On the surface tension, most of the students pointed out to be the same, the one responsible for the floating of the dye in the milk.
misconceptions.prevalence: most of the students
misconceptions.population: students in the Psychedelic Milk activity
misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular forces: a methodological proposal of teaching based on experimentation

papers.paper_title: Intermolecular Forces and the Languages of Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think molecular structure and macroscopic properties are not explicitly connected.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular structure is directly connected to observable properties such as boiling point and melting point through intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use the molecular structure to infer the dominant intermolecular forces and then connect those forces to the observed property trend (e.g., stronger intermolecular forces generally correspond to higher boiling or melting points).
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "for many students structure and properties were not explicitly connected"
misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces and the Languages of Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students fail to represent an intermolecular force as an interaction between molecules.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: An intermolecular force is an attraction between separate molecules, not a property of one molecule alone.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify two or more molecules and reason about the attractions between them, rather than treating the force as something within a single molecule.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "only 10−30% of students represented each IMF as an interaction between molecules"
misconceptions.prevalence: only 10–30% of students represented each IMF as an interaction between molecules
misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces and the Languages of Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think boiling involves breaking covalent bonds.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling is a phase change that overcomes intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds within molecules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should recognize that molecules remain intact during boiling; energy is used to separate molecules from each other, not to break the bonds within them.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "boiling involves breaking covalent bonds"
misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces and the Languages of Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think any molecule containing oxygen and hydrogen can form hydrogen bonds.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires a hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom and an appropriate acceptor; not every O/H-containing molecule qualifies in the same way.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should examine the bonding arrangement and molecular structure, not just the presence of O and H atoms, to determine whether hydrogen bonding is possible.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "any molecule with O and H (even CH3OCH3 and CH3COH) can form hydrogen bonds"
misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces and the Languages of Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogenation must decrease molecular weight to explain the large drop in melting point.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogenation changes molecular shape and saturation, which alters packing and intermolecular forces; it does not need to decrease molecular weight to lower melting point.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should compare the structures before and after hydrogenation, note changes in unsaturation and packing, and then relate those structural changes to melting point rather than assuming mass decrease.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "because of the large decrease in melting point, hydrogenation must somehow decrease the molecular weight rather than change the molecular shape"
misconceptions.prevalence: a few students
misconceptions.population: students in the 2023–2024 general chemistry course (n = 63 for language identification; n = 70 for prediction assessments)
misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces and the Languages of Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a double bond directly makes intermolecular forces stronger and therefore requires a higher melting point.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Double bonds, especially cis double bonds, change molecular shape and packing, often lowering melting point by reducing intermolecular attractions between molecules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason that molecular geometry affects how well molecules pack together; poorer packing weakens intermolecular interactions and lowers melting point.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "making the forces stronger which requires a higher melting point"
misconceptions.prevalence: a number of students
misconceptions.population: students in a follow-up 3 weeks after the activity
misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces and the Languages of Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a C=C bond has higher energy than a C–C bond, so more heat is needed to break it during melting.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Melting does not involve breaking covalent C=C or C–C bonds; the change in melting point is due to intermolecular forces and molecular packing, not bond strength within the molecule.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should distinguish covalent bond energies from intermolecular interactions and use structural packing arguments to explain melting point differences.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "a C=C bond has higher energy than a C–C bond, thus requiring more energy (heat) to break down and melt"
misconceptions.prevalence: a number of students
misconceptions.population: students in a follow-up 3 weeks after the activity
misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces and the Languages of Chemistry

papers.paper_title: Problem-Based Learning in 9th Grade Chemistry Class: 'Intermolecular Forces'

misconceptions.subtopic: Relative strength of intermolecular vs intramolecular forces
