misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think intermolecular bonding is as strong as intramolecular bonding.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are much weaker than intramolecular bonds such as covalent or ionic bonds.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between forces holding molecules together and bonds holding atoms together within a molecule. Boiling overcomes intermolecular attractions without breaking covalent bonds, so far less energy is needed for vaporization than for bond breaking.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The alternate conception that intermolecular bonding is as strong as intramolecular bonding was quite prevalent"
misconceptions.prevalence: 26.3% of responses
misconceptions.population: control group students on the post-test (N=38)
misconceptions.source_title: Problem-Based Learning in 9th Grade Chemistry Class: 'Intermolecular Forces'

misconceptions.subtopic: Presence of hydrogen bonds in molecules containing hydrogen
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think there are hydrogen bonds between all molecules that contain hydrogen.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding only occurs when hydrogen is directly bonded to a highly electronegative atom such as N, O, or F and interacts with a lone pair on another electronegative atom.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check the bonding environment of hydrogen, not merely the presence of hydrogen. Hydrogen must be covalently attached to N, O, or F and the acceptor atom must have lone pairs; otherwise hydrogen bonding does not occur.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "There are hydrogen bonds between all molecules which contain hydrogen."
misconceptions.prevalence: 34.2% of responses
misconceptions.population: control group students on the post-test (N=38)
misconceptions.source_title: Problem-Based Learning in 9th Grade Chemistry Class: 'Intermolecular Forces'

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think nonpolar molecules can become polar and therefore all molecules have dipole characteristics / dipole-dipole forces.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Only polar molecules have permanent dipoles and dipole-dipole forces; nonpolar molecules do not become polar just because they are liquid or because London dispersion forces are present.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine polarity from molecular structure and electronegativity differences, then decide whether permanent dipole-dipole interactions are possible. Nonpolar molecules can still have London dispersion forces, but they do not have permanent dipoles.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "nonpolar molecules can become polar, therefore all existing molecules have dipole characteristics"
misconceptions.prevalence: 21.1% of responses
misconceptions.population: control group students on the post-test (N=38)
misconceptions.source_title: Problem-Based Learning in 9th Grade Chemistry Class: 'Intermolecular Forces'

papers.paper_title: Student Discovery of the Relationship between Molecular Structure, Solubility, and Intermolecular Forces

misconceptions.target_misconception: Intermolecular forces are forces within a molecule rather than attractions between molecules.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are attractive forces between separate molecules or particles, not bonds within a molecule.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular bonding from intermolecular attraction: covalent bonds hold atoms together inside a molecule, whereas intermolecular forces act between molecules and influence bulk properties like solubility.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: students maintain their initial misconceptions, such as that intermolecular forces are attractive forces within a molecule.
misconceptions.population: general chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Student Discovery of the Relationship between Molecular Structure, Solubility, and Intermolecular Forces

misconceptions.target_misconception: Any molecule containing hydrogen atoms can hydrogen-bond.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires hydrogen covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom such as N, O, or F, plus a suitable lone-pair acceptor.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check the bonding environment of hydrogen, not just its presence. If hydrogen is bonded to carbon only, the molecule does not serve as a hydrogen-bond donor in the usual chemistry sense.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: intuitive reasoning could cause students to incorrectly guess that all molecules containing hydrogen atoms are capable of hydrogen-bonding.
misconceptions.population: students taking the prelaboratory assessment
misconceptions.source_title: Student Discovery of the Relationship between Molecular Structure, Solubility, and Intermolecular Forces

papers.paper_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think intermolecular forces are located within a single molecule rather than between separate molecules.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces act between molecules, not inside one molecule.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify two or more separate molecules and place the interaction in the space between them, because IMFs arise from attractions between molecules.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "a majority of students draw representations showing that IMFs are located within a single molecule rather than between separate molecules"
misconceptions.prevalence: Cohort 1 drawings: hydrogen bonding 72% (N=68) within; dipole-dipole 61% (N=57) within; LDFs 55% (N=52) within. Cohort 2 drawings: hydrogen bonding 56% (N=90) within; dipole-dipole 58% (N=93) within; LDFs 56% (N=89) within.
misconceptions.population: General chemistry college students; Cohort 1 N=94, Cohort 2 N=160
misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonding is the covalent O-H bond within ethanol, or otherwise a bond inside one molecule.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen attached to O, N, or F in one molecule and a lone pair on O, N, or F in another molecule.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should locate hydrogen bonding between two molecules and recognize that the covalent O-H bond is not the hydrogen bond; the hydrogen donor must be bonded to O, N, or F and attract a heteroatom on a different molecule.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "72% (N = 68) clearly represented hydrogen bonding as an O−H bond within a single molecule of ethanol."
misconceptions.prevalence: 72% (N=68) within; only 15% (N=14) correctly indicated hydrogen bonding occurs between separate molecules
misconceptions.population: Cohort 1 general chemistry students, N=94
misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a hydrogen-bonding representation can show only one molecule or no molecule at all.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: To represent hydrogen bonding, students should draw at least two molecules and show the interaction between them.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should include multiple molecules because hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular interaction; a single isolated molecule cannot show the between-molecule attraction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "54% (N = 51) of students drew only one molecule or none at all (even though they were explicitly asked to draw three molecules)."
misconceptions.prevalence: 54% (N=51) drew only one molecule or none
misconceptions.population: Cohort 1 general chemistry students, N=94
misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think dipole-dipole interactions occur within a single molecule, for example as bonds or interactions among parts of the same ethanol molecule.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interactions are attractions between the partial charges of different polar molecules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify two polar molecules and place the interaction between them, because dipole-dipole is an intermolecular force arising from charge separation across separate molecules.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the majority of students (61%, N = 57) in Cohort 1 drew dipole−dipole interactions as occurring within the ethanol molecule"
misconceptions.prevalence: Cohort 1: 61% (N=57) within; Cohort 2: 58% (N=93) within
misconceptions.population: General chemistry college students; Cohort 1 N=94, Cohort 2 N=160
misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students describe dipole-dipole as a bond rather than an intermolecular interaction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole is an intermolecular attraction, not a covalent bond.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between a covalent bond that holds atoms together within a molecule and an intermolecular attraction that acts between molecules; the term bond should not be used for dipole-dipole.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Dipole−dipole is 'a pretty weak bond between polar molecules.'"
misconceptions.prevalence: Documented in student written responses; no overall percentage given in the paper
misconceptions.population: Cohort 1 general chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think London dispersion forces occur within a single molecule, or as bonds within the molecule.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces are intermolecular attractions between molecules caused by temporary induced dipoles.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify that dispersion forces arise from interactions between separate particles/molecules, not from bonds inside one molecule.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "55% (N = 52) for LDFs"
misconceptions.prevalence: Cohort 1: 55% (N=52) within; Cohort 2: 56% (N=89) within
misconceptions.population: General chemistry college students; Cohort 1 N=94, Cohort 2 N=160
misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think London dispersion forces are simply a property that all substances have, rather than an interaction between particles.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: All molecules can experience London dispersion forces, but LDFs are still intermolecular forces arising from temporary dipoles between molecules or atoms.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should say that dispersion forces exist because of temporary electron fluctuations that create attractions between particles; universality does not mean they are an intrinsic property located within one molecule.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "26% (N=24) of students who explicitly stated in their written responses that LDFs are present for all molecules or always present."
misconceptions.prevalence: 26% (N=24) explicitly said LDFs are present for all molecules or always present
misconceptions.population: Cohort 1 general chemistry students, N=94
misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students use atom and molecule interchangeably when describing IMFs, such as referring to an atom when they mean a molecule or vice versa.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms and molecules are different entities; IMFs usually describe interactions between molecules (or particles), not confusion between the two terms.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should name the correct level of organization: an atom is a single atom, while a molecule is a bonded collection of atoms; the interaction should be described using the appropriate entity.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students often used atom to mean molecule (or vice versa)"
misconceptions.prevalence: Documented qualitatively in student responses; no overall percentage given
misconceptions.population: Cohort 1 general chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students use bond and interaction interchangeably, treating IMFs as bonds in the same sense as covalent bonds.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are attractions or interactions between molecules; covalent bonds are intramolecular bonds within a molecule, except that hydrogen bond is a special term for an IMF.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular covalent bonding from intermolecular attraction and reserve bond language for covalent bonds or clearly identified hydrogen bonds when appropriate.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "some students used the terms bond and interaction interchangeably."
misconceptions.prevalence: Documented qualitatively in student responses; no overall percentage given
misconceptions.population: Cohort 1 general chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

papers.paper_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think intermolecular forces are bonds within molecules rather than attractions between molecules.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are attractions between molecules, not within molecules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular bonding from intermolecular attraction by asking whether the interaction is holding atoms together inside one molecule or attracting separate molecules to each other.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "They are forces, often referred to as 'bonds', between (not within) molecules."
misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat intermolecular forces as comparable in strength to, or not clearly weaker than, ionic and covalent bonds.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are generally much weaker than intramolecular ionic and covalent bonds.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the type of interaction and recognize that IMFs are secondary attractions between molecules, so they are weaker than chemical bonds holding atoms together within a molecule.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "these forces are ... almost always weaker than intramolecular bonds such as ionic and covalent"
misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe hydrogen bonding can only occur between hydrogen and nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, or carbon.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding involves hydrogen bonded to N, O, or F interacting with a lone pair on N, O, or F; carbon is not a hydrogen-bonding partner in the usual definition.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify that H-bond donors are H attached to N/O/F and acceptors are lone pairs on N/O/F, then verify whether both parts of the interaction are present.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "A hydrogen bond is a rather strong bond and - can only occur between hydrogen and nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, or carbon."
misconceptions.population: Student preactivity response
misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a hydrogen bond is simply a weak bond between hydrogen atoms.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction involving hydrogen attached to an electronegative atom and a lone pair on another electronegative atom; it is not a bond between two hydrogen atoms.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check the donor-acceptor requirement for hydrogen bonding and recognize that hydrogen atoms do not hydrogen-bond to each other directly.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Weak bond between hydrogen atoms."
misconceptions.population: Student preactivity response
misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students can memorize textbook definitions of IMFs without understanding how molecules interact in three dimensions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should connect verbal definitions of IMFs to the 3D arrangement and interaction of molecules at the microscopic level.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use molecular geometry and intermolecular contact points to explain attraction rather than only reciting a definition.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students often can provide textbook level definitions but leave general chemistry and enter into organic chemistry without a thorough conceptual understanding of IMFs"
misconceptions.population: College chemistry students discussed in cited literature
misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may be able to give correct definitions from drawings but still lack a 2D-to-3D mental model of intermolecular interactions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should translate among symbolic, 2D, and 3D representations and use 3D structure to reason about intermolecular interactions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should interpret a structural drawing in terms of 3D molecular shape, electron distribution, and possible intermolecular contacts before deciding on IMF type or strength.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "These drawings reveal students' ability to provide definitions, but this does not necessarily translate to a 2D or 3D understanding."
misconceptions.population: Students in CLUE-related assessments cited by the paper
misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

misconceptions.subtopic: Incomplete or incorrect understanding from memorization
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students who memorize the term hydrogen bonding may have an incomplete or incorrect understanding of what it is.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding should be understood as a specific intermolecular attraction with defined structural and electronic requirements.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should move beyond memorized wording and determine whether the molecular structures satisfy the requirements for hydrogen bonding.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "when students solely memorize the terms, they have an incomplete or incorrect understanding of hydrogen bonding"
misconceptions.population: Organic chemistry students cited in prior work
misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

misconceptions.subtopic: Physical properties and molecular level causes
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students fail to connect macroscopic properties such as boiling point to the molecular-level arrangement and interactions causing them.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point and similar properties should be explained by the strength and nature of intermolecular interactions among molecules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should relate a higher or lower boiling point to the energy required to overcome intermolecular attractions and to molecular structure and polarity.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students often fail to connect these concepts to what is occurring on the molecular level in terms of the consequential three-dimensional arrangements of the interacting molecules"
misconceptions.population: College chemistry students discussed in cited literature
misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students misconceive the factors that determine the strength of intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: IMF strength depends on molecular features such as polarity, shape, accessibility of lone pairs, and the type of intermolecular interaction present.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should examine molecular structure, polarity, and geometry to decide which intermolecular attractions are possible and how strong they are likely to be.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students may also misconceive the factors that affect the strength of IMFs"
misconceptions.population: College chemistry students discussed in cited literature
misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

papers.paper_title: Teaching Intermolecular Forces to First-Year Undergraduate Students

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe dispersion (London) forces are negligible compared with hydrogen bonding and dipole-dipole forces.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dispersion forces are significant intermolecular forces and often increase with the number of electrons in a molecule.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should recognize that electron-rich, more polarizable molecules experience stronger dispersion forces, which can strongly affect physical properties such as boiling point.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the widespread misconception that dispersion (London) forces are of negligible strength when compared with hydrogen-bonding and dipole—dipole (Keesom) forces."
misconceptions.population: Introductory chemistry students (implied by the paper's discussion of first-year instruction)
misconceptions.source_title: Teaching Intermolecular Forces to First-Year Undergraduate Students

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that intermolecular forces have a simple, universal, one-to-one correlation with boiling points across all compounds.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point is often correlated with intermolecular-force strength, but there are exceptions and anomalies, so boiling point is only a reasonably good measure rather than an exact universal proxy.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should compare structures, intermolecular interactions, and additional factors such as molecular polarity and surface charge effects before inferring IMF strength from boiling point alone.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it may be assumed that all of these physical properties necessarily have a similar, simple correspondence to IMFs as that which is generally shown by boiling points."
misconceptions.population: First-year undergraduate students
misconceptions.source_title: Teaching Intermolecular Forces to First-Year Undergraduate Students

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe melting point should show the same neat trend with intermolecular forces as boiling point does.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Melting point is influenced by both enthalpy and entropy factors, so it may not correlate simply or consistently with intermolecular-force strength.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason that melting depends on $Delta_{fus}H$ and $Delta_{fus}S$ and that symmetry, crystal packing, and disorder can change melting points independently of IMF strength.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the correlation of IMFs with many physical properties is not necessarily as straightforward as is generally the case with boiling points and vapor pressures."
misconceptions.population: First-year undergraduate students
misconceptions.source_title: Teaching Intermolecular Forces to First-Year Undergraduate Students

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assume viscosity should track intermolecular-force strength in the same straightforward way as boiling point.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Viscosity depends on both intermolecular forces and molecular shape/entanglement, so structural effects can dominate and invert the expected trend.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should consider how molecular shape affects surface contact and entanglement when comparing viscosities, not just the number or type of intermolecular forces present.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "their viscosities show a strong and unexpected trend in the opposite direction."
misconceptions.population: First-year undergraduate students
misconceptions.source_title: Teaching Intermolecular Forces to First-Year Undergraduate Students

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assume surface tension should always increase in the same direction as intermolecular-force strength across a homologous series.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Surface tension can increase or decrease depending on whether enthalpy or entropy effects dominate; it is not guaranteed to follow a simple IMF trend.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should evaluate the balance of enthalpic and entropic contributions to surface tension rather than expecting a universal monotonic relationship with IMF strength.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the surface tension, in defiance of expectations, shows exactly the opposite trend."
misconceptions.population: First-year undergraduate students
misconceptions.source_title: Teaching Intermolecular Forces to First-Year Undergraduate Students

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe intermolecular forces are the sole influence governing physical properties such as melting point, viscosity, or surface tension.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Physical properties are affected by intermolecular forces along with other factors such as molecular symmetry, shape, entropy, crystal structure, and bonding directionality.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify all relevant factors for the property in question and not attribute changes to IMFs alone.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "may mistakenly lead students to believe that IMFs are the sole influence that needs to be considered."
misconceptions.population: Students in introductory chemistry contexts
misconceptions.source_title: Teaching Intermolecular Forces to First-Year Undergraduate Students

papers.paper_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

misconceptions.target_misconception: Surface tension is a force, or force per unit area, rather than energy required to increase unit surface area.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Surface tension is work/energy required to increase the unit surface area (J/m^2).
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the macroscopic phenomenon to the definition of surface tension as energy needed to create more surface; the unit should be interpreted as energy per area, not force.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: Most responses were "force (N)" or "force per unit area  (N/m^2)".
misconceptions.prevalence: 12/16 students gave incorrect unit responses; only 1/16 gave the correct answer.
misconceptions.population: 16 undergraduates majoring in chemistry education in Korea
misconceptions.source_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

misconceptions.target_misconception: Surface tension can be predicted only from intermolecular interaction indicators such as boiling point, hydrogen bonding, or molecular weight; molecular area is not considered as a factor.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Surface tension depends on both intermolecular interaction and molecular area (or number of molecules per unit area).
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from the definition of surface tension as work per unit area and recognize that both the energy contribution from intermolecular interaction and the area occupied by molecules affect the value; therefore, liquids with similar or stronger interactions can still have lower surface tension if molecular area differs.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: Students attempted to predict the degree of surface tension only by intermolecular interaction. No one described it in terms of molecular area or unit area.
misconceptions.prevalence: 16/16 students used only intermolecular interaction in the preconception test for question 2.
misconceptions.population: 16 undergraduates majoring in chemistry education in Korea
misconceptions.source_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

misconceptions.target_misconception: Surface tension acts inward on the liquid surface.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Surface tension acts parallel to the surface.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between fewer interactions at the surface and the actual direction of the tension force/work; the surface molecules are in force equilibrium, and the surface tension direction is parallel to the interface.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: Most students expressed that an inward direction.
misconceptions.prevalence: 12/16 students answered inward; 3/16 outward; 1/16 inward and outward; 0/16 correct.
misconceptions.population: 16 undergraduates majoring in chemistry education in Korea
misconceptions.source_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

misconceptions.subtopic: Explaining the water/ethylene glycol/diethylene glycol/ethanol counterexample
misconceptions.target_misconception: If surface tension data do not match the predicted order based on intermolecular forces, the data are likely invalid due to experimental error.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The measured anomaly should be accepted as valid and explained by a scientifically grounded model that includes both intermolecular interaction and molecular area.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate whether the measurements are trustworthy, then revise the explanation if the data are valid rather than dismissing them; the anomaly should trigger reconsideration of the model, not rejection of the results.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: I think intermolecular forces, that is, the number of hydrogen bonding and the boiling point have a great influence. In the experiment, between diethylene glycol and ethylene glycol, the surface tension of the latter was larger, which was contrary to my expectation. But the difference could be regarded as an experimental error, so my thought has not changed.
misconceptions.prevalence: 1/16 students
misconceptions.population: 16 undergraduates majoring in chemistry education in Korea
misconceptions.source_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

misconceptions.target_misconception: Anomalous surface tension measurements can be accepted as valid, but no explanation is needed or possible.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Valid anomalous data should be explained using a coherent scientific account, ideally integrating intermolecular interaction with molecular area.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the anomaly to test and refine their conception, producing an explanation that links the observed values to molecular structure and unit area rather than stopping at description.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: They believed anomalous data were valid, but there were not any attempts to explain the anomaly.
misconceptions.prevalence: 2/16 students
misconceptions.population: 16 undergraduates majoring in chemistry education in Korea
misconceptions.source_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

misconceptions.target_misconception: Surface tension is influenced more by hydrogen bonding than by dispersion force, without a basis in the definition of surface tension.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Surface tension should be explained from the work/energy per unit area, considering both intermolecular interaction and molecular area, not by an unsupported ranking of interaction types alone.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the strength/type of intermolecular interactions to surface tension through the surface-area definition and explain why those interactions matter in relation to molecular area.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Surface tension is influenced greater by hydrogen bonding than by dispersion force."
misconceptions.prevalence: 2/16 students
misconceptions.population: 16 undergraduates majoring in chemistry education in Korea
misconceptions.concept_category: response to anomalous data / peripheral theory change
misconceptions.source_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

misconceptions.target_misconception: Surface tension is determined by intermolecular interaction plus intermolecular accessibility, where molecular spacing/accessibility is treated as the causal factor instead of molecular area.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Surface tension is explained by intermolecular interaction together with molecular area (number of molecules per unit area), not by a vaguely defined accessibility factor.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should relate any structural factor to the surface-area definition and show how molecular area changes the number of molecules per unit area and thus the energy required to create surface.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: Student S12 thought that the difference in molecular area could affect intermolecular accessibility (the degree to which molecules approach each other), resulting in changes in intermolecular interaction and hence in surface tension.
misconceptions.prevalence: 1/16 students
misconceptions.population: 16 undergraduates majoring in chemistry education in Korea
misconceptions.concept_category: response to anomalous data / peripheral theory change
misconceptions.source_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

misconceptions.target_misconception: Surface tension depends on molecular weight because heavier molecules cannot be pulled apart well during measurement, so gravity affects the measured surface tension directly.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Surface tension is a surface property arising from intermolecular interactions and molecular area; it is not directly explained by molecular weight or gravity in the way described.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should avoid attributing surface tension to gravitational weight of molecules and instead reason about surface energy, intermolecular interactions, and the surface-area term.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The reason why the surface tension of diethylene glycol is lower than that of ethylene glycol is that diethylene glycol is much heavier. Surface tension is a force that pulls molecules from each other, and if molecules are too heavy, it will be difficult to pull them from each other."
misconceptions.prevalence: 1/16 students
misconceptions.population: 16 undergraduates majoring in chemistry education in Korea
misconceptions.concept_category: response to anomalous data / peripheral theory change
misconceptions.source_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

papers.paper_title: Using Computer-Based Visualization Strategies to Improve Students' Understanding of Molecular Polarity and Miscibility

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe a molecule with polar bonds must be polar, even if the molecular geometry is symmetrical.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular polarity depends on the vector sum of bond dipoles; symmetrical molecules can be nonpolar when bond dipoles cancel.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine whether the molecule has polar bonds, then consider the 3D shape and whether the bond dipoles cancel. If the geometry is symmetrical, the molecule can have zero net dipole even with polar bonds.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "symmetrical molecules with polar bonds are non-polar because they have no positive or negative end."
misconceptions.prevalence: Control group scored 0.9/2 vs experimental group 1.6/2 on classifying symmetric molecules with polar bonds as nonpolar.
misconceptions.population: Traditional students majoring in natural sciences in two sections of second-semester introductory chemistry (N=36 control, N=36 experimental).
misconceptions.source_title: Using Computer-Based Visualization Strategies to Improve Students' Understanding of Molecular Polarity and Miscibility

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students explain that oil and water do not mix only by stating that one is polar and the other is nonpolar, treating 'like dissolves like' as a memorized rule rather than an explanation.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oil and water are immiscible because water molecules are more strongly attracted to each other than to nonpolar oil molecules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare intermolecular attractions: water-water attractions are stronger than water-oil attractions, so mixing is unfavorable and the liquids separate.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "More than 80% of the students in the control group responded with the idea that water is polar and oil is nonpolar or that 'like dissolves like' a mere statement of the rule with no real explanation of why it is valid."
misconceptions.prevalence: More than 80% of the control group; just over 30% of the experimental group gave the rule without explanation.
misconceptions.population: Introductory chemistry students in the control and experimental groups.
misconceptions.source_title: Using Computer-Based Visualization Strategies to Improve Students' Understanding of Molecular Polarity and Miscibility

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe there are no attractions between oil and water molecules.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: There are attractions between all molecules; oil and water simply have much weaker cross-attractions than water-water attractions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize intermolecular attractions are universal but differ in strength. Water molecules preferentially attract each other more strongly than they attract nonpolar oil molecules.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "similar numbers of students in each group suggested that there are no attractions between oil and water molecules (18%)"
misconceptions.prevalence: 18% in each group.
misconceptions.population: Students in both control and experimental groups.
misconceptions.source_title: Using Computer-Based Visualization Strategies to Improve Students' Understanding of Molecular Polarity and Miscibility

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe oil and water molecules repel each other.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oil and water do not repel each other; they are immiscible because water-water attractions are stronger than water-oil attractions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish repulsion from weak attraction. Separation occurs because the system lowers energy by keeping stronger like-like interactions rather than because unlike molecules repel.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "similar numbers of students in each group suggested that there are no attractions between oil and water molecules (18%) or that oil and water molecules repel each other (7%)."
misconceptions.prevalence: 7% in each group.
misconceptions.population: Students in both control and experimental groups.
misconceptions.source_title: Using Computer-Based Visualization Strategies to Improve Students' Understanding of Molecular Polarity and Miscibility

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen molecules attract water oxygen atoms, or more generally that all H and O atoms attract each other regardless of charge.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Water molecules attract each other through the H of one water to the O of another water, but hydrogen gas does not provide opposite charges for strong H-O attraction to water.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify partial charges first: attraction occurs between opposite charges. Water has polar O-H bonds and partial charges; H2 is nonpolar and should not be shown attracting water's O atoms in this context.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "This question was designed to determine whether students believed that all H and O atoms are attracted to each other or if they recognized that H and O atoms are attracted to each other only when they have opposite charges."
misconceptions.population: Students responding to the conceptual question on intermolecular attractions in immiscible mixtures.
misconceptions.source_title: Using Computer-Based Visualization Strategies to Improve Students' Understanding of Molecular Polarity and Miscibility

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students omit the attraction between sodium ions and chloride ions when describing an aqueous sodium chloride system, focusing only on ion-water attractions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A complete description includes water-water attractions, Na+ to water oxygen attractions, Cl- to water hydrogen attractions, and Na+ to Cl- attractions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should account for all relevant intermolecular/ion-ion attractions in the system, not only solvation interactions. Both ion-water and ion-ion attractions matter in the aqueous mixture.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "A majority of the responses from students in the control group recognized attractions between the water molecules and the ions in sodium chloride but ignored the attractions of the water molecules to each other and of the sodium ions to the chloride ions"
misconceptions.prevalence: A majority of the control group; experimental students also tended to ignore only the sodium ion-chloride ion attractions.
misconceptions.population: Students in the control group and experimental group answering the aqueous sodium chloride attraction question.
misconceptions.source_title: Using Computer-Based Visualization Strategies to Improve Students' Understanding of Molecular Polarity and Miscibility

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students give incomplete explanations of how soap removes grease, omitting the dual hydrophobic/hydrophilic nature of soap and its role as a molecular bridge.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Soap molecules have both hydrophobic and hydrophilic ends; the hydrophobic end interacts with grease, the hydrophilic end interacts with water, and soap helps emulsify grease so it can be washed away.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain that soap is amphiphilic, orient itself with the hydrophobic tail in grease and hydrophilic head in water, and thereby form micelles/emulsions that allow grease to disperse in water.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Both instructors agreed that a correct response should include four concepts: (i) soap is a special molecule in that it has a hydrophobic end and a hydrophilic end; (ii) soap is attracted to water by its hydrophilic end; (iii) soap is attracted to the grease by its hydrophobic end; and (iv) soap acts as a 'molecular bridge'"
misconceptions.prevalence: Students who viewed the elpot maps gave more complete responses; 61% experimental vs 39% control provided completely correct responses.
misconceptions.population: Students in the control and experimental groups answering the soap/grease question.
misconceptions.source_title: Using Computer-Based Visualization Strategies to Improve Students' Understanding of Molecular Polarity and Miscibility

papers.paper_title: Using Molecular Dynamics Simulation To Reinforce Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonds are fixed bonds rather than dynamic intermolecular interactions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonds are temporary intermolecular interactions that continually form and break as molecules move.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that intermolecular attractions depend on molecular positions and thermal motion, so hydrogen bonding is not permanent; as molecules move, bonds can form and dissociate repeatedly.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: students have a tendency to think of hydrogen bonds as fixed bonds rather than dynamic intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.population: students in the chemistry courses described in the article
misconceptions.source_title: Using Molecular Dynamics Simulation To Reinforce Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces

misconceptions.subtopic: Acid dissociation and molecular dynamics limitations
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think molecular dynamics simulations can model the dissociation of strong acids in water by breaking and forming covalent bonds.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: These simulations do not change covalent bonds; they are suitable for intermolecular interactions, not chemical dissociation reactions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intermolecular forces from intramolecular covalent bonding and reason that a model based on fixed covalent structures cannot represent proton transfer or bond breaking/forming in acid dissociation.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: trying to simulate the dissociation of a strong acid in water will fail, because in that case, intramolecular bonds are being broken and formed.
misconceptions.population: students using molecular dynamics simulations
misconceptions.source_title: Using Molecular Dynamics Simulation To Reinforce Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may expect molecular dynamics simulations to give exact quantitative values, such as the exact boiling point of a substance.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: MDS is better for qualitative or relative predictions, such as comparing boiling points, not exact agreement with experiment.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the simulation to compare relative intermolecular strength and relative boiling behavior, but not infer an exact boiling point from the temperature at which aggregation ceases.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: trying to determine the exact boiling point of a substance by finding the temperature at which the molecules no longer associate with each other would be unwise.
misconceptions.population: students using molecular dynamics simulations
misconceptions.source_title: Using Molecular Dynamics Simulation To Reinforce Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces

misconceptions.subtopic: Periodic boundary conditions and empty space
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think the empty space in a low-density simulation cell is physically unrealistic and therefore invalidates the simulation.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In these simulations, empty space can be treated as a nonpolar environment, and low density can be used to improve efficiency without changing the final outcome.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should understand that the model is designed to represent intermolecular interactions efficiently; the low-density setup is an intentional simplification, not a claim that real condensed phases contain that much empty space.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: While the use of low densities may seem unrealistic, they need not be cause for concern. Empty space in a cell should be viewed as a nonpolar environment.
misconceptions.population: students constructing simulation cells
misconceptions.source_title: Using Molecular Dynamics Simulation To Reinforce Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces

papers.paper_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a state change breaks the covalent bonds within a molecule, so the molecule changes into different substances.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: During a physical change of state, intermolecular forces are overcome but intramolecular covalent bonds remain intact.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between forces between molecules and bonds within molecules, and reason that melting/boiling changes molecular arrangement and spacing, not molecular composition.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "when water changes in state, its chemical bond in the molecule does not be destroyed"
misconceptions.prevalence: Question 2: 12.70% alternative conception; Question 4: 11.11% alternative conception
misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe water changes its composition when ice melts, so liquid water is not the same substance as ice.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ice, liquid water, and water vapor are the same substance; the molecular composition of water remains H2O across state changes.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that state changes alter physical arrangement and intermolecular attractions, while the molecule H2O itself stays the same.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "water will change to hydrogen gas"
misconceptions.prevalence: Question 2: 12.70% alternative conception
misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that when water becomes gas, the oxygen and hydrogen atoms separate and become free atoms or separate gases.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: When water evaporates or boils, water molecules separate from each other, but each molecule remains H2O; atoms do not split apart.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that vaporization changes the spacing and motion of molecules, not the atoms within each molecule.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "oxygen atom and hydrogen atom will separate when it reaches the gas state"
misconceptions.prevalence: Question 3: 46.03% alternative conceptions
misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

misconceptions.subtopic: Formation of hydrogen and oxygen gases
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that phase change produces hydrogen gas and/or oxygen gas from water.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Phase change does not decompose water; it remains H2O unless a chemical reaction occurs.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that boiling or melting is a physical change, so only the arrangement/state changes, not the chemical identity of the substance.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "water will change to hydrogen and oxygen gas when the state changed"
misconceptions.prevalence: Described qualitatively in the discussion; included within Question 3 alternative conceptions (46.03%)
misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think intramolecular covalent bonds are the forces that break during a change of state.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are the attractions relevant to changes of state; intramolecular covalent bonds are not broken in ordinary phase changes.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify that the change of state depends on forces between molecules, so the correct force name is intermolecular force.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the bond between N and H atom is destroyed"
misconceptions.prevalence: Question 4: 11.11% alternative conception
misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe ammonia is an ionic substance rather than a covalent molecular substance.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ammonia (NH3) is a covalent molecular compound; its phase behavior is governed by intermolecular forces such as hydrogen bonding.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify NH3 as molecular/covalent, then reason that phase change involves overcoming intermolecular attractions, not ionic bonding.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it was an ionic substance"
misconceptions.prevalence: Question 4: included in the 11.11% alternative conception responses
misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

misconceptions.subtopic: Covalent bond treated as intermolecular force
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students classify a covalent bond as an intermolecular force.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Covalent bonds are intramolecular bonds within a molecule; intermolecular forces are separate attractions between molecules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish bonds within NH3 from attractions between NH3 molecules and select an intermolecular force such as hydrogen bonding.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Covalence bond as an intermolecular force"
misconceptions.prevalence: Question 5: 7.94% alternative conception
misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

misconceptions.subtopic: Wrong force named for boiling point difference
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the boiling point difference between ammonia and methane is explained by covalent bonding or by the number of hydrogen atoms, rather than by intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ammonia has hydrogen bonding, while methane has only London dispersion forces; these intermolecular forces explain the boiling point difference.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the intermolecular forces present in each substance and link stronger intermolecular attraction to a higher boiling point.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the difference of boiling point depending on the number of hydrogen atom in a molecule"
misconceptions.prevalence: Question 6: 23.81% alternative conception
misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that any substance containing hydrogen must have hydrogen bonding, including methane.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires hydrogen bonded to N, O, or F; mere presence of hydrogen is not sufficient.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check which atom hydrogen is bonded to and whether the molecule has an appropriate electronegative partner before naming hydrogen bonding.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "methane and ammonia have hydrogen bond because both of them have hydrogen in their molecules"
misconceptions.prevalence: Question 6: included in the 23.81% alternative conception responses
misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

misconceptions.subtopic: Covalent substances have highest boiling points
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe substances with covalent bonds always have the highest boiling points compared with other substances.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point depends on the strength of intermolecular forces and particle interactions, not simply on whether a substance is covalent.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the actual intermolecular forces present and recognize that covalent bonding within molecules does not determine ordinary boiling point by itself.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "substance with covalent will have the highest boiling point"
misconceptions.prevalence: Question 6: included in the 23.81% alternative conception responses
misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat properties such as pressure, temperature, boiling point, structure of an atom, and electron configuration as if they are not consistently categorized; the paper notes opposite answers for similar items, indicating confusion about which are macroscopic versus sub-microscopic.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Macroscopic properties are bulk, observable properties; sub-microscopic properties concern particles and their structure/configuration.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should ask whether the property describes the bulk sample that can be directly observed/measured (macroscopic) or the particles/particles' arrangement and electron structure (sub-microscopic).
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "About a half of the students tested had difficulty in answering Question 1 correctly"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: About half of students (average performance in Question 1: 58% correct; 40–64% correct by item)
all_misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students (n=148 total; 46 first year, 55 second year, 47 third year)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that a statement like 'copper metal conducts electricity because all metals conduct electricity' is an explanation rather than just a description or classification.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: An explanation must give the mechanism at the particle level, not merely cite a general rule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish a general descriptive statement from a mechanism-based explanation by asking whether the statement says why at the particle level; for metal conduction, the explanation should refer to electron flow in metals.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "two-thirds of the students thought erroneously that 'copper metal conducts electricity because all metals conduct electricity' was an explanatory statement."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Two-thirds of students (Question 2(d))
all_misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not know that liquid water consists of H2O molecules; some may not represent liquid water at the molecular level correctly.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Liquid water is made of H2O molecules as the stable particles present.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the substance and recall its stable molecular particles; for liquid water, the particles are intact H2O molecules, not separate atoms or ions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "more than 60 % of the students tested did not know that the particles that exist in liquid water (Question 3(c)) ... are H2O molecules."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: More than 60% incorrect
all_misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that water vapour contains particles other than intact H2O molecules, including H2 and O2 molecules or H atoms and O atoms, or that H2O decomposes on boiling.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Water vapour consists of H2O molecules; boiling is a phase change, not decomposition.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that a phase change changes only particle spacing/arrangement, not chemical identity; therefore molecules remain H2O in the vapour.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The main error in Question 4 was due to students thinking that H2O molecules in liquid water decompose into H2 and H2 0 molecules when it is boiled."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: More than 60% incorrect on related item(s); Question 4 average 24% correct
all_misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students consider only the solute particles in aqueous solutions and do not recognize that water molecules are also present in aqueous sodium chloride and glucose solutions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Aqueous solutions contain H2O molecules along with the dissolved solute particles.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that 'aqueous' means the solvent is water, so water molecules remain in the solution as part of the particle mixture.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the main source of error was due to students not recognizing that aqueous solutions always contain H2O molecules: they considered only the solute particles."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Described as the main source of error; Question 3(f) and 3(g) were very poorly answered (overall average for Question 3: 19% correct)
all_misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think molecules are distributed uniformly between the liquid and vapour phases in a closed vessel at equilibrium.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: At liquid-vapour equilibrium, the same substance is present in both phases, but particle density is much higher in the liquid than in the vapour; the distribution is not uniform across phases.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from phase density: particles are closely packed in the liquid and much more dispersed in the vapour, even though exchange balances at equilibrium.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The majority thought, surprisingly, that the molecules are distributed uniformly in the liquid and vapour phases (response (e))."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Majority of students chose the incorrect uniform-distribution option; only about a quarter correct on Question 5
all_misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the main reason a gas expands on heating at constant pressure is simply the increase in temperature or the increase in molecular speed.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Heating increases molecular speed, which leads to greater spacing between molecules; the increase in volume is due to increased space between molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect higher temperature to faster molecular motion, then infer that faster motion at constant pressure requires a larger average separation, increasing gas volume.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The majority of students thought erroneously that response (e) was correct. Increase in temperature cannot, however, be considered to be the reason for the increase in gas volume when it is heated: it is an experimental fact. Similarly, increase in the speed of the molecules (response (c)) is not the main reason for the increase in volume."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Only about 15% correct on Question 10
all_misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the bonds that break when ice melts are covalent O-H bonds within H2O molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Melting breaks intermolecular forces between water molecules, not the covalent bonds inside each molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular bonds, which hold atoms together within a molecule, from intermolecular bonds, which hold molecules together; melting disrupts the latter only.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "More than half of the students tested had difficulty and they thought that the bonds that break when ice melts are covalent O-H bonds within the molecules."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: More than half incorrect; Question 11 average 42% correct
all_misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students write reaction equations in molecular form (e.g. HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O) when the question asks for the particles actually involved, i.e. ions/electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: For ionic reactions, equations should be written using the reacting ions and relevant particles only, such as H+ and OH- for acid-base neutralization.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the species actually present and changing in solution, omit spectator ions, and write the balanced ionic equation based on particles involved.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Most students wrote the equations correctly in terms of molecules. For example, about 70 % of them wrote correctly the equation for the reaction between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide using molecules (HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O)."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: About 70% gave the molecular equation instead of the requested particle-level equation for Question 12(d)
all_misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not write reactions in terms of bonds broken and formed, missing that chemical change involves breaking and making specific covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Chemical reactions can be represented by counting bonds broken in reactants and bonds formed in products.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should translate each molecule into its bond structure, then count bonds broken and formed while conserving atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The very poor performance was due to students not writing the given balanced equations in terms of the bonds in the reactant and product molecules."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Less than 10% correct on Question 13
all_misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot write the half-equation for removal of two electrons from a copper atom.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Removing two electrons from copper is Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e-.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that electron loss produces a positively charged ion and balance charge and electrons on both sides.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it was surprising that they could not write the simple equation for the removal of two electrons from a copper atom (Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-)."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: About 30% could not answer part 12(a)
all_misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe solid NaCl conducts electricity simply because it contains Na+ and Cl- ions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Solid NaCl does not conduct electricity because its ions are not mobile; conductivity requires mobile ions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish the presence of ions from their mobility: in a solid lattice the ions are fixed, so current cannot flow.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "(b) Solid NaCl consists of Na+ ions and Cl– ions and hence will conduct electricity"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: About 54% correct, so about 46% held the misconception
all_misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not correctly relate molecular mass to molecular speed, or cannot order gases by speed and density using mass reasoning.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: At the same temperature, lighter gas molecules move faster than heavier ones; gas density at fixed temperature and pressure increases with molecular mass.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare relative molecular masses: lower mass means higher average speed and lower density under the same T and P.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Student performance in the next question, which tests explanation of molecular speed and gas density in terms of the mass of the molecules, was very poor."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Only about 20% correct on Question 15
all_misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students struggle to connect molecular shape and intermolecular forces to density and melting point in packed hydrocarbon solids.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular shape affects packing efficiency and intermolecular interactions, which in turn affect density and melting point.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare linear vs branched molecules: better packing usually gives higher density and, depending on packing/intermolecular contacts, affects melting point.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Though Question 16 appears to be more difficult than Question 15, because its solution needs the correlation of density/melting point with some properties of molecules and intermolecular forces, student performance was much better."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: About half correct; about half incorrect on Question 16
all_misconceptions.population: BSc first-, second-, and third-year chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Conceptions about the Sub-Microscopic Approach to Explanations in Chemistry Throughout their BSc Degree Course

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Some first-year students do not recognize that a functional group can affect a molecule's boiling point, implying they think compounds with the same carbon atoms should have the same boiling point or that functional group differences are not important.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Functional groups can change the type and strength of intermolecular forces, which changes boiling point; alcohols boil higher than ethers because alcohols can form hydrogen bonds while ethers cannot.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the functional groups, identify whether hydrogen bonding is possible, and then infer that stronger intermolecular forces lead to a higher boiling point.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Some first-year students seem unaware that a functional group can affect a molecule's boiling point."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 50% of first-year students answered correctly; 100% of third-year students answered correctly
all_misconceptions.population: First-year (2023) and third-year (2021) chemistry education students; 10 students in each cohort
all_misconceptions.concept_category: boiling point factors / functional group effects
all_misconceptions.source_title: University Students' Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Comparison of First & Third-Year Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Several first-year students believe that the most volatile compounds are the ones with the highest boiling points and molar masses, and that higher molar mass means lower boiling point because the intermolecular bonds are weaker in larger nonpolar hydrocarbon molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Higher molar mass and greater polarizability generally strengthen London dispersion forces, which can raise boiling point; nonpolar molecules still experience van der Waals (dispersion) forces.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should relate molecular size and electron cloud polarizability to dispersion forces, then predict that stronger dispersion forces usually increase boiling point rather than decrease it.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Several first-year students assume that the most volatile compounds are the compounds with the highest boiling points and molar masses."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 50% of first-year students answered correctly; 100% of third-year students answered correctly
all_misconceptions.population: First-year (2023) and third-year (2021) chemistry education students; 10 students in each cohort
all_misconceptions.concept_category: boiling point factors / molar mass and dispersion
all_misconceptions.source_title: University Students' Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Comparison of First & Third-Year Students

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Polarizability, atomic size, and steric effects
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Some students failed to connect larger atomic size with easier polarization, suggesting they do not reason that a larger iodine atom is more polarizable than bromine because its valence electrons are less tightly held by the nucleus.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A larger atom with more weakly held valence electrons is more easily polarized, which strengthens London dispersion forces and can affect boiling point.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare atomic size, infer electron-cloud polarizability, and then connect greater polarizability to stronger dispersion forces and higher boiling point.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "They failed to realize that the size of the iodine atom is greater than the bromine atom, so the valence electron in the iodine atom is weakly bound by the nucleus more than the bromine atom."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 70% of third-year students answered correctly; 20% of first-year students answered correctly
all_misconceptions.population: First-year (2023) and third-year (2021) chemistry education students; 10 students in each cohort
all_misconceptions.source_title: University Students' Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Comparison of First & Third-Year Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Some first-year students appear to think that the higher the hydrocarbon compound's molar mass, the lower its boiling point because of weaker bonds between hydrocarbon molecules and their nonpolar character, rather than recognizing that nonpolar molecules still interact through van der Waals forces.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nonpolar molecules do experience London dispersion forces; as molar mass and polarizability increase, these forces generally become stronger and can increase boiling point.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the molecule as nonpolar, then apply London dispersion forces rather than dismissing intermolecular interactions altogether.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "They failed to recognize that the van der Waals forces exist in non-polar molecules."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 50% of first-year students answered correctly
all_misconceptions.population: First-year (2023) chemistry education students; 10 students in the cohort
all_misconceptions.concept_category: nonpolar molecules / van der Waals forces
all_misconceptions.source_title: University Students' Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Comparison of First & Third-Year Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Some students did not identify London dispersion forces as the interaction between methane molecules, implying they may think nonpolar molecules have no intermolecular forces or choose stronger polar interactions instead.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Methane is nonpolar, so the dominant intermolecular force between methane molecules is London dispersion force.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine that methane is nonpolar, then select London dispersion forces as the appropriate intermolecular interaction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the interaction between the methane molecules is London dispersion forces because methane is a nonpolar molecule."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 20% of first-year students answered correctly; 50% of third-year students answered correctly
all_misconceptions.population: First-year (2023) and third-year (2021) chemistry education students; 10 students in each cohort
