all_misconceptions.source_title: University Students' Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Comparison of First & Third-Year Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may incorrectly think hydrogen bonding occurs whenever a molecule contains hydrogen atoms, rather than only when hydrogen is covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom and interacts with a lone pair on another electronegative atom.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires H covalently bonded to N, O, or F and attraction to a lone pair on another electronegative atom.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should inspect the bonding environment of hydrogen and verify whether the donor atom is sufficiently electronegative before concluding that hydrogen bonding is possible.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students assume hydrogen bonds involve hydrogen atoms, occurring when a C atom binds to an H atom in the molecule."
all_misconceptions.population: Students discussed in cited prior research (Cooper et al., 2015; related studies mentioned in the paper)
all_misconceptions.source_title: University Students' Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Comparison of First & Third-Year Students

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Phase change and bond breaking in water
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Heating water breaks the covalent bond between the O and H atoms in the water molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Phase changes such as heating, melting, or evaporation do not break intramolecular covalent O–H bonds in water; they overcome intermolecular attractions between molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular bonds from intermolecular forces: heating supplies energy to separate water molecules from each other during a phase change, but the O–H covalent bonds within each molecule remain intact unless a chemical reaction occurs.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "there was a covalent bond break between the O and H atoms in the water molecule due to heating"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 24.6% of 69 students
all_misconceptions.population: Grade XI high school students (n=69 for the IFDI misconception table; overall class XI sample n=101)
all_misconceptions.source_title: 2.2 Research instruments

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Comparison of intermolecular and intramolecular forces
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Intermolecular forces are stronger than intramolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intramolecular bonds are stronger than intermolecular forces; intermolecular forces are weaker attractions between molecules compared with covalent/ionic bonds within molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the kinds of interactions: bonds holding atoms together inside a molecule require more energy to break than the attractions between separate molecules, so intermolecular forces cannot be stronger than intramolecular bonds.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Intermolecular force is stronger than intramolecular force"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 23.1% of 69 students
all_misconceptions.population: Grade XI high school students (n=69 for the IFDI misconception table; overall class XI sample n=101)
all_misconceptions.source_title: 2.2 Research instruments

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The concave shape of a liquid surface is caused by dipole–dipole intermolecular force.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The shape of a liquid surface (e.g., meniscus) is determined by the balance of adhesive and cohesive forces with the container surface, not simply by dipole–dipole attraction alone.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from the interactions between the liquid and the container: if adhesion and cohesion differ, the liquid surface curves accordingly; the shape is not directly explained by naming one type of intermolecular force without considering the solid–liquid interactions and relative strengths.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the surface shape of concave fluids is influenced by dipole–dipole intermolecular force"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 29.2% of 69 students
all_misconceptions.population: Grade XI high school students (n=69 for the IFDI misconception table; overall class XI sample n=101)
all_misconceptions.source_title: 2.2 Research instruments

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: During melting and freezing, the volumes of ice and water are the same.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ice and liquid water have different volumes for the same mass because water expands on freezing and contracts on melting; density changes accompany the phase change.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare densities of the two phases: because the arrangement of water molecules in ice is more open than in liquid water, a given mass occupies a larger volume as ice than as liquid water.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "in the smelting and freezing process, the volume of ice and water is the same"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 27.7% of 69 students
all_misconceptions.population: Grade XI high school students (n=69 for the IFDI misconception table; overall class XI sample n=101)
all_misconceptions.source_title: 2.2 Research instruments

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Vapor pressure and intermolecular force strength
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Substances with strong intermolecular forces have large vapor pressures.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Stronger intermolecular forces lead to lower vapor pressure because molecules are less able to escape from the liquid into the gas phase.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect vapor pressure to molecular escape from the liquid surface: if attractions between molecules are strong, fewer molecules leave the liquid, so vapor pressure is lower, not higher.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "substances that have strong intermolecular forces have large vapor pressures"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 26.2% of 69 students
all_misconceptions.population: Grade XI high school students (n=69 for the IFDI misconception table; overall class XI sample n=101)
all_misconceptions.source_title: 2.2 Research instruments

all_misconceptions.topic: Boiling point trends and intermolecular forces
all_misconceptions.subtopic: Hydrogen bonding as evidence for higher boiling point
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that a substance's higher boiling point can be explained without linking it to stronger intermolecular forces and the extra energy required to overcome them, or they give only a surface-level mention of hydrogen bonding with no causal mechanism.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A higher boiling point is caused by stronger intermolecular forces; molecules with stronger attractions require more energy to separate before boiling occurs.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the compound with stronger intermolecular forces, explain that these stronger attractions make molecules harder to separate, and state that more energy is needed to overcome those interactions, leading to a higher boiling point.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students may be able to easily make a claim, they can struggle with identifying appropriate evidence or being able to clearly link evidence to the claim through reasoning"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 40% of Cohort 1 provided no explanation or non-normative responses; 50% of Cohort 4 gave the most sophisticated reasoning including energy
all_misconceptions.population: General chemistry students across four cohorts (Cohort 1 N=119; Cohort 2 N=106; Cohort 3 N=86; Cohort 4 N=70)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of three-dimensional learning interventions on student understanding of structure-property relationships

all_misconceptions.topic: Boiling point trends and intermolecular forces
all_misconceptions.subtopic: Correct boiling point ranking for ethanol vs dimethyl ether
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students incorrectly choose dimethyl ether or cannot predict the higher-boiling compound when comparing ethanol and dimethyl ether.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ethanol has the higher boiling point than dimethyl ether because ethanol can form hydrogen bonds in addition to dipole-dipole interactions and London dispersion forces.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the intermolecular forces present in each compound, recognize that ethanol has hydrogen bonding while dimethyl ether does not, and conclude that ethanol’s stronger overall intermolecular attraction gives it the higher boiling point.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The majority of students in the control group incorrectly identified the claim"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: In Cohort 1, 35% selected ethanol as the correct claim before intervention; this increased to 52% in Cohort 2 and 80% in Cohort 3
all_misconceptions.population: General chemistry students in the structure-property assessment at the end of GC2
all_misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of three-dimensional learning interventions on student understanding of structure-property relationships

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students draw hydrogen bonding within a molecule as if it were a covalent bond between H and O rather than as an intermolecular, non-covalent attraction between separate molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is a non-covalent interaction between different molecules, not a bond within one molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify donor and acceptor sites, then draw the hydrogen bond between molecules with a dashed or dotted line to show an intermolecular attraction rather than a covalent bond inside the ethanol molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students have difficulty differentiating between bonding and intermolecular forces"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Less than 20% of Cohort 1 correctly represented hydrogen bonding as between molecules; 52% of Cohort 2; 57% of Cohort 3; 79% of Cohort 4
all_misconceptions.population: General chemistry students drawing hydrogen bonding for three ethanol molecules
all_misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of three-dimensional learning interventions on student understanding of structure-property relationships

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think covalent bonds are broken during the boiling process.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling separates molecules by overcoming intermolecular forces; covalent bonds within molecules are not broken when a liquid boils.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular covalent bonds from intermolecular attractions and reason that heat supplied during boiling is used to overcome intermolecular forces between molecules, not to break covalent bonds inside molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "along with the misunderstanding that covalent bonds are broken during the boiling process"
all_misconceptions.population: Students answering questions on hydrogen bonding and boiling point explanations
all_misconceptions.concept_category: phase change / bonding vs intermolecular forces
all_misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of three-dimensional learning interventions on student understanding of structure-property relationships

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students omit or fail to use the idea that stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to overcome, or they do not connect energy to the boiling point difference.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to overcome, which leads to a higher boiling point.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare interaction strengths, state that stronger attractions are harder to overcome, and infer that more energy is needed to boil the substance with stronger intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students were more likely than Cohorts 1-3 to also include the ideas of energy needed to overcome stronger forces for a more sophisticated explanation"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 17-33% for Cohorts 1-3 versus 50% for Cohort 4
all_misconceptions.population: Students responding to Question 6 on the structure-property assessment
all_misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of three-dimensional learning interventions on student understanding of structure-property relationships

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students explain boiling point by saying one substance has 'more bonds' that must be broken to boil.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point depends on intermolecular force strength, not on having more covalent bonds to break.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should not count bonds in the molecule; instead, they should focus on the strength and type of intermolecular forces between molecules and the energy required to overcome them.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Because ethanol will have more bonds than dimethyl ether, therefore have more bonds to break to reach a boiling point"
all_misconceptions.population: Students coded as giving non-normative reasoning in Question 6
all_misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of three-dimensional learning interventions on student understanding of structure-property relationships

all_misconceptions.subtopic: London dispersion forces and molecular size
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the relative boiling point can always be predicted only by the simple rule that a molecule with hydrogen bonding must boil higher than one with only London dispersion forces, and they do not apply this to exceptions where a larger molecule with stronger LDFs can boil higher than a smaller molecule with weak H-bonding.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point depends on the overall balance of intermolecular forces; a larger, more polarizable molecule can have stronger London dispersion forces and a higher boiling point than a smaller molecule even if the smaller one can hydrogen bond weakly.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Compare the size/polarizability and the types of intermolecular forces in both molecules, then weigh which set of attractions is stronger overall rather than relying on a single surface rule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “they are often unable to reason that a large molecule with high LDFs may have a higher boiling point than a small molecule with weak H-bonding.”
all_misconceptions.population: college freshman-level chemistry students
all_misconceptions.concept_category: boiling point trends / LDF vs hydrogen bonding
all_misconceptions.source_title: Gamifying intermolecular forces: Improving student performance outcomes for college freshman-level intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may fail to recognize that a molecule can be capable of hydrogen bonding even when it is not a typical alcohol or common textbook example.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding occurs when a molecule has H bonded to N, O, or F and a suitable lone-pair acceptor; uncommon or unstable molecules can still be hydrogen-bond donors/acceptors if they meet the structural criteria.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Inspect the functional groups and Lewis structure for N–H, O–H, or F–H bonds and lone pairs on N/O/F, then decide whether hydrogen bonding is possible regardless of whether the molecule is a familiar example.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students were not significantly better or worse at recognizing that methylimine is ‘capable’ of hydrogen bonding as a cause for its higher boiling point compared to ethene.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Pre-activity correct responses: 60.6%; post-activity correct responses: 61.9%
all_misconceptions.population: students in the freshman-level IMF activity (matched n = 236 responses)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Gamifying intermolecular forces: Improving student performance outcomes for college freshman-level intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not correctly determine how molecular geometry affects polarity, leading them to miss that a cis isomer can have stronger dipole-dipole interactions than the trans isomer.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular geometry determines whether bond dipoles cancel; a cis isomer may be polar while the trans isomer is nonpolar or less polar, so the cis isomer can have stronger dipole-dipole interactions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Draw or interpret the molecular geometry, add bond dipoles as vectors, and decide whether a net dipole remains; if the cis isomer has a net dipole and the trans does not, the cis isomer has stronger dipole-dipole forces.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students were not significantly better or worse at recognizing that the cis- isomer of dichloro-difluroxenon has stronger dipole-dipole interactions than the trans- isomer.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Pre-activity correct responses: 63.1%; post-activity correct responses: 67.4%
all_misconceptions.population: students in the freshman-level IMF activity (matched n = 236 responses)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Gamifying intermolecular forces: Improving student performance outcomes for college freshman-level intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may fail to recognize that cis and trans alkene isomers can differ in polarity and dipole-dipole forces.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The cis isomer of dichloroethene has a net dipole and therefore stronger dipole-dipole interactions than the trans isomer, whose dipoles cancel more effectively.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Use the molecular geometry to assess whether the bond dipoles cancel; then compare the strength of dipole-dipole interactions based on the net molecular dipole.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students were significantly better at recognizing that the cis- isomer of dichloro-ethene has stronger dipole-dipole interactions than the trans- isomer”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Pre-activity correct responses: 55.1%; post-activity correct responses: 66.1%
all_misconceptions.population: students in the freshman-level IMF activity (matched n = 236 responses)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Gamifying intermolecular forces: Improving student performance outcomes for college freshman-level intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Hydrogen bonding and boiling point comparison
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may incorrectly think that a substance with fewer hydrogen-bonding opportunities can still have the higher boiling point, rather than connecting more hydrogen bonding to stronger intermolecular attraction and higher boiling point.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: More hydrogen bonding generally increases intermolecular attraction and raises boiling point; glycerol has more hydrogen bonding than pentanol, so glycerol boils higher.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Count the hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors available, compare the extent of hydrogen bonding in each molecule, and infer that more extensive hydrogen bonding usually raises boiling point.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students are significantly better at recognising that glycerol has more hydrogen bonding than pentanol as a cause for glycerol having the higher boiling point.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Pre-activity correct responses: 69.1%; post-activity correct responses: 76.3%
all_misconceptions.population: students in the freshman-level IMF activity (matched n = 236 responses)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Gamifying intermolecular forces: Improving student performance outcomes for college freshman-level intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Comparing LDFs and dipole-dipole interactions in sulfur oxides
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think sulfur trioxide should have dipole-dipole interactions like sulfur dioxide, or may not understand that the stronger LDFs of the larger molecule can outweigh sulfur dioxide's dipole-dipole interactions in boiling point comparison.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Sulfur trioxide is nonpolar and has no dipole-dipole interactions; its larger electron cloud gives stronger London dispersion forces than sulfur dioxide, contributing to the higher boiling point.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Determine whether the molecule has a net dipole. If not, rule out dipole-dipole forces, then compare size/polarizability to judge London dispersion strength and its effect on boiling point.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students are significantly better at recognising that sulfur trioxide does not have dipole-dipole interactions, but has significantly stronger LDFs when compared to sulfur dioxide's weaker LDFs and dipole-dipole interaction, as a cause for sulfur trioxide having the higher boiling point.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Pre-activity correct responses: 30.9%; post-activity correct responses: 41.5%
all_misconceptions.population: students in the freshman-level IMF activity (matched n = 236 responses)
all_misconceptions.concept_category: polarity / LDF vs dipole-dipole interactions / boiling point trends
all_misconceptions.source_title: Gamifying intermolecular forces: Improving student performance outcomes for college freshman-level intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Dipole-dipole interactions occur within a single molecule, not between two molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interactions are intermolecular forces that occur between separate molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify that the interaction is between the partial positive end of one polar molecule and the partial negative end of another polar molecule, not between atoms within the same molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “a large portion of the students believed that intermolecular forces were within a single molecule rather than between”
all_misconceptions.population: students in general chemistry; discussion references prior work
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Any molecule containing nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine can hydrogen bond.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires a hydrogen atom bonded to N, O, or F and interaction with a lone pair on N, O, or F; the presence of N, O, or F alone is not sufficient.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check both the donor and acceptor conditions for hydrogen bonding, rather than assuming that the presence of N, O, or F automatically makes a molecule hydrogen-bonding capable.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students often generalize principles associated with intermolecular forces such that any molecule with either nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine carries the ability to hydrogen bond”
all_misconceptions.population: students in general chemistry; prior literature summarized in the paper
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Lone pairs or open electron sites are places that should bond with another atom, so the dipole-dipole interaction is treated like a covalent bond formation site.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interactions are attractions between partial charges on different molecules; lone pairs may influence polarity and molecular shape but are not themselves bonding sites for intermolecular force formation.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use molecular polarity and partial charges to locate the attraction between molecules, not infer that a lone pair is an available bonding site that must be filled.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the lone pairs represent sites that are free to bond with other atoms.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in 5 students in Version 1 (Sawyer, Sasha, Sadie, Sabrina, Sebastian) when discussing Lewis dot structures; also discussed as a broader pattern in the Discussion
all_misconceptions.population: Version 1 students in second semester general chemistry (n=9 in Version 1; 18 total interviewed)
all_misconceptions.concept_category: bonding availability / intermolecular vs intramolecular forces
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: If a representation shows no explicit lone pairs or bonds, the atom has an 'open spot' that needs to be filled by an intermolecular interaction to satisfy the octet.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Missing dots or bonds in a representation do not mean an atom needs an additional bond; dipole-dipole interactions depend on partial charges between molecules, not octet completion in the displayed model.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should interpret the representation in terms of electron distribution and polarity, and recognize that intermolecular attractions do not add bonds to complete octets.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students considered the space around each atom as the location where dipole-dipole interactions could occur”
all_misconceptions.population: students in both protocol versions; especially Version 1 space-filling and chemical formula tasks
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Molecular geometry is explicitly shown in Lewis dot structures, so a Lewis structure can be read as linear unless lone pairs are added mentally afterward.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lewis structures encode connectivity and lone pairs, and molecular geometry must be inferred using electron-domain considerations; lone pairs change shape and therefore polarity.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should examine the presence and arrangement of lone pairs to infer the true molecular geometry, then determine whether the molecule is polar and where dipole-dipole attraction can occur.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students carried the assumption that molecular geometry was explicit in Lewis dot structures”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in 3 students in Version 2 (Regan, Rachel, Rebecca) before correction
all_misconceptions.population: Version 2 second semester general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Linear and nonpolar assumption for SeO2
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Selenium dioxide is linear and nonpolar when first viewed in Lewis dot form because lone pairs are not initially considered.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Selenium dioxide is bent because lone pairs on selenium affect bond angle, making the molecule polar.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should count electron domains and include lone pairs in VSEPR reasoning; the bent geometry creates a net dipole that allows dipole-dipole interactions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “designated the molecule as linear and non-polar, without taking into account the influence of lone pairs”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in 3 students in Version 2 before they corrected themselves
all_misconceptions.population: Version 2 students working on Lewis dot structures
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The larger atom in a ball-and-stick or space-filling model is the preferred location for dipole-dipole interaction because larger size means stronger attraction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interaction location is determined by molecular polarity and partial charges, not by atomic size; size in these models is not itself a proxy for dipole-dipole strength.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use electronegativity and molecular geometry to identify partial positive and negative regions, then place the interaction between opposite partial charges on different molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the bigger the two atoms that are bonding are, the weaker the forces are.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in multiple Version 1 students; 3 students (Sandeep, Spencer, Sebastian) explicitly began to use size in ball-and-stick tasks, and 1 student (Sandeep) stayed with size in space-filling
all_misconceptions.population: Version 1 second semester general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: In space-filling models, larger atom size directly corresponds to higher electronegativity and therefore identifies the interaction site.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atom size in a space-filling model is a graphical convention and is not equivalent to electronegativity; the interaction site should be inferred from polarity and partial charge, not from visual size alone.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish the representational cue of atomic size from chemical properties such as electronegativity, and use electron distribution to determine the dipole-dipole interaction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “I think it's just because seeing how one ball can be bigger than the other throws you off easily.”
all_misconceptions.population: Version 1 students; discussed in relation to space-filling representations
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Atoms in the molecules carry fixed valence charges or ionic charges that can be used to predict dipole-dipole attraction by pairing opposite charges.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interactions arise from partial charges in polar covalent molecules; atoms do not need to be treated as ionic species with fixed charges from the periodic table.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use electronegativity differences and molecular geometry to identify partial positive and partial negative ends, then connect those ends between molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “began assigning charges to each of the atoms in the molecules”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in 4 students in Version 2 (Ria, Rachel, Rebecca, Richard) in the space-filling task
all_misconceptions.population: Version 2 second semester general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A central atom cannot participate in or be used to locate dipole-dipole interactions because it is already in the middle of the molecule and is not available to connect.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The relevant interaction site is the region of partial charge in the molecule, which may involve a central atom’s bonded environment; being central does not by itself prevent intermolecular attraction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate the molecule’s polarity from electronegativity and geometry, rather than excluding atoms solely because of their position in the structure.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “I don't know about this one because chlorine is the central... and I don't really know how it's going to connect to the hydrogen.”
all_misconceptions.population: Version 2 chemical formula task; reported for Rachel and also discussed for Ranger and Richard
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A triple bond or greater number of bonds directly means a stronger dipole-dipole interaction or stronger intermolecular attraction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond order affects intramolecular bonding, but dipole-dipole interactions depend on molecular polarity and the magnitude/direction of partial charges between molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should not infer intermolecular force strength from the number of covalent bonds; instead they should analyze electronegativity differences and geometry to locate the partial charges that attract between molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the number of bonds signifies the strength of dipole-dipole interactions in the molecule.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in Version 2 ball-and-stick task; explicitly noted for Ria, and Rebecca linked affinity to number of bonds
all_misconceptions.population: Version 2 second semester general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole—dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Dipole-dipole forces occur within a single molecule at polar bonds rather than only between molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole forces are intermolecular attractions between separate molecules, not bonds within one molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first determine the molecular dipole for each molecule from bonded-atom electronegativity differences, then identify that the attractive interaction occurs between the positive end of one molecule and the negative end of another molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "identify the pair(s) of atoms where the strongest intermolecular force would occur?"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 11 of 18 participants consistently showed dipole-dipole as an intramolecular force; 61% in prior work drew dipole-dipole within a molecule.
all_misconceptions.population: Second semester general chemistry students (18 interview participants); prior cited study of students drawing ethanol molecules.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Any positive and negative partial charges or dipoles anywhere in a molecule pair can be directly connected as the location of dipole-dipole interaction, including when the charges were inferred from unbonded atoms or different molecules without first establishing molecular dipoles correctly.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole attraction should be based on the interaction between the positive end of one molecular dipole and the negative end of another molecular dipole, derived from correct bonded-atom polarity analysis.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare electronegativities only for bonded atoms to identify bond dipoles, combine bond dipoles to determine each molecule's polarity, and then use the positive and negative molecular ends to locate the intermolecular attraction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "In this case, since F would have the more negative partial charge in the iodine monofluoride and then Se would have the positive dipole on the selenium dioxide. It makes sense that they're connected."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 10 of 18 participants used opposite charges attract as a basis; some varied in how they determined molecular dipoles.
all_misconceptions.population: Second semester general chemistry interview participants
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Electronegativity should be compared between atoms on different molecules to decide where dipole-dipole attraction occurs, rather than only between bonded atoms within a molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electronegativity is used first between bonded atoms to determine bond polarity; intermolecular dipole-dipole location is then inferred from the resulting molecular dipoles.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify bonded atoms, subtract electronegativity values only for those bonded pairs, decide which bonds are polar, determine each molecule's dipole, and then place the intermolecular force between opposite molecular ends.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I think the sulfur [in SCl2] and the nitrogen [in NH3] might be able to, just because the electronegativity difference is 0.5."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in approach 1B and 2A/2B; e.g., one participant in approach 1B and three participants in approach 2A compared atoms on different molecules.
all_misconceptions.population: Second semester general chemistry interview participants
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Electronegativity can be compared between unbonded atoms within the same molecule to decide where dipole-dipole attraction is located.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electronegativity comparisons for bond polarity must be made only between atoms that share a chemical bond.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should restrict electronegativity differences to bonded atoms, use those bond polarities to infer molecular polarity, and then locate dipole-dipole attraction between molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the chlorine [in CH3Cl] does have a stronger electronegativity than the hydrogen atoms [in CH3Cl]. So that tells me that the chlorine is found to be partially negative."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented for Lam in approach 1C; Lam compared unbonded atoms within one molecule in one prompt.
all_misconceptions.population: One second semester general chemistry interview participant (Lam)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Any atom pair whose electronegativity difference is greater than 0.5 is the site of dipole-dipole interaction, even if the pair is within a molecule and not a bond site for intermolecular attraction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A difference greater than 0.5 is used to classify a bond as polar covalent, not to directly locate an intermolecular dipole-dipole force.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the 0.5 threshold only to decide bond polarity for bonded atoms, then use the set of bond dipoles to determine molecular polarity and the intermolecular attraction between molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "bonds between S and chloride [in SCl2], and N and hydrogen [in NH3] are all polar bonds because the difference between electronegativity of S and Cl is 0.5."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 4 participants consistently used bonded-atom EN differences above 0.5 to assign dipole-dipole location within a molecule; additional students used this idea inconsistently.
all_misconceptions.population: Second semester general chemistry interview participants
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The atom pair with the largest electronegativity difference is automatically where dipole-dipole force occurs.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Largest electronegativity difference does not by itself determine the location of dipole-dipole force; bond polarity and molecular dipoles must be considered.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare bonded atoms only, determine which bonds are polar, build each molecular dipole, and then identify the positive-to-negative attraction between molecules rather than simply choosing the maximum EN difference.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I feel like the more [EN] difference there is between the two, the more that they're going to interact."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 4 participants (Ethan, Feng, Kavita, Mason) used the largest EN difference approach.
all_misconceptions.population: Second semester general chemistry interview participants
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The atom with the biggest electronegativity value is the one that attracts the other molecule most strongly and therefore marks the dipole-dipole location.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electronegativity is used comparatively to create bond dipoles; the larger raw value alone is not the site of intermolecular attraction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use electronegativity differences between bonded atoms to establish polarity, then use the resulting molecular dipole directions to locate the intermolecular force.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it's [N in NH3] more electronegative, so connect that to chlorine because that's [Cl in SCl2] also the most electronegative."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 3 participants (Ethan, Lam, Quinn) focused on the biggest EN values; Quinn used it consistently across all four prompts.
all_misconceptions.population: Second semester general chemistry interview participants
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The largest atoms in the two molecules are the ones that will experience dipole-dipole attraction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole attraction depends on molecular polarity arising from bond polarity and molecular shape, not on atomic size.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should ignore atom size as the basis of intermolecular attraction, determine bond polarities from electronegativity differences, identify molecular dipoles, and then place the dipole-dipole interaction between opposite molecular ends.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the I [in IF] is significantly bigger than the F [in IF]...It makes me feel that the I should have more attraction to it"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 1 participant (Ethan) used atomic size as the basis in the prompts where size was visually explicit.
all_misconceptions.population: One second semester general chemistry interview participant (Ethan)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Bent molecular shape itself means the bonds inside that molecule are the dipole-dipole force location.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular shape helps determine molecular polarity, but dipole-dipole forces occur between molecules, not inside the bent molecule's bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use shape together with bond polarity to infer whether a molecule has a net dipole, then use the positive and negative ends of two molecules to locate the intermolecular attraction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "because dipole-dipole exists where...molecules are bent, and these [sulfur to chlorine bonds] are in a bent shape right here. So these two bonds would be dipole-dipole."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 1 participant (Danh) consistently used molecular shape in all four prompts.
all_misconceptions.population: One second semester general chemistry interview participant (Danh)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: If a molecule is not bent, it has no dipole and therefore cannot participate in dipole-dipole interactions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular polarity depends on the vector sum of bond dipoles and overall geometry; a molecule can have a dipole even if a student does not recognize a bent shape in the representation.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine the bond dipoles from electronegativity differences, consider the molecular geometry, and decide whether the bond dipoles cancel or produce a net molecular dipole rather than using bend/no-bend as the only criterion.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "when asked whether there was a dipole in IF, Danh replied there was not a dipole because it did not show a bent geometry."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 1 participant (Danh) explicitly said IF had no dipole because it was not bent.
all_misconceptions.population: One second semester general chemistry interview participant (Danh)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Approaches to Determining the Location of Intermolecular Force between Two Distinct Molecules

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Intermolecular forces occur within a single molecule rather than between molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are interactions between molecules, not intramolecular forces within one molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the two separate molecules in the task and determine the strongest attractive interaction between them based on their electrostatic properties, not on bonds within one molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "over half of participants held the conception that intermolecular forces occur within a single molecule rather than between molecules."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: over half of participants (from Cooper et al., cited in paper)
all_misconceptions.population: general chemistry students in prior study cited by the paper
all_misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A lone pair on an atom is a direct indicator that a hydrogen can bond there in intermolecular force tasks.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding occurs between a hydrogen attached to N, O, or F and a lone pair on another electronegative atom; lone pairs alone are not simply 'bonding sites' by themselves.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the intermolecular force definition and identify complementary partial positive and partial negative regions between different molecules rather than treating any lone pair as an available bond site.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Because I have a lone pair ... the hydrogen could bond there."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 5 students
all_misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
all_misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: An atom's octet state or how 'surrounded' it is determines whether it can participate in intermolecular interactions, and an incomplete octet means it is a bonding site.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular interactions are determined by partial charges and electrostatic attraction between molecules, not by whether an atom has a full octet or appears 'surrounded'.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should look for electrostatic complementarity between molecules and connect partial positive regions to partial negative regions, rather than inferring intermolecular interaction sites from octet completeness.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it doesn't have its full like ... it's not like surrounded"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 5 students
all_misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
all_misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: An uneven distribution of electrons or extra lone pairs in a Lewis structure directly means the atom has a negative charge and is attractive for intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Partial charges arise from differences in electron density and electronegativity across the molecule, not simply from counting lone pairs or noticing an 'uneven' Lewis structure.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from electronegativity and electron density to determine where partial positive and partial negative regions exist, then infer the likely intermolecular interaction site from those partial charges.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "there's an extra lone pair on the side and that gives it a negative charge."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: part of the 5-student availability-for-bonding group
all_misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
all_misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Electronegativity values can be subtracted within a single molecule to decide which molecule has the strongest intermolecular force.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electronegativity differences within a bond help infer bond polarity and molecular polarity, but intermolecular force strength is determined by interactions between molecules, not by the molecule with the largest internal electronegativity difference.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first use electronegativity differences to infer bond polarity and then use molecular polarity and complementary partial charges to determine the strongest force between two molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "participants subtracted the provided elemental electronegativity values within the same molecule and identified the one with the largest difference as having the strongest intermolecular force."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 5 students
all_misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
all_misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A Lewis structure's drawn appearance can be taken as the actual molecular geometry; for example, a molecule that appears linear in the Lewis structure is treated as linear and nonpolar.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Actual molecular geometry must be inferred from structure and electron-domain arrangement, not from the flat Lewis drawing; molecular shape determines polarity and thus intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use VSEPR or equivalent geometry reasoning to determine the true 3D shape, then decide whether the molecule is polar and what intermolecular force is strongest.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "if it was linear for example, then you couldn't because it pulls equally in both directions, so no dipole"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: mentioned for Ellie
all_misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
all_misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The explicit lone pairs shown in a Lewis structure are the key features for determining intermolecular force strength and location, so forces are treated as if they depend on structural placeholders rather than molecule-to-molecule electrostatics.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular force location should be based on electrostatic attraction between partial charges on different molecules; explicit lone pairs are not the force itself.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should translate the structural information into polarity and partial charges, then identify where opposite charges on separate molecules attract.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the explicit lone pairs on the Lewis Dot structure as indicators of available interaction sites."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 5 students
all_misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
all_misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

all_misconceptions.subtopic: color interpretation in electrostatic potential maps
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The colors on an electrostatic potential map indicate force strength or magnitude of intermolecular attraction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The colors on an electrostatic potential map represent relative electron density/partial charge, not intermolecular force strength itself.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should interpret the color key as electron-density information, identify partial positive and partial negative regions, and then reason about which molecules will attract each other.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "several participants carrying intramolecular force conceptions viewed the colors on the EPM as a measure of force strength/magnitude."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: several participants
all_misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
all_misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Symmetrical nonpolar molecules should lack areas of high and low electron density on an EPM because opposing dipoles cancel out.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Even symmetric molecules can show regions of different electron density on an EPM because the map displays local electron distribution; cancellation of the net dipole does not mean the map is uniform.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between overall molecular polarity and local electron-density variation, recognizing that a nonpolar molecule can still have electron-density gradients across bonds and atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "several participants seemed to hold the conception that the EPM of symmetrical molecules would be devoid of areas of high and low electron density because of the opposite but equal dipole moments."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: several participants
all_misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
all_misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: London dispersion forces result from random electron movement being directly visible as changing electron density on the map, so a static EPM can misrepresent dispersion as non-random or non-physical.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces arise from temporary fluctuations in electron distribution; an EPM is a static representation of electron density, not a movie of electron motion.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should understand that an EPM shows a snapshot of electron density and that dispersion forces are described by temporary induced dipoles and fluctuating electron motion, not fixed map colors alone.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the EPM presentation of electron density as a static characteristic which dissuaded students from a conception of London dispersion forces that result from random electron movement."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: several participants
all_misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
all_misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: More electron density, more bonds, or a more 'balanced' electron-density pattern means a molecule is stronger and therefore has stronger intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular force type and strength depend on the nature of intermolecular electrostatic interactions between molecules, not on how hard it seems to pull a molecule apart or on the number of bonds within it.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the types of intermolecular attractions possible between two molecules and use polarity/partial charges, not internal bonding or perceived molecular stability, to judge the strongest intermolecular force.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "CCl4 has overall higher electron density, which I'm pretty sure means that it's harder to pull the atoms apart from each other in the molecule, which would mean that it's stronger."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Ivy; part of intramolecular-force-conception group of 5
all_misconceptions.population: general chemistry II interview participants
all_misconceptions.source_title: An Investigation into Dissonance-Induced Changes in Intermolecular Force Conceptions through Electrostatic Potential Maps

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the rubber stopper pops out because the total amount of matter/number of moles increases, the solution becomes more filled, or air is released/fills the tube, rather than because hydrogen gas pressure builds up.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The stopper is ejected because the reaction produces H2 gas, increasing internal pressure above external pressure.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Identify that Mg reacts with HCl to form hydrogen gas; in a closed container the produced gas increases the internal pressure, and when this pressure exceeds the outside pressure the stopper is pushed out.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the rubber stopper to jump was due to increase the amount of matter”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 1: specific alternative conceptions 9.19% (8/87); partial understanding with specific alternative conception 12.64% (11/87)
all_misconceptions.population: 87 11th grade science students from three public schools in Erzurum, Turkey
all_misconceptions.source_title: 11th Grade Students' Understanding Level of Gases in terms of Some Chemical Variables and the Determination of Alternative Conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen in the acid is a hydrogen element/ion that flies away as a gas or decomposes, rather than recognizing molecular hydrogen gas produced by the reaction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen gas is H2 formed by chemical reaction; H+ ions are not the same as hydrogen gas particles.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Distinguish ions from molecules and use the reaction equation to see that H+ ions are reduced to form H2 gas, which accumulates and raises pressure.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the hydrogen element and Mg metal reacted, the pressure increased”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Reported in group discussions; no percentage given
all_misconceptions.population: 9 students in group discussions (from the same 87-student sample)
all_misconceptions.source_title: 11th Grade Students' Understanding Level of Gases in terms of Some Chemical Variables and the Determination of Alternative Conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think tire pressure rises because of elevation changes, outdoor pressure changes, or because the accelerator pedal presses on the wheels, rather than because heating from friction increases molecular kinetic energy and pressure.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Tire pressure increases when friction heats the tire, increasing the kinetic energy of gas molecules and their collisions with the tire walls.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Link friction to temperature rise; higher temperature means faster-moving gas molecules and more forceful/more frequent collisions with the tire wall, which raises pressure in a fixed volume.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “Pressure from the accelerator pedal increases the gas pressure on the wheels.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 2: specific alternative conceptions 18.39% (16/87); partial understanding with specific alternative conception 26.43% (23/87)
all_misconceptions.population: 87 11th grade science students from three public schools in Erzurum, Turkey
all_misconceptions.source_title: 11th Grade Students' Understanding Level of Gases in terms of Some Chemical Variables and the Determination of Alternative Conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat the ideal gas law as meaning pressure and volume always change inversely in every context and apply it without considering the specific variables held constant or the actual cause of pressure change.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The relationship between pressure and volume depends on the conditions; in a tire, heating increases molecular kinetic energy and pressure, and volume is not simply inferred from pressure alone.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Use the full gas model: friction raises temperature, higher temperature raises molecular kinetic energy, and that increases pressure at approximately constant volume. Do not infer a universal inverse pressure-volume relation without identifying the fixed variables.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “As the pressure increases, the volume decreases”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 2: partial understanding with specific alternative conceptions 26.43% (23/87)
all_misconceptions.population: 87 11th grade science students from three public schools in Erzurum, Turkey
all_misconceptions.source_title: 11th Grade Students' Understanding Level of Gases in terms of Some Chemical Variables and the Determination of Alternative Conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that as you go higher, pressure increases and therefore the balloon volume increases or stays fixed, rather than recognizing that external pressure decreases with altitude and the balloon expands.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: At higher altitude external pressure decreases, so the balloon volume increases.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Compare the balloon’s internal gas pressure with the outside pressure; when outside pressure drops, the balloon expands until a new equilibrium is reached.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “As you go higher, the pressure becomes higher. Pressure and volume are inversely proportional.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 3: specific alternative conceptions 9.19% (8/87); partial understanding with specific alternative conception 14.94% (13/87)
all_misconceptions.population: 87 11th grade science students from three public schools in Erzurum, Turkey
all_misconceptions.source_title: 11th Grade Students' Understanding Level of Gases in terms of Some Chemical Variables and the Determination of Alternative Conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think gases expand in the cold or that decreasing temperature makes volume increase, rather than contract.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lower temperature causes gas volume to decrease at constant pressure.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Use the particle model: cooling lowers molecular kinetic energy, particles move more slowly, and the gas occupies less volume.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “Gases expand in the cold environment.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 3: specific alternative conceptions included this statement; no exact count given for this specific misconception
all_misconceptions.population: 87 11th grade science students from three public schools in Erzurum, Turkey
all_misconceptions.source_title: 11th Grade Students' Understanding Level of Gases in terms of Some Chemical Variables and the Determination of Alternative Conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think no expansion occurs in a deflated/air-drained environment, or that the balloon volume decreases because there is no external air pressure or no oxygen.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: With lower external pressure, the balloon expands; the absence of external air does not prevent expansion.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Reason from pressure balance: if outside pressure is removed or reduced, the gas inside the balloon expands until internal and external pressures balance.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “No expansion occurs when the air is deflated.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 3: specific alternative conceptions 9.19% (8/87) included no-understanding/incorrect claims around this idea; exact count for this exact statement not separated
all_misconceptions.population: 87 11th grade science students from three public schools in Erzurum, Turkey
all_misconceptions.source_title: 11th Grade Students' Understanding Level of Gases in terms of Some Chemical Variables and the Determination of Alternative Conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think gases become bulkier or that intermolecular distance increases when gas liquefies or when gas changes to solid.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: When a gas liquefies, particles come closer together and intermolecular distance decreases; going from gas to liquid to solid generally decreases spacing.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Use the particle model of states of matter: gases have the largest spacing, so condensation or solidification reduces spacing between particles.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “If the gaseous material liquefies, it becomes bulky.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 4: specific alternative conceptions 8.04% (7/87)
all_misconceptions.population: 87 11th grade science students from three public schools in Erzurum, Turkey
all_misconceptions.source_title: 11th Grade Students' Understanding Level of Gases in terms of Some Chemical Variables and the Determination of Alternative Conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think increasing pressure creates more substance between molecules or increases intermolecular distance, instead of reducing the distance by compressing the gas.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: At constant temperature, higher pressure compresses gas particles, decreasing intermolecular distance.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: If pressure increases while temperature is constant, the volume decreases; with the same amount of gas in less volume, particles are closer together.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “Increased pressure results in more substances between molecules.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 4: specific alternative conceptions included this statement; group discussion examples provided, no exact count for this exact misconception
all_misconceptions.population: 87 11th grade science students from three public schools in Erzurum, Turkey
all_misconceptions.source_title: 11th Grade Students' Understanding Level of Gases in terms of Some Chemical Variables and the Determination of Alternative Conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think increasing temperature weakens intermolecular bonds/interaction in gases in a way that directly explains particle spacing, rather than using kinetic particle motion and volume changes appropriately.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Temperature changes particle kinetic energy; it does not mean bonds simply weaken in the way students described. Increased temperature at constant volume is not reasoned as bond weakening increasing spacing.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Relate temperature to kinetic energy and collisions, then use the correct state/pressure-volume relationship to infer particle spacing, not a vague bond-breaking explanation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “If the temperature increases at a constant volume, the intermolecular bond weakens.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 4: specific alternative conceptions included this statement; no exact count given
all_misconceptions.population: 87 11th grade science students from three public schools in Erzurum, Turkey
all_misconceptions.source_title: 11th Grade Students' Understanding Level of Gases in terms of Some Chemical Variables and the Determination of Alternative Conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe intermolecular forces are stronger than intramolecular forces, for example that a hydrogen bond is stronger than a covalent bond.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intramolecular bonds are generally much stronger than intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should compare the types of interactions involved and recognize that covalent bonds hold atoms together within a molecule, whereas intermolecular forces act between molecules and are weaker.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "IMFs are stronger than intramolecular forces (for example hydrogen bond is stronger than covalent bond)"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Video with multiple representations approach to promote students' conceptual understanding of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think IMFs are present only in polar molecular substances such as water.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces occur between molecules and can occur in many substances, including nonpolar substances through dispersion forces.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify the type of particles present and then determine which intermolecular attractions can operate between them, rather than restricting IMFs to polar substances only.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "IMFs are present in polar molecular substancessuch as water"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Video with multiple representations approach to promote students' conceptual understanding of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think IMFs occur within a covalent molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces act between molecules, not within a covalent bond framework of a single molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should distinguish between bonds within molecules and attractions between separate molecules; if the interaction is inside one molecule, it is intramolecular, not intermolecular.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "IMFs occur within a covalent molecule"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Video with multiple representations approach to promote students' conceptual understanding of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that intramolecular bonds break when a substance changes state, rather than the intermolecular forces between molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: During a change of state, intermolecular forces are overcome or rearranged; covalent bonds within molecules usually remain intact.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason that melting or boiling changes the arrangement and separation of molecules without changing the identity of the molecules themselves.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Intramolecular bonds break on change of state, rather than IMFs"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Video with multiple representations approach to promote students' conceptual understanding of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think IMFs are the forces within the molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: IMFs are forces between molecules, while forces within a molecule are intramolecular bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify whether the interaction is inside one molecular structure or between separate molecules, then classify it accordingly.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "IMFs are the forces within the molecule"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Video with multiple representations approach to promote students' conceptual understanding of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe strong intermolecular forces exist in a continuous covalent network solid as if those solids were held together by IMFs.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Continuous covalent network solids are held together by covalent bonds throughout the structure, not by intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should distinguish a network solid from a molecular solid by checking whether the structure is a continuous covalent lattice or discrete molecules held together by attractions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Strong IMFs exist in a continuous covalent (network) solid"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Video with multiple representations approach to promote students' conceptual understanding of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think intermolecular forces are influenced by gravity.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces arise from electrostatic interactions between molecules, not gravity.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should explain molecular attractions in terms of charge distribution, polarity, and induced dipoles rather than macroscopic gravitational effects.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "IMFs are influenced by gravity"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Video with multiple representations approach to promote students' conceptual understanding of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe intermolecular forces lead to reactions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Chemical reactions involve breaking and forming chemical bonds; intermolecular forces mainly affect physical properties and phase behavior.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should separate physical attractions between molecules from bond rearrangements that produce new substances in reactions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "IMFs led to reactions"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Video with multiple representations approach to promote students' conceptual understanding of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe unpaired electrons are necessary for hydrogen bonds to form.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom and a lone pair on a neighboring electronegative atom; unpaired electrons are not the requirement.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify the donor hydrogen and acceptor lone pair involved in hydrogen bonding rather than looking for unpaired electrons.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Unpaired electrons are necessary for hydrogen bonds to form"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Video with multiple representations approach to promote students' conceptual understanding of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Intermolecular forces are forces that occur between atoms to form molecules or compounds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are attractive forces between molecules or particles of different molecules, not the forces that make atoms bond within a molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between intramolecular bonds, which hold atoms together inside a molecule, and intermolecular forces, which act between separate molecules and influence physical properties such as boiling point.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Intermolecular forces are forces that occur between atoms to form molecules or compound"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: It takes a high boiling point to break the bonds in a liquid phase.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling occurs when intermolecular attractions between molecules are overcome; boiling point is related to the strength of intermolecular forces, not to breaking covalent bonds inside molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to separate molecules into the gas phase, so higher boiling point indicates stronger attractions between molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "It takes a high boiling point to break the bonds in a liquid phase."
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.concept_category: strength of IMFs and effect on boiling point
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The greater the boiling point, the more difficult it is for the forces between the molecules of the compound to be broken so that the forces between the molecules are stronger.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A higher boiling point indicates stronger intermolecular forces between molecules, because more energy is needed to overcome those attractions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect boiling point to the amount of energy needed to separate molecules, and infer that stronger intermolecular attractions cause a higher boiling point.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The greater the boiling point, the more difficult it is for the forces between the molecules of the compound to be broken so that the forces between the molecules are stronger"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
