all_misconceptions.concept_category: strength of IMFs and effect on boiling point
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: London forces are forces that occur between nonpolar molecules and permanent dipoles.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces arise from instantaneous induced dipoles and occur in all atoms and molecules, though they are the only intermolecular force in nonpolar substances.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify London dispersion as temporary electron-density fluctuations that induce attractions, rather than as attraction between a nonpolar molecule and a permanent dipole.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "London forces are forces that occur between nonpolar molecules and dipole permanent."
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: London forces occur in ethanol between the ethyl group and the OH group.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ethanol molecules experience London dispersion forces as well as dipole-dipole interactions and hydrogen bonding between molecules; London forces are not a force between parts of one ethanol molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that intermolecular forces act between separate ethanol molecules, while the ethyl group and OH group are parts of the same molecule and are connected by covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "London forces occur in ethanol i.e. between ethyl and OH"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: London forces occur in CH4 due to the tetrahedral shape of the CH4 molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Methane has London dispersion forces because it is nonpolar and all molecules have temporary induced dipoles; its tetrahedral shape alone is not the reason London forces exist.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from electron distribution and molecular polarity, not from shape alone, and understand that dispersion forces arise from temporary fluctuations in electron density.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "London forces occur in CH4 due to the tetrahedral shape of the CH4 molecule"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: London force is a nonpolar force.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces are intermolecular attractions caused by instantaneous induced dipoles; they are not defined simply as a 'nonpolar force'.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain dispersion forces in terms of temporary electron redistribution and induced attractions, rather than labeling them as nonpolar without mechanism.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "London force is a nonpolar force"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: London force occurs between positive and negative ions on a molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces are not ion-ion attractions; they are weak intermolecular attractions due to induced dipoles in electron clouds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish dispersion forces from electrostatic attraction between ions and from other types of intermolecular forces based on charge, polarity, and electron fluctuation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "London force occurs between positive and negative ions on a molecule"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The London force is a force of attraction that occurs between atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces are attractions between atoms or molecules arising from temporary induced dipoles, but the concept should not be reduced to a generic atom-to-atom attraction; the mechanism matters.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the force to induced dipoles and recognize where it operates, rather than simply saying it is any attraction between atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The London force is a force of attraction that occurs between atoms"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Nonpolar molecules can undergo permanent dipoles.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nonpolar molecules do not have permanent dipoles; they can only develop temporary induced dipoles that give rise to dispersion forces.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine polarity from molecular symmetry and bond dipoles and understand that London forces come from temporary, not permanent, dipoles in nonpolar molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Nonpolar molecules can undergo permanent dipoles"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The bonds in CH4 and O2 are weak bonds and this explains their low boiling point.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Low boiling points of CH4 and O2 are due to weak intermolecular dispersion forces between molecules, not because the covalent bonds inside the molecules are weak.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate intramolecular covalent bond strength from intermolecular force strength, and relate low boiling point to weak attractions between molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The bond in the compounds CH4 and O2 is a weak bond"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.concept_category: strength of IMFs and effect on boiling point
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Low boiling point is due to London force being very weak and not related to the number of electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion force strength increases with greater polarizability, which is often related to more electrons and larger electron clouds; these stronger dispersion forces can raise boiling point.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should relate electron count and polarizability to the strength of London dispersion forces, then connect stronger dispersion forces to higher boiling point.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students think that the low boiling point is due to the London force which is indeed very weak and is not related to the number of electrons"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.concept_category: strength of IMFs and effect on boiling point
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: HCl molecules are polar, so the interaction between HCl molecules is simply a polar intermolecular force.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole forces are attractions between the opposite partial charges of neighboring polar molecules; naming a substance as polar is not yet an explanation of the specific intermolecular interaction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify partial positive and partial negative ends on adjacent polar molecules and explain the attraction between them.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "HCI molecules are polar molecules, so the interaction between HCI molecules is a polar intermolecular force"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: H atoms are positive atoms and Cl atoms are negative atoms, producing attractive forces.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Partial charges in HCl arise from unequal electron sharing, but atoms are not fully positive or fully negative; dipole-dipole attraction is between partial charges of separate polar molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use electronegativity to assign partial charges and then describe attraction between the positive end of one molecule and the negative end of another, not between fully charged atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "H atoms as positive atoms and Cl as negative atoms produce attractive forces"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A polar molecule has a positive dipole and negative dipole in the polar region.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A polar molecule has regions of partial positive and partial negative charge, and dipole-dipole forces are attractions between these regions on neighboring molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should understand dipoles as separated centers of partial charge, not as two independent 'positive' and 'negative' dipoles within one region.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "This polar molecule has a positive dipole and negative dipole in the polar region"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Polar molecules have permanent dipoles so that positive dipoles will bind to negative dipoles.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Polar molecules have permanent molecular dipoles, and dipole-dipole attraction occurs between the partial positive end of one molecule and the partial negative end of another molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should describe the interaction as attraction between opposite partial charges on different molecules rather than using the phrase 'positive dipoles bind to negative dipoles'.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Polar molecules have permanent dipoles so that positive dipoles will bind to negative dipoles."
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonds are formed due to shared electron usage.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction involving H bonded to N, O, or F interacting with a lone pair on another electronegative atom; it is not the covalent sharing of electrons within a bond.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish covalent electron sharing inside a molecule from hydrogen bonding between molecules based on electronegativity and lone pairs.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonds are formed due to shared electron usage"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonds occur between N and H atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding occurs when H bonded to N, O, or F in one molecule interacts with a lone pair on N, O, or F in another molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify both the donor atom bonded to H and the acceptor lone pair on a neighboring molecule, rather than describing it as simply between N and H atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonds occur between N and H atoms"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonds use PEB for bonding.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is based on electrostatic attraction between a hydrogen attached to N, O, or F and a lone pair on another molecule, not a generic 'PEB' concept as a bonding type.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain the specific donor-acceptor interaction involved in hydrogen bonding rather than using an unsupported abbreviation or vague bonding label.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonds uses PEB fot bonding"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonds occur between atoms in a molecule, not intermolecular.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular force between molecules, not a bond within one molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine whether the interaction is within one molecule or between separate molecules; hydrogen bonding is between molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students define that hydrogen bonds occur between atoms in a molecule, not intermolecular"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The difference in electronegativity of covalent compounds affects the boiling point.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point depends on the strength of intermolecular forces present; electronegativity differences matter insofar as they influence molecular polarity and hydrogen bonding, but boiling point is not directly determined by covalent bond electronegativity differences alone.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should link molecular structure and polarity to intermolecular forces, then connect those forces to boiling point.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students assume that the difference in electronegativity of covalent compounds affects the boiling point."
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The strength of the hydrogen bond is affected by the difference in electronegativity between H and N, O, and F.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bond strength depends on the polarity of the H-X bond and the availability of a lone pair on a neighboring electronegative atom, along with molecular environment; it is not simply a direct function of electronegativity difference alone.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should consider the donor-acceptor geometry and the intermolecular context, not only the electronegativity difference between atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The strength of the hydrogen bond is affected by the difference in electronegativity between H and the elements N, O, and F."
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bond strength is affected by PEB.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bond strength depends on the intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen donor and an electronegative acceptor, not on a vague PEB factor.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should base the explanation on donor-acceptor interactions and molecular structure, rather than an unsupported abbreviation or unrelated factor.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bond strength is affected by PEB"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The strength of hydrogen bonds is related to the acidity of the substance.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bond strength is not the same as acidity; acidity concerns proton donation, whereas hydrogen bonding concerns intermolecular attraction involving H attached to N, O, or F and a lone pair on another molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate acid-base behavior from intermolecular attraction and not use acidity as the basis for hydrogen bond strength.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The strength of hydrogen bonds is related to the acidity of the substance"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonding occurs at the H atom with one of the F, O, and N atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding occurs between H bonded to N, O, or F in one molecule and a lone pair on N, O, or F in another molecule, not simply at an H atom with one of those atoms in the same molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify hydrogen bonding as an intermolecular donor-acceptor interaction and specify the two molecules involved.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students assume that hydrogen bonding occurs at the H atom with one of the F, O, and, N atoms."
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonding occurs between O and H atoms in ether molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ethers do not hydrogen bond to each other as donors because they lack an O-H bond; oxygen in ether can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor but not a donor.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check whether the molecule has an H attached to O, N, or F to donate a hydrogen bond and whether another molecule has a lone-pair acceptor.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonding occurs between O and H atoms in ether molecules"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The bond between H and O in an alcohol molecule is a hydrogen bond.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The H-O bond within an alcohol is a covalent intramolecular bond; hydrogen bonding is the intermolecular attraction between alcohol molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish the covalent O-H bond inside the alcohol from the hydrogen bond that forms between the hydrogen of one molecule and the oxygen lone pair of another.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The bond between the elements H and O in the alcohol molecule is a hydrogen bond"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonding is present in the OH group of polar molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is not determined just by the presence of an OH group or polarity; it requires a hydrogen attached to N, O, or F and an acceptor lone pair on a neighboring molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate both donor and acceptor requirements and remember that not every polar molecule with an OH group necessarily participates in hydrogen bonding the same way.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonding is present in the OH group of polar molecules"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonding occurs in methane (C and H atoms).
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Methane does not form hydrogen bonds because H is bonded to carbon, not to N, O, or F, and methane lacks a sufficiently electronegative donor/acceptor system for hydrogen bonding.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check the identity of the atom bonded to hydrogen and apply the rule that hydrogen bonding requires H attached to N, O, or F.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonding occurs in methane (C and H atoms)"
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students in a general chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students attribute the yellowish-green colour of chlorine to chlorine atoms or chlorine molecules rather than to the macroscopic substance.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The colour is a macroscopic property of chlorine gas, not of isolated chlorine atoms or molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should distinguish the substance level from the particle level and explain colour as a property of the bulk sample under the given conditions, not as a property of individual atoms or molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the yellowish green colour of chlorine is due to chlorine atoms"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 8.5% secondary school; 15.2% university for chlorine molecules; 8.5% secondary school for chlorine atoms
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the water molecule itself has a boiling point of 100 °C.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point is a property of the substance water, not of a single molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason that phase change temperatures describe the bulk substance at a given pressure, so the correct statement refers to liquid water as a substance.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The water molecule has a boiling point of 100 °C at 1-atm pressure."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 10.0% secondary school
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe branched organic compounds have stronger Van der Waals forces than straight-chain isomers.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: For isomeric hydrocarbons, a less branched structure usually has greater surface contact and stronger intermolecular dispersion forces, giving a higher boiling point.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should compare molecular shape and surface area: greater contact surface allows stronger dispersion interactions, so the straight-chain isomer boils higher than the branched one.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Van der Waals forces are more intense in branching organic compounds."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 34.0% secondary school
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think Van der Waals forces become more intense simply as molar mass increases.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point depends on several factors, including surface area and molecular shape; molar mass alone does not determine intermolecular-force strength in such comparisons.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should compare the specific structural features of the molecules rather than using only molar mass; for isomers with equal molar mass, shape and contact area affect dispersion forces.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Van der Waals forces are more intense as molar mass increases."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 8.0% secondary school; 23.0% university
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe sodium iodide can dissolve in nonpolar solvents or that NaI is a molecule that dissolves there.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ionic sodium iodide dissolves in polar solvents such as water because ion-dipole interactions stabilize the ions in solution.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify NaI as an ionic compound, then match it with polar solvents that can solvate and stabilize separated ions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The NaI molecules can be dissolved in nonpolar solvents."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 10.0% secondary school
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think solid or molten/dissolved NaCl conducts because it has free electrons like a metal.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: NaCl conducts when molten or dissolved because ions are mobile charges; in the solid, ions are fixed in the lattice.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should distinguish metallic conduction from ionic conduction and reason that electrical current in ionic compounds is carried by moving ions, not electrons.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "NaCl solid, molten or in solution, has free electrons that conduct electricity."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 22.0% secondary school; 13.0% university
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think NaCl exists as a molecule that dissociates into ions which conduct electricity.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: NaCl is an ionic compound made of ions in a lattice; when molten or dissolved, the ions become mobile and conduct electricity.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify the substance as an ionic lattice rather than a molecule, and explain conduction by the movement of ions in the molten or aqueous state.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "NaCl molecule, molten or in solution, dissociates into a sodium ion and a chloride ion which are the conductors of the electric current."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 14.0% secondary school; 11.0% university
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe graphite conducts electricity because its layers can slide over each other.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Graphite conducts because of delocalized electrons within layers, not because layers slide.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect conductivity to mobile charged particles; in graphite, delocalized electrons are available for charge transport.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Graphite conducts electricity because the layers of hexagonal carbon rings can slide over each other."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 22.0% secondary school
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe graphite conducts because its layers are bonded by Van der Waals forces.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Graphite conducts due to delocalized electrons in its structure, while Van der Waals forces are not the reason for conductivity.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify the charge carriers in graphite as delocalized electrons and not confuse weak intermolecular forces with electrical conduction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Graphite conducts electricity because the layers of hexagonal carbon rings are bonded by Van der Waals forces."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 20.0% secondary school; 12.0% university
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe diamond conducts electricity because it is a covalent 3D network with free electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Diamond does not conduct electricity because its electrons are localized in covalent bonds and there are no mobile charge carriers.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should distinguish diamond from graphite and reason that a covalent network does not automatically imply conductivity; mobile electrons or ions are needed.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Diamond conducts electricity because is a three-dimensional network with covalent bonds between carbon atoms. Electrons are free and can conduct electrical current."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 13.0% secondary school
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think NaCl is a molecular substance.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: NaCl is an ionic compound composed of ions in a lattice, not molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should classify NaCl by the presence of ions and ionic lattice structure, not by imagining discrete molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "NaCl is a molecular substance."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 16.0% secondary school
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonds form in any molecule that contains H together with F, N, or O, even if H is not directly bonded to those atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A hydrogen bond requires hydrogen directly bonded to N, O, or F and attraction to a lone pair on another electronegative atom.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should check the bonding environment: only H attached to N/O/F can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and an acceptor atom with lone pairs is needed.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "H atoms plus atoms of N, or O or F"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 19.0% secondary school; 16.0% university
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonds are stronger in compounds with nitrogen because nitrogen is more electronegative than oxygen.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: For the comparison in the paper, ethanol has stronger hydrogen bonding than ethylamine because oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should compare the electronegativity of the atom bonded to hydrogen and the resulting hydrogen-bond strength, using the given molecules and their donor atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "N atom is more electronegative than O"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 15.0% secondary school
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonds are stronger in compounds containing more hydrogen atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen-bond strength depends on electronegativity and the donor-acceptor interaction, not simply on the number of hydrogen atoms present.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should focus on the nature of the hydrogen bond-forming atoms and the interaction, rather than counting hydrogens in the formula.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "containing more hydrogen atoms"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 13.0% secondary school
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think iodine is a molecular substance whose covalent bonds between iodine atoms are broken at the boiling point.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: At the boiling point, intermolecular forces are overcome; covalent bonds within molecules are not broken for molecular iodine.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should distinguish intramolecular covalent bonds from intermolecular forces and know that boiling separates molecules, not atoms within molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "iodine is a molecular substance with covalent bonds between iodine atoms that are broken at the boiling point"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 34.2% secondary school; 19.2% university
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students classify HF as covalent simply because it consists of two non-metals sharing electrons, ignoring intermolecular forces and the substance type.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: HF is a molecular substance with covalent H–F bonds between atoms and intermolecular forces, including van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonding, between molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should classify the substance by both intra- and intermolecular forces and not stop at the fact that the atoms share electrons.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "HF is a covalent substance since consists of two non-metallic elements bonded by sharing electrons."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 27.8% secondary school; 8.0% university
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students classify HF as ionic because of the electronegativity difference between H and F.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: HF is not ionic; it is a polar covalent molecular substance with hydrogen bonding between molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use electronegativity difference to judge bond polarity, but also recognize that H–F is still covalent rather than ionic.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "HF is an ionic substance since the difference in electronegativity of H and F atoms allows establishing and ionic bond."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 15.2% secondary school; 9.0% university
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think SiO2 is a molecular substance because it is made of two non-metallic elements linked by covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SiO2 is a covalent network solid, not a molecular substance.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should recognize that covalent bonding can extend in a network, so the presence of covalent bonds does not imply discrete molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "SiO2 is a molecular substance since it consists of two non-metallic elements linked by covalent bonds."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 29.0% secondary school; 17.2% university
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students identify the arrangement of electron pairs around the central atom with the geometry of the molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular geometry is the spatial arrangement of the atoms (nuclei) around the central atom; electron-pair arrangement determines it but is not the same as the molecular shape.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should first determine Lewis structure and electron-pair arrangement, then derive the actual molecular shape from atomic positions and bond angles.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Identify the arrangement of electron pairs around the central atom with the geometry of the molecule."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 19.0% secondary school
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students attribute the shape of a molecule to the electron pairs, both lone and bonded, rather than to the atom arrangement.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The shape of a molecule is the spatial arrangement of atoms around the central atom, while lone and bonded electron pairs are used to predict it.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should distinguish electron-pair geometry from molecular geometry and use the latter to describe the positions of atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Attribute the shape of the molecule to the electron pairs, both lone and bonded."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 50.6% secondary school; 83.8% university
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think bond polarity determines the shape of a molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond polarity influences molecular polarity, but molecular shape is determined by the arrangement of electron pairs and the positions of atoms.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should separate the question of molecular geometry from the question of whether bonds are polar; geometry comes from electron-pair repulsions and atom positions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Bond polarity determines the shape of a molecule."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 15.2% secondary school
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assume tetrahedral geometry is enough to cancel bond dipoles regardless of the atoms attached to the central atom.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Polarity depends on both molecular geometry and the identity/polarity of the bonds; tetrahedral geometry alone does not guarantee nonpolarity.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should evaluate the symmetry of the whole molecule and the nature of the substituent atoms before concluding that dipoles cancel.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "tetrahedral geometry is a necessary and sufficient condition to cancel the bond dipole moments regardless of the atoms bonded to the central atom."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 21.5% secondary school; 15.2% university
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students identify the Lewis structure with the molecular shape and make wrong predictions of geometry and polarity.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lewis structure is used to infer electron-pair arrangement and then molecular geometry and polarity, but it is not itself the molecular shape.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should derive the Lewis structure first, then use it to determine electron-pair geometry, molecular geometry, and polarity separately.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Identify the Lewis structure with the shape of the molecule and make wrong predictions of the geometry and polarity of molecules."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 15.0% secondary school
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think H2S is linear because the two lone pairs are balanced and the resultant dipole moment is zero.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: H2S is bent; lone pairs affect its geometry, but they do not make it linear or necessarily zero-dipole by simple balancing.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use VSEPR to determine that electron pairs around sulfur produce a bent molecular geometry, then assess polarity from the actual geometry and bond dipoles.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "H2S molecule is linear because the two lone electron pairs are balanced and the resultant dipole moment is zero."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 10.0% secondary school
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe any molecule with lone electron pairs is polar.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and molecular geometry; lone pairs do not automatically make a molecule polar.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should determine whether bond dipoles cancel based on the full 3D geometry, not simply count lone pairs.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "All molecules having lone electron pairs are polar."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 25.3% secondary school; 12.0% university
all_misconceptions.population: 79 high school students; 99 first-year university students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student's Misconceptions on Chemical Bonding: A Comparative Study between High School and First Year University Students

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Electrostatic nature and relationship to bonds
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think intermolecular forces are not electrostatic attractions and are fundamentally different from chemical bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are electrostatic attractions, like other chemical bonds, though they involve different particles and are much weaker than conventional bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that attraction between particles is an electrostatic phenomenon. They should compare the interacting particles and see that intermolecular forces are attractions between molecules, not a separate non-electrostatic category.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "intermolecular forces were just another type of chemical bond"
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry students in Singapore (Grades 11 and 12); the paper is textbook analysis, not a direct student interview study.
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analysis of two textbooks on the topic of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think intermolecular forces are not especially weak, or may not distinguish their weakness from covalent, ionic, and metallic bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are much weaker than conventional chemical bonds such as ionic, covalent, and metallic bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare bond types by interaction strength and particle separation, understanding that intermolecular attractions are weaker because the particles are farther apart and the electrical dipoles are weaker.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Vander Waals' bonds are, ofcourse, much weaker than covalent and ionic bonds."
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry students in Singapore (Grades 11 and 12); inferred misconception discussed by the authors.
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analysis of two textbooks on the topic of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think van der Waals forces do not exist between gas particles and therefore do not affect gases.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces act between gas particles too and help explain why real gases deviate from ideal-gas behavior.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should consider that gas particles still attract each other, especially when they are close enough, so deviations from pV = nRT arise from intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students might think that there were no van der Waals forces between gases"
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry students in Singapore (Grades 11 and 12); discussed as a likely student difficulty.
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analysis of two textbooks on the topic of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think boiling breaks intermolecular forces completely so that no intermolecular forces remain in the gas state.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling overcomes enough intermolecular attraction for particles to separate into the gas phase, but it does not mean intermolecular forces cease to exist as a concept for gases.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between overcoming attractions during a phase change and the general presence of weak attractions between particles under all conditions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "could gtve students the itnpression that when a liquid was boiled, intermolecular forces would be broken resulting in no intermolecular forces between the particles in a gas"
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry students in Singapore (Grades 11 and 12); inferred from textbook language.
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analysis of two textbooks on the topic of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think molecular polarity can be identified without using the vector sum of bond dipoles and molecular geometry, or may not use net dipole moment to predict polarity.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A molecule is polar when its bond dipoles do not cancel; molecular geometry must be considered through VSEPR and the vector sum of dipole moments to determine the net dipole moment.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first determine the molecular shape using VSEPR, then identify individual bond dipoles from electronegativity differences, and finally add them vectorially to decide whether the molecule has a net dipole moment.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the net dipole moment of a molecule"
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry students in Singapore (Grades 11 and 12); identified as a missing concept likely to contribute to misconceptions.
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analysis of two textbooks on the topic of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think bond polarity is not connected to electronegativity differences and displacement of shared electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Differences in electronegativity cause unequal sharing of bonding electrons, creating a polar bond with a dipole moment.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the electronegativities of the bonded atoms, infer electron density shift toward the more electronegative atom, and then conclude that the bond is polar.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Differences in electronegativity between two atoms cause the displacement of the shared electrons between them."
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry students in Singapore (Grades 11 and 12); treated as essential but insufficiently integrated content.
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analysis of two textbooks on the topic of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think hydrogen bonding is simply a generic strong intermolecular attraction rather than a specific interaction involving H bonded to N, O, or F and attraction to a lone pair on another N, O, or F.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is a specific interaction between an electron-deficient H attached to N, O, or F and a lone pair on another N, O, or F atom.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the donor atom bonded to H, the acceptor atom with a lone pair, and recognize the special requirement for N, O, or F in hydrogen bonding.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonding is defined as the attraction of an electron deficient hydrogen atom"
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry students in Singapore (Grades 11 and 12); the paper discusses likely misconceptions from textbook treatment.
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analysis of two textbooks on the topic of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Strength ranking among HF, H2O, and NH3
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think hydrogen-bond strength follows the same order as bond polarity alone, or that water should have the strongest hydrogen bonding because it forms the highest boiling point.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen-bond strength depends on both bond polarity and lone-pair availability; in the paper’s cited comparison the strength order is HF > H2O > NH3, while water’s highest boiling point is due to more extensive hydrogen bonding, not stronger individual hydrogen bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare both donor bond polarity and acceptor lone-pair availability, then separately consider how many hydrogen bonds each molecule can form to explain boiling point trends.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The strength of the hydrogen bonding as follows: H-F>H-O>H-N"
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry students in Singapore (Grades 11 and 12); discussed as a possible student at a loss when comparing boiling points.
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analysis of two textbooks on the topic of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think the substance with the strongest hydrogen bonding must always have the highest boiling point.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point depends on the overall extent and pattern of intermolecular attractions, not only on the strength of an individual hydrogen bond; water’s higher boiling point is due to more extensive hydrogen bonding network formation.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare both bond strength and the number of hydrogen bonds each molecule can form per molecule, then use that to explain the macroscopic boiling point trend.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "water had the highest boiling point of the three substances based only on the strength of hydrogen bonding"
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry students in Singapore (Grades 11 and 12); explicitly discussed by the authors.
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analysis of two textbooks on the topic of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think hydrogen bonding is only intermolecular and may not recognize intramolecular hydrogen bonding when groups capable of hydrogen bonding are close together.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding can be intramolecular as well as intermolecular, depending on molecular structure and proximity of donor and acceptor sites.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should inspect the molecular structure to determine whether H-bond donors and acceptors can interact within the same molecule or between different molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonding can be intermolecular or intramolecular in nature."
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry students in Singapore (Grades 11 and 12); discussed as a topic insufficiently covered.
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analysis of two textbooks on the topic of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Intramolecular hydrogen bonding effect on properties
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think the presence of hydrogen-bonding groups always increases intermolecular hydrogen bonding and therefore does not reduce boiling or melting points.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intramolecular hydrogen bonding can reduce the number of sites available for intermolecular hydrogen bonding, which can lower boiling point or melting point.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine whether hydrogen bonding is internal to one molecule or between molecules; if internal bonding ties up donor/acceptor sites, fewer intermolecular attractions are possible.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "limit number of sites available for intermolecular hydrogen bonding"
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry students in Singapore (Grades 11 and 12); identified as an omitted idea likely to cause confusion.
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analysis of two textbooks on the topic of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think instantaneous dipole-induced dipole interactions occur only in non-polar molecules and not in polar molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: All molecules, including polar molecules, possess instantaneous dipole-induced dipole interactions; polar molecules also have permanent dipole-permanent dipole interactions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that electron clouds fluctuate in every molecule, so dispersion forces are always present alongside any other intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "instantaneous dipole-induced dipole interactions do exist in polar molecules"
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry students in Singapore (Grades 11 and 12); highlighted as an omitted emphasis in the textbook analysis.
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analysis of two textbooks on the topic of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think the strength of instantaneous dipole-induced dipole interactions depends only on the number of electrons, or only on molecule size/shape, without considering surface area of contact.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The strength of dispersion forces depends on both electron number/polarisability and molecular surface area or contact area.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare electron count and molecular shape/surface area to determine how easily electron clouds are distorted and how much contact can occur between molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The greater the surface area of contact between molecules"
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry students in Singapore (Grades 11 and 12); treated as a likely misconception due to insufficient discussion in the textbooks.
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analysis of two textbooks on the topic of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think instantaneous dipole-induced dipole interactions can never be stronger than hydrogen bonding.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In some cases dispersion forces can be stronger than hydrogen bonding, depending on molecular size, surface area, and polarisability.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare all relevant intermolecular-force contributions rather than assuming one force type is always strongest in every substance.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "instantaneous dipole-induced dipole interactions can stronger be than hydrogen-bonding"
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry students in Singapore (Grades 11 and 12); identified as a missing comparison in the texts.
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analysis of two textbooks on the topic of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: There are only two kinds of bonds: covalent and ionic; anything else is just a force or not a proper bond.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Chemical bonding includes more than just covalent and ionic bonds; metallic bonding is also a real bonding type, and intermolecular forces are different from bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish among covalent, ionic, and metallic bonding, and separately identify intermolecular forces as attractions between molecules rather than as bond types within all substances.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: There are only two kinds of bonds: covalent bonds and ionic bonds. Anything else is just a force
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Electrons are ions, and bonding occurs between electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrons are not ions; chemical bonding involves interactions between atoms/ions, not bonds between electrons themselves.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that ions are charged atoms or groups of atoms, while electrons are subatomic particles. Bonding is explained by electrostatic attraction or electron sharing/transfer between atoms, depending on bond type.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Electrons are ions and bonding occurs between the
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Atoms bond mainly to balance their total charge or because they are 'charged', rather than through electrostatic attraction and lower-energy configurations.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms bond because electrostatic interactions and energy considerations lead to stable bonding arrangements; atoms are not bonding simply to equalize total charge.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that bonding results from attractions between oppositely charged nuclei and electrons, or ions in ionic bonding, and that bonding leads to lower-energy, more stable arrangements such as full valence shells or favorable electrostatic configurations.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: atoms want to balance their total charge and thus bond with other
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Atoms bond because they 'want' to get filled shells, implying a teleological goal rather than an explanation based on electronic structure and stability.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms bond to achieve lower-energy, more stable electron configurations; the octet/duet pattern is an outcome of electronic structure, not a purpose.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect valence electron arrangement and electrostatic stability to bonding, explaining that atoms form bonds because the resulting configuration is energetically favorable.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: to produce filled shells rather than filled shells being the
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Atoms/particles 'want' to give or lose electrons because they desire to lose energy or because shells are 'full'.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electron transfer is explained by energetic and electrostatic considerations, not by particle desire or intention.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain ionic bonding with the tendency of systems to reach a lower-energy, more stable arrangement, not as an action motivated by atoms' intentions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: it desire to lose energy
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A covalent bond is simply the sharing of electrons, with little or no recognition of the electrostatic attraction involved.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A covalent bond is an attractive interaction between nuclei and shared electrons; electron sharing is part of the model, but the bond is the result of electrostatic attraction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should describe covalent bonding as shared electron density between atoms that creates attraction between nuclei and the shared electron pair, stabilizing the molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: A covalent bond holds atoms together because the bond is sharing electrons.
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Metals can form covalent bonds with non-metals, so metallic substances are interpreted through covalent bonding ideas.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Metallic bonding is distinct from covalent bonding; metals are held together by metallic bonding, not by covalent bonds with non-metals.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify metallic bonding as a lattice of positive metal ions and delocalized electrons, separate from covalent bonding between non-metal atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: metals such as
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: All covalent bonds are equally shared; bond polarity is determined only by the number of valence electrons or is ignored.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond polarity depends on differences in electronegativity between bonded atoms, leading to unequal sharing of electrons in polar covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare electronegativities of the two atoms to determine whether electrons are shared equally or unequally, which in turn determines bond polarity.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Equal sharing of the electron pair occurs in all covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Molecular shape is due only to repulsion between bonding electron pairs, ignoring the role of lone pairs.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular shape is determined by repulsions among all electron pairs around the central atom, including bonding and lone pairs.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should count both bonding and non-bonding electron pairs around the central atom and use electron-pair repulsion to predict molecular geometry.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: molecules due only to the repulsion between the bonding electron pairs.
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A molecule is polar simply because it contains polar bonds, or nonpolar molecules are those with atoms of similar electronegativity.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular polarity depends on the vector sum of bond dipoles and molecular geometry; polar bonds do not always make a polar molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine bond polarity from electronegativity differences and then consider the symmetry of the molecular shape to decide whether dipoles cancel or produce a net molecular dipole.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: molecule is polar because it has polar bonds.
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Nitrogen and other atoms can share electron pairs without regard to the octet rule, or students treat the octet rule as allowing incorrect bonding patterns.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms in main-group covalent molecules generally seek stable valence shells consistent with the octet rule, with known exceptions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should count valence electrons, determine how many electrons each atom needs to complete its valence shell, and then use that to predict the number of shared electron pairs and likely bonding pattern.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Nitrogen atoms can share five electron pairs in bonding.
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Molecular solids are interpreted as continuous covalent lattices with strong bonds, or as made of discrete molecular species in all network solids.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Covalent network solids consist of atoms linked in extended networks; molecular solids are made of discrete molecules held together by intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between a molecular solid and a network covalent solid by identifying whether the solid consists of discrete molecules or an extended lattice of atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: molecular solids is due to strong bonds in the continuous covalent lattices.
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Graphite conducts electricity because it has layers of carbon atoms that can slip over each other, linking conductivity to physical sliding rather than delocalized electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Graphite conducts electricity because it contains delocalized electrons that can move through the structure.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the presence of mobile electrons in graphite's layered structure and connect those electrons to electrical conduction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Graphite conducts electricity because it has layers of carbon ato
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Ionic substances are made of discrete molecules or ion pairs such as Na+ and Cl− units.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ionic substances form extended ionic lattices of oppositely charged ions, not discrete molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that ionic compounds are held together in a crystal lattice by electrostatic attractions among many ions, so formulas like NaCl represent ratios, not molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Ionic substances are discrete
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Number of ionic bonds in lattices
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: An ion forms only one ionic bond, usually to the atom/ion involved in electron transfer.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In an ionic lattice, each ion interacts electrostatically with multiple surrounding ions; ionic bonding is not a one-to-one bond.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that lattice ions are surrounded by several oppositely charged ions and that bonding in ionic solids is a network of attractions rather than discrete pairwise bonds.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: An ionic bond only occurs between the ato
all_misconceptions.concept_category: number of ionic bonding in lattices
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Bonds exist only for the specific ion pair that exchanged electrons with each other.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In ionic lattices, ions are attracted to multiple counter-ions; bonding is not limited to the original electron-transfer pair.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should understand that after electron transfer, ions become part of a lattice in which each ion is surrounded by many oppositely charged ions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Bonds are only for
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Ionic interactions are 'just forces' and not real bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ionic bonding is a real electrostatic bond arising from attraction between oppositely charged ions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain ionic bonding as mutual electrostatic attraction in a lattice, not as something weaker or qualitatively different from bonding.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Ionic bonds are not real bonds in the sense of covalent bonds
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The result of ionic bonding is neutralization or the canceling of charges leading to discrete neutral molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ionic bonding forms electrically neutral formula units within an extended ionic lattice; ions remain charged and are held together by electrostatic attraction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that electron transfer creates ions that attract one another in a lattice, while the compound as a whole is neutral because charges balance in the formula unit.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: The result of the attraction between the two oppositely charged ions
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Ionic bonding is the transfer of electrons rather than the attraction of ions that results after transfer; electron transfer is the bond itself.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electron transfer produces ions, and ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between the resulting ions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate the process of electron transfer from the bonding force: transfer creates charged ions, and attraction between those ions constitutes the bond.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Ionic bonds are the transfer of electrons, rather than the attractions of the ions that result from the transfer of electrons.
all_misconceptions.concept_category: transfer of electrons in ionic bonding
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A sodium atom can only form one ionic bond because it has only one valence electron to donate.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ionic bonding in solids is not limited to a single one-to-one bond; an ion can attract many oppositely charged ions in the lattice.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect valence electron donation to ion formation, then understand that the resulting ion participates in multiple lattice attractions rather than a single bond.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: A sodium atom can only form one ionic bond, because it only has one electron in its outer shell to donate
all_misconceptions.concept_category: number of ionic bonding in lattices
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Metals are molecular in nature, and metallic bonding is not a real bond like covalent bonding.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Metallic bonding is a real bonding type in which metal cations are held together by delocalized electrons in an extended lattice.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should describe metals as non-molecular, with positive metal ions in a lattice and delocalized electrons providing cohesion and conductivity.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Metals are
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Intermolecular forces are the forces within a molecule or within a continuous covalent solid.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces act between molecules; intramolecular forces act within molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish whether an attraction is holding atoms together inside a molecule or attracting separate molecules to one another.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: students often incorrectly identify intermolecular forces as the forces within a molecule or continuous covalent solid
all_misconceptions.concept_category: general alternative conceptions on intermolecular forces
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Intermolecular forces are the same as covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are weaker attractions between molecules and are different from the covalent bonds inside molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the location and strength of the interactions, recognizing that covalent bonds hold atoms together within a molecule while intermolecular forces hold molecules together.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: equate intermolecular forces with covalent bonds
all_misconceptions.concept_category: general alternative conceptions on intermolecular forces
all_misconceptions.source_title: A review of chemical bonding studies: needs, aims, methods of exploring students' conceptions, general knowledge claims and students' alternative conceptions
