all_misconceptions.topic: Conservation of matter in chemical reactions
all_misconceptions.subtopic: Mass, atoms, and molecules before and after reaction
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe mass can change during a chemical reaction, or that the number of molecules must stay the same, or that atoms and moles are simply proportional in a way that ignores conservation of atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In a chemical reaction, total mass is conserved in a closed system and the number of atoms of each element is conserved, although the number of molecules may change as new substances form.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify that chemical reactions rearrange atoms into new molecules without creating or destroying atoms. Therefore, the mass of the system and the number of each type of atom stay the same, while molecule count may change depending on the reaction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Mass can change after chemical reaction"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Q1 pre-survey: 20% NPU; 30% PSM; 50% PSU. Also, 10% of all students selected the correct option but lacked a sound explanation.
all_misconceptions.population: CHEM 115/115L students, Fall 2018 (N=10 pre-survey; N=8 post-survey)
all_misconceptions.source_file: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and/College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and the Impact on Research Instrumentation

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Identity of gas in boiling water
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the bubbles in boiling water are air, oxygen gas, hydrogen gas, oxygen, or heat instead of water vapor.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The bubbles are water vapor (steam), i.e. gaseous water produced during boiling.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that heating liquid water gives water molecules enough energy to enter the gas phase; the bubbles are composed of water molecules, not air or decomposition products.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "25% of their sample of 17-year-old chemistry students thought that the bubbles in boiling water were made of air"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: The paper cites prior studies and also reports student responses on Q2; in the present study, Q2 had 50% PSU and 50% PSM in the pre-survey.
all_misconceptions.population: Prior study cited in the paper: 17-year-old chemistry students; present study: CHEM 115/115L students
all_misconceptions.source_file: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and/College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and the Impact on Research Instrumentation

all_misconceptions.topic: Chemical reaction stoichiometry and particle count
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students identify only the product formula or give an incorrect atom ratio, failing to determine how many S and O atoms are present after the reaction. Some wrote formulas such as '2SO3' without evaluating the reactant ratio, or treated the product as just a rearrangement of listed atoms without checking stoichiometric limits.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should use the balanced equation 2S + 3O2 → 2SO3 to determine the product and the number of leftover atoms/molecules from the limiting reactant relationship.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should count atoms on both sides of the balanced equation, apply the 2:3 stoichiometric ratio, and determine how many SO3 units can form and what remains unreacted.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "It represents 2SO3"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Q3 pre-survey: 20% NPU; 50% PSM; 30% PSU. The most frequently selected answer was the wrong option for 50% of students.
all_misconceptions.population: CHEM 115/115L students, Fall 2018
all_misconceptions.source_file: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and/College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and the Impact on Research Instrumentation

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think water 'splits up and combine,' turns into oxygen and hydrogen, or that evaporation means water disappears rather than remaining as water molecules in the gas phase.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Evaporation is a physical change in which water molecules remain H2O but move farther apart and disperse into the gas phase.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain that intermolecular attractions are overcome, molecules separate, and the molecules remain intact as H2O in the vapor phase.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "water split up and combine"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Q4 pre-survey: 40% PSM and 60% PSU; Q6 pre-survey also showed 40% PSM. Interview responses documented this misconception explicitly.
all_misconceptions.population: CHEM 115/115L students, Fall 2018
all_misconceptions.source_file: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and/College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and the Impact on Research Instrumentation

all_misconceptions.subtopic: What happens to water on a drying plate
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe drying water no longer exists, goes into the plate, or changes into oxygen and hydrogen, rather than evaporating as water molecules into the air.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: When water dries, it evaporates into the air as water molecules; the substance remains matter and does not vanish or decompose.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize evaporation as a physical change where liquid water molecules escape into the gas phase, preserving matter.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Water does not exist anymore"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Q6 pre-survey: 10% NPU; 40% PSM; 60% PSU. The paper also notes this as a 'lack of understanding of evaporation.'
all_misconceptions.population: CHEM 115/115L students, Fall 2018
all_misconceptions.source_file: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and/College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and the Impact on Research Instrumentation

all_misconceptions.subtopic: What exists between molecules in a gas
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe there is matter, air, water vapor, atmosphere, or even a bond between oxygen molecules in the space between gas particles, rather than empty space.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Between gas molecules there is mostly empty space; gas particles are separated and do not have matter filling all the space between them.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the particulate model to infer that gas particles are far apart with essentially nothing between them except empty space.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "There is always a matter between oxygen molecules"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Q7 pre-survey: 10% NPU; 20% PSM; 70% PSU. The paper states that some students thought there was something between the molecules.
all_misconceptions.population: CHEM 115/115L students, Fall 2018
all_misconceptions.source_file: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and/College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and the Impact on Research Instrumentation

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Effect of pressure on particle size and motion
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that decreasing pressure makes particles grow larger, that increasing pressure changes particle size, or that pressure changes the number of particles rather than their spacing and motion.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Changing pressure affects the spacing and frequency of collisions among gas particles, not the size of the particles themselves.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that gas particles are essentially incompressible at this level; reduced pressure lets them spread out more, while increased pressure packs them closer together.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Pressure would force the molecules to grow larger"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Q8 pre-survey: 60% PSM and 40% PSU. The paper also notes that some students thought pressure affected molecule size.
all_misconceptions.population: CHEM 115/115L students, Fall 2018
all_misconceptions.source_file: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and/College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and the Impact on Research Instrumentation

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think reduced pressure means particles stop moving, do not spread out, or grow larger instead of becoming more dispersed.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: At lower pressure, gas particles occupy a larger volume and are farther apart while remaining the same particles.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should infer from gas laws and the particle model that lowering pressure increases spacing between particles, not particle size.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The particles wont be moving as fast if pressure is reduced"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Q8 pre-survey and post-survey responses included PSM; the paper discusses pressure-related misconceptions in this item.
all_misconceptions.population: CHEM 115/115L students, Fall 2018
all_misconceptions.source_file: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and/College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and the Impact on Research Instrumentation

all_misconceptions.topic: State of matter in liquids and solids
all_misconceptions.subtopic: Microscopic interpretation of evaporation and boiling
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students explain phase change only at the macroscopic level, for example saying 'all water is evaporated' without referring to particles, or treating evaporation as disappearance of water rather than molecular motion and separation.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A correct explanation of phase change must describe molecular behavior: molecules remain intact and move into the gas phase with increased spacing and motion.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the visible disappearance of liquid to particle-level motion and intermolecular forces, not to disappearance of matter.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "All water is evaporated"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Discussed in the Q4 interview analysis as an example of a student lacking PNM-level explanation.
all_misconceptions.population: CHEM 115/115L students, Fall 2018
all_misconceptions.concept_category: phase change / macroscopic vs microscopic reasoning
all_misconceptions.source_file: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and/College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: College Students Conceptions of Particulate Nature of Matter and the Impact on Research Instrumentation

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A hydrogen bond is a covalent bond, or a bond formed by hydrogen with another atom as if it were an intramolecular covalent bond.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom and a nearby electronegative atom with a lone pair; it is not itself a covalent bond.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the donor atom bonded to H, recognize the partial positive charge on H and partial negative charge/lone pair on the acceptor, and explain the attraction between molecules rather than drawing a new covalent bond.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the majority of the students who gave the wrong answer in the pretest and all the students who gave the wrong answer in the posttest depicted the hydrogen bond as a covalent bond in their drawing."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 31 students in the pretest; 8 students in the posttest (wrong answers to Q1A)
all_misconceptions.population: 52 grade 12 Turkish students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Scientific Argumentation in Teaching Hydrogen Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonding occurs only when hydrogen is bonded to fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen, and only these atoms can participate.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is not restricted to only F, O, or N; it can occur with other electronegative atoms or groups, and the key condition is a hydrogen attached to an electronegative atom interacting with a nearby acceptor.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should examine the polarity of the bond and the availability of lone pairs/partial charges, rather than memorizing only the NOF list.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "they defined the bond over water, hydrogen fluoride, and ammonia molecules and defined the bond as weak interactions occurring intermolecule between fluoride, oxygen, and nitrogen atoms and hydrogen atom."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 18 students in the pretests; 15 students in the posttests used surface-level symbolic representations without moving beyond this idea
all_misconceptions.population: 52 grade 12 Turkish students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Scientific Argumentation in Teaching Hydrogen Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot identify which atom is the hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor and instead treat hydrogen bonding as merely an attraction between hydrogen and any electronegative atom.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The hydrogen-bond donor is the X–H group where X is electronegative, and the acceptor is a nearby electronegative atom with a lone pair; the acceptor is not just any atom in the molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine where hydrogen is covalently bonded, then locate the nearby lone-pair-bearing electronegative atom that attracts the δ+ hydrogen.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "they were unable to identify the hydrogen donor or acceptor atom."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Nearly all students in the pretests and nearly half in the posttests
all_misconceptions.population: 52 grade 12 Turkish students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Scientific Argumentation in Teaching Hydrogen Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonding between two water molecules is formed by a bond between the hydrogen atoms of the two water molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In water, hydrogen bonding is the attraction between the partially positive hydrogen of one molecule and the partially negative oxygen of another molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should mark oxygen as the acceptor and hydrogen as the donor across two molecules, using partial charges and lone pairs.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "four students showed this bond between the hydrogen of two water molecules in the pretests."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 4 students in the pretests
all_misconceptions.population: 52 grade 12 Turkish students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Scientific Argumentation in Teaching Hydrogen Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonding in amines, ethers, aldehydes, or similar organic molecules is not recognized, or students say no hydrogen bond exists when it actually can.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecules such as amines, ethers, alcohols, carboxylic acids, and some aromatic hydroxy compounds can participate in hydrogen bonding when the structural requirements are met.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should inspect the functional group, identify electronegative atoms and lone pairs, and determine whether suitable donor and acceptor sites are present.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The common mistake about these molecules in the pretests was that the hydrogen bond was established between hydrogens in an amine molecule and oxygen in a water molecule."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 15 students identified hydrogen bonding between amine groups; 11 correctly identified with water; common mistake noted in pretests
all_misconceptions.population: 52 grade 12 Turkish students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Scientific Argumentation in Teaching Hydrogen Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Ether molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with one another or with water because students focus only on the absence of an O–H bond.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Although ethers cannot donate hydrogen bonds, their oxygen lone pairs allow them to accept hydrogen bonds from water; they do not hydrogen-bond to each other as donors, but they can interact with water.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish hydrogen-bond donor from acceptor and recognize the acceptor role of the ether oxygen.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "In the pretests, 19 students stated that no hydrogen bond was established between ether molecules, and eight students asserted that no hydrogen bond was established between ether and water molecules."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 19 students (ether-ether); 8 students (ether-water) in pretests
all_misconceptions.population: 52 grade 12 Turkish students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Scientific Argumentation in Teaching Hydrogen Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonding in carboxylic acids is limited to the O–H group only, and the hydrogen of the O–H group in the acid hydrogen-bonds to water oxygen as the only relevant interaction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Carboxylic acids can hydrogen-bond through both donor and acceptor sites; the carbonyl oxygen and hydroxyl hydrogen both matter for intermolecular interactions and interactions with water.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should examine both oxygens and the hydroxyl hydrogen, then use partial charges and lone pairs to decide donor and acceptor roles.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The number of students who showed the hydrogen bond between ethanolic acid within only the OH group was large."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Described as a common error; 19 students stated an acid-water interaction involving the O–H hydrogen and water oxygen
all_misconceptions.population: 52 grade 12 Turkish students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Scientific Argumentation in Teaching Hydrogen Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a hydrogen atom attached to carbon in an organic molecule can form a hydrogen bond with oxygen in another molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A hydrogen bond generally requires hydrogen bonded to a sufficiently electronegative atom such as N, O, or F; C–H is not usually considered an effective hydrogen-bond donor in this context.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check the electronegativity of the atom bonded to H and only treat H as hydrogen-bond donor when the X–H bond is sufficiently polar.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Another misconception some students had was the establishment of a hydrogen bond between the hydrogen (H) atom attached to carbon (C) in organic molecules and oxygen in other molecules."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Not quantified; reported as another misconception in Question 2
all_misconceptions.population: 52 grade 12 Turkish students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Scientific Argumentation in Teaching Hydrogen Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Boiling point differences can be explained only by saying a substance has a stronger hydrogen bond, without connecting this to molecular structure or other factors.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point differences should be explained by comparing molecular structure, polarity, hydrogen-bonding ability, and intermolecular force strength in relation to the actual molecules involved.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify which molecules can hydrogen-bond, compare the number/strength of interactions, and connect that to energy needed for vaporization.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The fact that students presented their warrants for their statements in a, b, c, and d as 'having stronger hydrogen bond' indicated that they understood the establishment of hydrogen bonds between molecules."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Shown as a pattern in Question 2 responses; many students gave only this warrant
all_misconceptions.population: 52 grade 12 Turkish students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Scientific Argumentation in Teaching Hydrogen Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Differences in boiling point or solubility are explained by saying a substance is denser, or that density alone determines molecular attractions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Density is not the fundamental cause of hydrogen bonding or boiling-point differences; the relevant factors are polarity, molecular size, electronegativity, and intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should relate the property to intermolecular interactions and molecular structure rather than to density alone.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "In the pretests, 13 students presented their warrants, mentioning that 'its density is greater' for a, b, and c; however, only four students detailed it..."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 13 students in the pretests used density as a warrant; 4 elaborated
all_misconceptions.population: 52 grade 12 Turkish students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Scientific Argumentation in Teaching Hydrogen Bonding

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Synthetic ordering instead of causal explanation
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students explain properties by memorized order patterns such as 'acid > alcohol > aldehyde' rather than by causal molecular reasoning.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Property comparisons should be justified by underlying molecular structure and intermolecular forces, not by memorized ranking strings.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect each compound’s structure to its hydrogen-bonding ability and polarity, then infer the property trend causally.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "irrelevant answers, such as efficient order, 'acid *>* alcohol > aldehyde' in d, e, and f, were encountered."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Not quantified; reported in the pretests
all_misconceptions.population: 52 grade 12 Turkish students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Scientific Argumentation in Teaching Hydrogen Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assume that if a compound is polar, or if it contains no hydrogen bond, then it must not interact with water or must be more volatile for that reason alone.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Water solubility and volatility depend on the actual intermolecular interactions available, including hydrogen bonding, dipole interactions, and functional groups; polarity alone is not enough.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify possible donor/acceptor sites and compare the strength and number of interactions with water.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The majority of these students stated that it was a polar molecule and that it was more volatile than alcohol as it contained no hydrogen bond."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 19 students stated no hydrogen bond for ether molecules; 8 said no hydrogen bond with water
all_misconceptions.population: 52 grade 12 Turkish students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Scientific Argumentation in Teaching Hydrogen Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: HF is a weak acid because of its strong hydrogen bonding or because boiling point and acidity are directly determined by hydrogen bonding strength alone.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: HF is weak because its dissociation in water is incomplete; hydrogen bonding can contribute to association, but acidity depends on the extent of proton release in water.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intermolecular hydrogen bonding from acid dissociation and use the extent of ionization in water to explain acidity.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonds are stronger than Van der Waals bonds... This special occasion derives from the greater electronegativity compared with that of fluorine"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Presented as Student 10's pretest reasoning
all_misconceptions.population: 52 grade 12 Turkish students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Scientific Argumentation in Teaching Hydrogen Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students can explain London dispersion forces only by naming the attraction from nonpermanent dipoles, without explaining how those dipoles arise.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The origin of London dispersion forces must be explained mechanistically in terms of electron movement creating temporary, nonpermanent dipoles.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect fluctuating electron clouds to temporary charge separation, then show how these induced dipoles lead to attraction between particles.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: they found students could often explain the cause of the attraction (nonpermanent dipoles) but rarely offered the mechanism by which these arise.
all_misconceptions.population: undergraduate students
all_misconceptions.source_file: Enhance explanations of intermolecular forces _ News _ RSC Education/Enhance explanations of intermolecular forces _ News _ RSC Education.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Enhance explanations of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe benzene contains fixed localized double bonds between particular carbon atoms rather than a delocalized bonding system.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In benzene, the pi electrons are delocalized around the ring and no single Lewis structure with fixed double bonds fully represents the molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that benzene is better represented by resonance or delocalized bonding models because all C–C bonds are equivalent and the bonding cannot be captured by one localized double-bond pattern.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “apparently they believed that there were double bonds in benzene.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Secondary school learners; described as a common view, but no count given for this misconception.
all_misconceptions.population: Secondary school learners
all_misconceptions.source_file: Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding/Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Exploring Tertiary Students' Understanding of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think covalent bonding means vague sharing of 'bits' of atoms or undefined material rather than sharing electrons or electron density between nuclei.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Covalent bonding involves sharing electron density, typically a shared pair of electrons, between atoms.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify that the bond is explained by electrons being shared between nuclei, not by atoms sharing unspecified pieces of themselves.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the bonding in molecular iodine as 'strong I think' ... she described the bond as consisting of the overlap of 'bits of iodines'.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in at least one secondary school learner; most learners could not clearly articulate what covalent meant.
all_misconceptions.population: Secondary school learners
all_misconceptions.source_file: Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding/Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Exploring Tertiary Students' Understanding of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the shared electrons are simply 'one from each atom' used to complete shells, without clearly distinguishing between the electron pair as the bond and shell completion as the consequence.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A covalent bond is a shared electron pair; full-shell stability is the result of sharing, not a separate material object being moved around.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain that each atom contributes electrons to a shared pair and that this shared electron density helps achieve a stable valence shell.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “They share two electrons because each of them needs to gain one to get a full shell.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Appeared in the discussion of several learners, especially secondary school learners and undergraduates; exact count not given.
all_misconceptions.population: Secondary school learners and undergraduates
all_misconceptions.source_file: Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding/Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Exploring Tertiary Students' Understanding of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe the number of valence electrons and the number of covalent bonds are the same thing.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Valence electrons are available for bonding, but the number of bonds a species forms is not identical to the number of valence electrons.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between the count of valence electrons and the bonding pattern; electrons may be paired, lone pairs, or involved in single/double bonds depending on structure.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “Some learners believe that the number of valence electrons and number of covalent bonds were one and the same”
all_misconceptions.population: Reported in the literature review as a documented misconception among learners
all_misconceptions.source_file: Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding/Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Exploring Tertiary Students' Understanding of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think non-polar molecules are formed simply between atoms of similar electronegativity, and that molecular polarity is determined by valence electron count, lone pairs, or ionic charge rather than electronegativity difference and geometry.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular polarity depends on bond polarity from electronegativity differences and the vector sum of bond dipoles, together with molecular geometry.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first assess whether each bond is polar from electronegativity differences, then consider the 3D arrangement of the bonds to determine whether dipoles cancel.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the number of valence electrons, the presence of lone pairs of electrons, or ionic charge determine molecular polarity”
all_misconceptions.population: Students reported in prior studies cited by the paper
all_misconceptions.source_file: Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding/Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Exploring Tertiary Students' Understanding of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think attraction between oppositely charged species causes neutralisation rather than bond formation.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Attraction between opposite charges can lead to bond formation; neutralisation is not the correct description of covalent bond formation.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that electrostatic attraction between nuclei and shared electrons stabilizes the bond, rather than assuming charges cancel to 'neutral'.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “attraction between two oppositely charged species was thought to result in neutralisation rather than bond formation”
all_misconceptions.population: Students reported in prior studies cited by the paper
all_misconceptions.source_file: Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding/Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Exploring Tertiary Students' Understanding of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think covalent bond formation involves transfer of electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Covalent bonding involves sharing electrons; electron transfer is characteristic of ionic bonding.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish covalent from ionic bonding by recognizing that covalent bonds are formed by shared electron pairs, not by complete electron transfer.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “believing that covalent bond formation involves the transfer of electrons”
all_misconceptions.population: Students reported in prior studies cited by the paper
all_misconceptions.source_file: Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding/Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Exploring Tertiary Students' Understanding of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Covalent vs ionic substances and models
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students use ball-and-stick models to conclude that the stick is a real individual covalent bond and that ionic substances are molecular in nature.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ball-and-stick models are representations; ionic solids are not molecular substances, and sticks are not physical bond objects.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should interpret models as symbolic representations, not as literal pictures of hidden objects, and should distinguish molecular covalent substances from ionic lattices.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “believing that the stick is an individual chemical covalent bond and that ionic substances are molecular in nature”
all_misconceptions.population: Students reported in prior studies cited by the paper
all_misconceptions.source_file: Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding/Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Exploring Tertiary Students' Understanding of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Bond as physical entity and energetics
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe a chemical bond is a physical entity that is broken to release energy and made by requiring energy input.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond breaking requires energy input and bond formation releases energy; a bond is an interaction, not a physical object.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use energy conservation to reason that making a bond lowers potential energy and releases energy, while breaking a bond raises potential energy and needs energy input.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “learners believed that bond breaking releases energy and bond making involves energy input.”
all_misconceptions.population: Students reported in prior studies cited by the paper
all_misconceptions.source_file: Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding/Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Exploring Tertiary Students' Understanding of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Relative strength of intermolecular and intramolecular forces
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe intermolecular bonding is stronger than intramolecular bonding.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intramolecular covalent bonds are generally much stronger than intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the energy required to break bonds within molecules versus forces between molecules and recognize that intermolecular forces are weaker.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “learners believe intermolecular bonding is stronger than intramolecular bonding”
all_misconceptions.population: Students reported in prior studies cited by the paper
all_misconceptions.source_file: Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding/Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Exploring Tertiary Students' Understanding of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Presence of intermolecular forces in polar substances
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe intermolecular forces are absent in polar molecular substances such as water.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Polar molecules such as water do have intermolecular forces, including hydrogen bonding and dipole-dipole interactions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that polarity creates intermolecular attractions between molecules, especially when H is bonded to highly electronegative atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “believe it is absent in polar molecular substances such as water”
all_misconceptions.population: Students reported in prior studies cited by the paper
all_misconceptions.source_file: Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding/Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Exploring Tertiary Students' Understanding of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students know carbon compounds are tetrahedral only as a rote label but cannot explain why; some treat tetrahedrality as just the default arrangement carbon 'always' has.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Tetrahedral geometry arises from arrangement of electron pairs and hybridized orbitals that minimize repulsion in sp3 environments.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect molecular shape to electron-pair repulsion and orbital arrangement, not merely memorize 'tetrahedral'.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “I know carbon is tetrahederal because carbon is always tetrahedral.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in some undergraduate and graduate learners; exact count not given.
all_misconceptions.population: Graduate learners
all_misconceptions.source_file: Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding/Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Exploring Tertiary Students' Understanding of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think atomic orbitals are 'a myth' or no longer relevant, and use molecular orbital ideas without clearly distinguishing atomic from molecular orbitals.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atomic orbitals are real conceptual entities used to build molecular orbitals; molecular orbitals extend over the whole molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should understand that molecular orbitals are formed from combinations of atomic orbitals, and that the two levels of description are distinct but related.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “atomic orbitals tend to be almost a myth.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in one undergraduate learner's explanation.
all_misconceptions.population: Undergraduate learner
all_misconceptions.source_file: Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding/Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Exploring Tertiary Students' Understanding of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think depiction A or C means there is a fixed double bond between specific carbon atoms, rather than a delocalized aromatic structure.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Benzene has delocalized pi electrons and equivalent C–C bonds; depictions with alternating single and double bonds are limited resonance representations.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should interpret resonance structures as alternative representations of a delocalized system, not as evidence for localized double bonds at fixed positions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “A and C you get the misconception that there's a double bond between two particular carbon atoms.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Seven graduate learners disliked depictions A and C because they implied this misconception.
all_misconceptions.population: Graduate learners
all_misconceptions.source_file: Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding/Exploring Tertiary Students  Understanding of Covalent Bonding.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Exploring Tertiary Students' Understanding of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Any attraction between oppositely charged species is an ionic bond, so Na+ interacting with water is treated as ionic bonding rather than ion-dipole attraction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The attraction between an ion and the partial charges on a polar molecule is an ion-dipole interaction, not an ionic bond.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Identify that water is a polar molecule with a partial negative charge on oxygen; the ion interacts electrostatically with that partial charge, so the correct intermolecular force is ion-dipole rather than bond formation between ions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "any interaction between opposite charged species is ionic bond"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 1: 21 (26%) had misconceptions; 11 (13%) answered correctly with correct explanation.
all_misconceptions.population: 82 first-year chemistry major teacher trainees at the University of Education, Winneba
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teacher Trainees' Alternative Conceptions about Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Na+ binds to water by forming an ionic bond, or water induces a negative charge in sodium and then bonds to it.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Na+ is attracted to the partial negative oxygen end of water through ion-dipole attraction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Reason from molecular polarity: the ion interacts with the negative end of a polar molecule without creating a new ionic bond or inducing charge as the explanation for the force.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the sodium ion will form ionic bond with the negative charge in water molecules and stay together"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 1: part of the 21 (26%) with misconceptions.
all_misconceptions.population: 82 first-year chemistry major teacher trainees at the University of Education, Winneba
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teacher Trainees' Alternative Conceptions about Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: London dispersion forces require a charge to be present to create the temporary instantaneous dipole.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces arise from temporary fluctuations in electron distribution, not from pre-existing charges.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Recognize that electrons are constantly moving; brief uneven electron distribution creates a temporary dipole that induces attraction between molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "a charge should be present to bring about the temporary instantaneous dipole"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 2: 30 (37%) had misconceptions; 20 (24%) showed correct understanding.
all_misconceptions.population: 82 first-year chemistry major teacher trainees at the University of Education, Winneba
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teacher Trainees' Alternative Conceptions about Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: London dispersion forces occur within a single molecule rather than between molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces are intermolecular attractions between separate molecules or particles.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Distinguish intramolecular bonding from intermolecular attraction; LDFs act between neighboring molecules due to instantaneous/induced dipoles.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the students perceived LDFs to occur within a single molecule rather than between molecules"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 2: part of the 30 (37%) with misconceptions.
all_misconceptions.population: 82 first-year chemistry major teacher trainees at the University of Education, Winneba
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teacher Trainees' Alternative Conceptions about Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The major attractive force between I2 molecules is a covalent-ionic interaction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The major attractive force between nonpolar I2 molecules is London dispersion force.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Since I2 molecules are nonpolar, the intermolecular attraction must be dispersion forces caused by temporary dipoles, not covalent or ionic interactions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "covalent–ionic interaction was the major attractive force that existed in different I2 molecules"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 3: 28 (33%) had misconceptions; 33 (40%) showed correct understanding.
all_misconceptions.population: 82 first-year chemistry major teacher trainees at the University of Education, Winneba
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teacher Trainees' Alternative Conceptions about Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Any molecule containing O and H forms hydrogen bonding, regardless of whether H is directly bonded to O in the molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires hydrogen to be directly bonded to an electronegative atom such as O, N, or F, and then interact with a lone pair on another electronegative atom.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Check the structural arrangement: H must be covalently attached to O/N/F; simply having O and H somewhere in the formula is not sufficient.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "hydrogen bonding in the given species occurred between hydrogen and oxygen atoms"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 4: 43 (53%) had misconceptions; 29 (35%) showed good understanding.
all_misconceptions.population: 82 first-year chemistry major teacher trainees at the University of Education, Winneba
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teacher Trainees' Alternative Conceptions about Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonding only occurs between O and H, not between N-H and F-H.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding can occur when H is directly bonded to O, N, or F.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Identify all three electronegative atoms that support hydrogen bonding; if hydrogen is attached to N or F, hydrogen bonding is also possible.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonding only occurs between 'O' and 'H' but not between N-H and F-H."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Listed among the major findings; reported in Question 4 misconceptions (43 students, 53%).
all_misconceptions.population: 82 first-year chemistry major teacher trainees at the University of Education, Winneba
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teacher Trainees' Alternative Conceptions about Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A molecule's atomic number predicts the strength of London dispersion force and therefore its boiling point.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion force generally increases with molecular size/molar mass and number of electrons, not simply atomic number.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Compare the molecules by electron count and polarizability; larger, more electron-rich nonpolar molecules have stronger dispersion forces and higher boiling points.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Atomic number predicts the strength of London dispersion force."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 5: 30 (37%) demonstrated misconceptions; 28 (34%) showed correct understanding.
all_misconceptions.population: 82 first-year chemistry major teacher trainees at the University of Education, Winneba
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teacher Trainees' Alternative Conceptions about Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.subtopic: London dispersion, dipole-dipole, and hydrogen bonding
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not distinguish among the three intermolecular force types and may treat them as interchangeable or as simple memorized labels rather than forces with different mechanisms and criteria for occurrence.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces, dipole-dipole interactions, and hydrogen bonding are distinct intermolecular forces with different causes and different conditions for when they occur.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the kind of particles present, determine whether bonds are polar, whether the molecule is polar, and then decide which intermolecular forces are possible based on those features before ranking their relative strengths.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: The emphasis is on three such forces - London dispersion forces, dipoledipole interactions, and hydrogen bonding.
all_misconceptions.source_file: Intermolecular Forces - Teacher Notes/Intermolecular Forces - Teacher Notes.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching Ideas and Suggestions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think that identifying intermolecular forces can be done without first determining whether bonds are polar and whether the molecule is polar or nonpolar.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: To identify intermolecular forces, students must first analyze Lewis structures and electronegativity to determine bond polarity and molecular polarity.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use a Lewis structure and electronegativity differences to decide if polar bonds are present, then use the molecular geometry to decide if the molecule is polar or nonpolar, and only then infer the intermolecular forces present.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Students will have to use a Lewis structure (provided) and an electronegativity table to determine the presence/absence of polar bonds and whether the substance consists of polar or nonpolar molecules.
all_misconceptions.source_file: Intermolecular Forces - Teacher Notes/Intermolecular Forces - Teacher Notes.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching Ideas and Suggestions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may believe the relative strength of intermolecular forces can be ranked directly from formulas alone without analyzing the type of forces present in the substances.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ranking intermolecular force strength requires determining which intermolecular forces are present in each substance, then comparing their relative strengths.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should infer the intermolecular forces from structure and polarity, and then compare those forces to rank the substances from weakest to strongest.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Finally, students will need to be able to rank the relative strength of the intermolecular forces for three susbtances if given their formulas.
all_misconceptions.source_file: Intermolecular Forces - Teacher Notes/Intermolecular Forces - Teacher Notes.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching Ideas and Suggestions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The temperature of a material changes during phase change.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: During a phase change, added energy goes into changing particle arrangement/intermolecular attractions rather than changing temperature.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that while a substance is melting or boiling, the temperature can remain constant because the energy input is used to overcome intermolecular attractions (increase potential energy) instead of increasing kinetic energy.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The temperature of a material changes during phase change."
all_misconceptions.population: students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: When you get something hot enough it will always turn into a gas.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Whether a substance becomes a gas depends on temperature and pressure; at high enough pressure or near the critical point, a substance may not simply become a normal gas and can exist as a supercritical fluid.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that heating increases particle kinetic energy, but pressure and intermolecular attraction also matter. At certain pressure-temperature conditions, the substance may boil, reach a critical point, or behave as a supercritical fluid rather than always becoming a gas.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "When you get something hot enough it will always turn into a gas."
all_misconceptions.population: students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Pressure doesn't matter for boiling temperature or state of matter.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point and state of matter depend on pressure as well as temperature; lowering pressure lowers boiling point.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that liquids boil when vapor pressure equals external pressure, so changing external pressure changes the temperature at which boiling occurs.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Pressure doesn't matter for boiling temperature or state of matter."
all_misconceptions.population: students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Intermolecular forces are attractions within molecules rather than between molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are attractions between separate molecules, or between distant parts of some very large molecules, not the covalent bonds holding atoms together within one molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular bonds from intermolecular attractions and identify that melting, boiling, and sticking involve interactions between molecules, not breaking covalent bonds inside a molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Intermolecular forces are attractions between molecules not within molecules."
all_misconceptions.population: students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonds are any covalent bond with hydrogen in it.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is a specific intermolecular attraction involving hydrogen bonded to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine interacting with N, O, or F on another molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the atoms involved and check whether the molecule has H directly bonded to N, O, or F and whether there is a nearby N, O, or F lone-pair acceptor for the intermolecular attraction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonds are any covalent bond with hydrogen in it."
all_misconceptions.population: students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond is always right in the middle.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bonding electron pairs in covalent bonds are not always centered; their position depends on the relative electronegativities of the bonded atoms and is shifted toward the more electronegative atom.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Compare the electronegativities of the bonded atoms. The atom with greater electronegativity attracts shared electrons more strongly, so the bonding pair is displaced toward that atom rather than sitting exactly midway.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond is always right in the middle"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 37% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The size of the atom affects the position of the bonding electron pair in a covalent bond.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The position of the bonding electron pair is determined by electronegativity differences, not atomic size.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Identify which atom is more electronegative; shared electrons are drawn toward that atom. Atomic size is not the deciding factor for bond-pair position in the model used here.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The size of the atom affects the position of the bonding electron pair in a covalent bond"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 17% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The lone pair of electrons affects the position of the bonding electron pair in a covalent bond.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond-pair position is explained by electronegativity differences between bonded atoms, not by the presence of lone pairs.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Determine electron density using electronegativity of the atoms involved in the bond. Lone pairs affect molecular shape, but they do not determine where a bonding pair sits within a covalent bond.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The lone pair of electrons affects the position of the bonding electron pair in a covalent bond"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 17% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The shape of the molecule is only due to the repulsion of the bonding electron pair.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular geometry is determined by repulsions among all electron domains, especially bonding pairs and lone pairs, according to VSEPR theory.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Count all electron domains around the central atom and consider that lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs. Use VSEPR to predict the 3D shape.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The shape of the molecule is only due to the repulsion of the bonding electron pair"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 41% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Lone pairs of electrons are considered to be included in molecular geometry.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lone pairs are part of electron geometry, but molecular geometry describes only the positions of atoms, not lone pairs.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: First determine electron geometry from all electron domains, then derive molecular geometry by ignoring lone pairs and looking only at the arrangement of atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Lone pairs of electrons are considered to be included in molecular geometry"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 18% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students are inverted in understanding the partial charge symbol.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The partial charge symbols delta-plus and delta-minus indicate the direction of electron density in a polar bond, with the more electronegative atom carrying partial negative charge.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Use electronegativity to decide which atom attracts electron density more strongly, then assign δ− to that atom and δ+ to the other atom.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Inverted in understanding the partial charge symbol"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 33% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Effect of lone pairs on shape
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Lone pairs of electrons do not affect the geometry of the molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lone pairs do affect molecular geometry because they occupy electron domains and exert repulsion that changes bond angles and shape.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: When applying VSEPR, include lone pairs as electron domains. Their stronger repulsion alters the arrangement of bonding pairs and thus the molecular shape.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Lone pairs of electrons do not affect the geometry of the molecule"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 23% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Effect of lone pairs on shape
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The geometry of the molecule is only affected by the lone pair of electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular geometry depends on the repulsions among all electron domains, not lone pairs alone.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Consider both bonding pairs and lone pairs together. Molecular shape emerges from the full set of electron-domain repulsions around the central atom.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The geometry of the molecule is only affected by the lone pair of electrons"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 13% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Lone pairs of electrons cause polarity in a molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and the symmetry of the molecular geometry; lone pairs influence polarity indirectly by affecting shape, not by directly causing polarity themselves.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Determine whether the molecule has polar bonds, then assess whether the geometry is symmetrical enough for dipoles to cancel. Lone pairs matter because they can make geometry asymmetrical.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Lone pairs of electrons cause polarity in a molecule"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 18% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Polar molecules will form when there is a large difference in electronegativity in the atoms that make up the molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A large electronegativity difference makes a bond polar, but molecular polarity also depends on molecular geometry and whether bond dipoles cancel.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Check bond polarity from electronegativity differences, then determine the 3D shape. If the dipoles do not cancel because of asymmetry, the molecule is polar.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Polar molecules will form when there is a large difference in electronegativity in the atoms that make up the molecule"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 11% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Chemical bonds are forces between molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Chemical bonds hold atoms together within a substance, whereas intermolecular forces act between molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Distinguish intramolecular bonding from intermolecular attractions. Determine whether the question asks about forces within a molecule/compound or between separate molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Chemical bonds are forces between molecules"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 43% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: H2S is a non-polar molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: H2S is polar because its bent shape and bond dipoles do not cancel completely.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Determine the H–S bond polarity from electronegativity, then evaluate the bent molecular geometry. Because the dipoles do not cancel, the molecule is polar.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "H2S is a non-polar molecule"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 19% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The electronegativity of an atom affects the geometry of the molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular geometry is determined by repulsions among electron domains, not by electronegativity directly.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Use VSEPR to count electron domains and predict shape. Electronegativity influences bond polarity, but shape comes from electron-pair repulsion.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The electronegativity of an atom affects the geometry of the molecule"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 12% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Polar molecules are formed when the difference in electronegativity between atoms is small.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A molecule with a small electronegativity difference is not necessarily polar; polarity depends on both bond polarity and molecular geometry.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Assess electronegativity difference to judge bond polarity, then check whether the molecular shape allows dipoles to cancel. A small difference alone does not create molecular polarity.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Polar molecules are formed when the difference in electronegativity between atoms is small"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 19% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Molecules become polar when the bonds formed between atoms are polar.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Polar bonds are necessary but not sufficient for molecular polarity; the molecular shape must also be asymmetrical so dipoles do not cancel.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Identify polar bonds, then examine geometry. If the bond dipoles cancel because the molecule is symmetrical, the molecule is nonpolar despite having polar bonds.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Molecules become polar when the bonds formed between atoms are polar"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 15% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: NaCl is a molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: NaCl is an ionic compound and is not a molecule; it forms a crystal lattice and is represented by an empirical formula.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Recognize that ionic compounds do not consist of discrete molecules. Describe NaCl as a lattice of ions with an empirical formula rather than as a molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "NaCl is a molecule"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 75% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Metal and non-metal elements can form covalent compounds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A metal reacting with a nonmetal typically forms an ionic compound due to electron transfer and large electronegativity difference.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Use the element types and electronegativity difference to infer bonding. Metal atoms tend to lose electrons and nonmetals tend to gain them, leading to ionic bonding.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Metal and non-metal elements can form covalent compounds"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 25% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The octet rule is used to determine molecular geometry.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The octet rule is a guide for stable electron configurations; it is not a rule for determining molecular geometry.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Use the octet rule to check whether atoms achieve stable valence-shell electron configurations, and use VSEPR—not the octet rule—to predict molecular shape.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The octet rule is used to determine molecular geometry"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 20% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: VSEPR theory states that molecular geometry is caused by the repulsion of bonding atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: VSEPR theory explains molecular geometry in terms of repulsion between electron pairs/domains, including lone pairs and bonding pairs, not repulsion between atoms.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Count electron domains around the central atom and apply electron-pair repulsion. Atoms themselves are not the source of the VSEPR repulsions; the electron domains are.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "molecular geometry is caused by the repulsion of bonding atoms"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 30% of students
all_misconceptions.population: 101 tenth-grade students at a public high school in Jakarta, Indonesia
all_misconceptions.source_title: Identifying Students' Misconceptions about Chemical Bonding Using a Four-Tier Diagnostic Test

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe sodium chloride exists as discrete molecules rather than as an ionic lattice.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice made of alternating ions, not discrete NaCl molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Reason from the crystal structure: electron transfer forms ions, and electrostatic attraction acts in all directions through a lattice rather than producing individual molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "many students believed that sodium chloride existed as molecules"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 80.4% of 119 Grade 10 students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think one sodium ion and one chloride ion form an 'ion pair molecule'.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ionic compounds do not consist of ion-pair molecules; they form extended ionic lattices.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Recognize that ionic bonding is non-directional and each ion is attracted to many oppositely charged ions in a lattice, not to a single partner molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "46.1% thought that one sodium ion and one chloride ion formed an 'ion pair molecule'"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 46.1% of 119 Grade 10 students

all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that when metals and non-metals combine, they form covalent bonds instead of ionic bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Metal–non-metal combinations typically form ionic bonds via electron transfer, not covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Identify the elements involved and determine whether electrons are transferred from a metal to a non-metal to form ions held by electrostatic attraction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "22.5%) also indicated that when atoms of metals and non-metals combine, they form covalent bonds instead of ionic bonds."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 22.5% of 119 Grade 10 students
all_misconceptions.population: Grade 10 students in a Singapore school
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the number of electrons transferred in ionic bonding depends only on the number of electrons the non-metal needs to achieve an octet.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electron transfer in ionic bonding depends on the overall electron changes of both atoms, leading to stable ions and an extended ionic lattice; it is not determined only by the non-metal's octet need.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Consider both the metal's tendency to lose electrons and the non-metal's tendency to gain electrons, then determine a charge balance that yields stable ions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the number of electrons transferred depends only on the number of electrons that the atoms of the non-metal need to achieve a stable octet"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 10% of 119 Grade 10 students
all_misconceptions.population: Grade 10 students in a Singapore school
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.subtopic: bond count determined by donated electron
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe an atom can form only one ionic bond because it donates only one electron, so bonding is limited to the specific atom that received that electron.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ions in an ionic lattice are attracted to many surrounding counterions; one electron transfer does not mean one bond to one fixed partner only.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: After electron transfer, think in terms of charge and omnidirectional electrostatic attraction in a lattice, not one-to-one molecular bonding.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "a sodium atom can only donate one electron, so it can form only one bond"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: described in interviews with Grade 12 students
all_misconceptions.population: Grade 12 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe ions are bonded only to the specific counterion involved in the electron transfer event.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ionic bonding is not a one-time pairing; each ion is surrounded by and attracted to multiple oppositely charged ions in the lattice.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Link electron transfer to ion formation, then reason that the resulting ions interact electrostatically with all neighboring opposite charges.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the chloride is bonded to the specific sodium atom that donated an electron to it"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: described in interviews with Grade 12 students
all_misconceptions.population: Grade 12 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think an ion is bonded to only one counterion, while interactions with the other surrounding ions are merely forces, not bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The ionic lattice is held together by electrostatic attraction in all directions; neighboring ion interactions are part of the lattice bonding, not merely weaker forces outside the bond.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Recognize that the lattice is a network of electrostatic attractions extending to all neighboring ions, not a single-bond-plus-forces model.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "a chloride ion is bonded to one sodium ion and attracted to a further five sodium ions, but just by forces and not bonds"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: described in interviews with Grade 12 students
all_misconceptions.population: Grade 12 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think attraction between oppositely charged ions neutralizes the charges and forms neutral molecules in the solid.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Attraction between ions does not neutralize them; ions remain charged within the ionic lattice.
