all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Track charge before and after bonding: electron transfer creates ions, and the lattice is stabilized by electrostatic attraction without charge cancellation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the attraction between oppositely charged ions in an ionic compound results in the neutralisation of the charges, leading to the formation of a lattice consisting of neutral molecules"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: described in interviews with 48 Grade 12 students
all_misconceptions.population: 48 Grade 12 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students try to assign each electron in a covalent bond to one of the bonded atoms, as if each electron belongs to a particular atom.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In a covalent bond, the bonding electrons are shared between atoms and occupy the region between nuclei.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Treat the pair of electrons as shared electron density between both nuclei, not as two separately owned electrons.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students would commonly identify and distinguish which electron in a covalent bond belonged to each of the bonded atoms"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: described for Grade 11 and 12 students
all_misconceptions.population: Grade 11 and 12 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the sharing of electrons is the force that holds atoms together in a molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A covalent bond is an electrostatic attraction between the shared electrons and the nuclei of the bonded atoms; the bond is not the electrons themselves.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Reason from electrostatic attraction: negatively charged shared electrons are attracted to both positively charged nuclei, creating the bond.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "considered the sharing of electrons as the 'force' holding the atoms in a molecule together instead of electrostatic attraction between the shared electrons and the nuclei involved"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: described for Grade 11 and 12 students
all_misconceptions.population: Grade 11 and 12 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.subtopic: pair of shared electrons equals bond
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe a covalent bond is simply a pair of shared electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction that holds the atoms together; shared electrons participate in the bond but are not themselves the bond.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Distinguish the physical particles (shared electrons) from the attractive interaction between nuclei and shared electrons that constitutes the bond.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "some of her students held the misconception that a covalent bond is a pair of shared electrons"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: described in interviews with Boo's students
all_misconceptions.population: Boo's students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think ionic bonds are electrostatic in nature but covalent bonds are not.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: All chemical bonds, including covalent bonds, are electrostatic in nature.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Apply the same electrostatic principle to covalent bonding: shared electrons are attracted to both nuclei, so the bond is electrostatic too.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "some of her interviewees held the misconception that an ionic bond is electrostatic in nature but not the covalent bond"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: described in interviews
all_misconceptions.population: Boo's interviewees
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think covalent bonds are broken when a substance changes state.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: For simple molecular substances, changing state usually breaks intermolecular forces between molecules, not the covalent bonds within molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Differentiate intramolecular covalent bonds from intermolecular attractions; phase changes overcome the weaker intermolecular forces first.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "21% of the students believed ... that covalent bonds were broken when a substance changed state"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 21% of the students in Tan and Treagust's study
all_misconceptions.population: Grade 10 students in a Singapore school
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.subtopic: covalent bonds weaker than ionic bonds because of low melting/boiling points
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students infer that covalent bonds are weaker than ionic bonds simply because covalent substances often have lower melting and boiling points.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lower melting and boiling points of many covalent substances are due to weaker intermolecular forces, not weaker covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Compare substance structure: covalent molecular substances usually have discrete molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces, whereas ionic substances form lattices with strong electrostatic attractions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "some of her interviewees believed that covalent bonds are weaker than ionic bonds because they had the notion that covalent substances generally have lower melting points and boiling points compared to ionic substances"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: described in interviews
all_misconceptions.population: Boo's interviewees
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students identify intermolecular forces as the forces within a molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces act between molecules, while covalent bonds act within molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Use the prefixes: 'inter' means between different molecules, and 'intra' or intramolecular means within a molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the students incorrectly identified intermolecular forces as the forces within a molecule"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: described in two studies involving Grade 11 and 12 students
all_misconceptions.population: Grade 11 and 12 students in Australia and Singapore
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.subtopic: strong intermolecular forces in network covalent solid
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think strong intermolecular forces exist in a continuous covalent network solid.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A continuous covalent network solid is held together by covalent bonds throughout the network, not by intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Recognize the structural difference between a molecular solid, where intermolecular forces dominate, and a network covalent solid, where atoms are linked by covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "others thought that strong intermolecular forces exist in a continuous covalent (network) solid"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: described in two studies involving Grade 11 and 12 students
all_misconceptions.population: Grade 11 and 12 students in Australia and Singapore
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the number of ionic bonds formed is determined by electrovalency or valency.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrovalency refers to ionic charge, not the number of ionic bonds formed; bond number is not determined by valency.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Separate ionic charge from lattice bonding: an ion’s charge indicates electron loss or gain, but the ionic lattice involves multiple electrostatic attractions not fixed one-to-one bond counts.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the number of ionic bonds formed is not determined by electrovalency"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: presented as a misconception to avoid
all_misconceptions.population: general secondary chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students infer from the formula NaCl that one sodium particle is bonded to one chlorine particle, analogous to HCl molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: NaCl is an ionic lattice formula unit, not evidence of discrete one-to-one molecules or bonded particle pairs.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Interpret ionic formulae as simplest ratios of ions in a lattice, unlike molecular formulae that represent actual molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students might have the idea that one particle of sodium is bonded to one particle of chlorine just as one atom of hydrogen is bonded to one atom of chlorine"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: suggested as a contributing misconception
all_misconceptions.population: secondary school students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students interpret the wires in a ball-and-stick model of sodium chloride as actual bonds of some sort.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Model sticks are representational aids and do not literally correspond to individual bonds in an ionic lattice.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Use the model as a visualization tool while remembering that ionic bonding is a three-dimensional, omnidirectional electrostatic lattice.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "many interpreted the six wires attached to each ball (ion) as each representing a bond of some sort"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: described among many Grade 12 students
all_misconceptions.population: Grade 12 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of chemical bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot determine whether a molecule is polar by analyzing the polarity of its bonds within the molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular polarity is determined from the bond polarities together with the molecular geometry and the vector sum of bond dipoles.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify polar bonds, determine the 3D shape of the molecule, and then combine the bond dipoles vectorially to decide whether there is a net dipole moment.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “many students could not determine the polarity of the molecules by analyzing the polarity of the bonds within the molecules”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: many students
all_misconceptions.population: Grade 11 and 12 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: CONTENT FRAMEWORK FOR INTER- MOLECULAR FORCES

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students hold alternative conceptions about intermolecular forces after instruction, but the provided paper excerpt does not specify the exact misconception statements.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces should be understood scientifically as attractions between particles that explain molecular properties and behavior.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect particle structure and interactions to observed properties using correct molecular-level reasoning.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Common alternative conceptions that students had pertaining to the topic of intermolecular forces were identified"
all_misconceptions.population: Junior college students
all_misconceptions.source_file: Junior college students' conceptions of intermolecular forces/Junior college students' conceptions of intermolecular forces.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Junior college students' conceptions of intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat intermolecular attractions as an invisible property that is only recognized through a phenomenon, rather than as real forces between molecules that explain the phenomenon.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are real attractive interactions between molecules/particles that can be used to explain observable bulk phenomena such as surface tension and solubility behavior.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the macroscopic observation to particle-level attractions: if water can hold many paper clips above the brim, the surface is being stabilized by cohesive intermolecular attractions, especially hydrogen bonding, rather than by an unexplained "trick" of the liquid.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students will explore, learn, and connect concepts of Intermolecular Forces (IMFs) to physical phenomena"
all_misconceptions.population: 9th-12th grade chemistry/physical science students
all_misconceptions.source_file: K20 LEARN _ The Attraction Is REAL/K20 LEARN _ The Attraction Is REAL.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Authentic Lessons for 21st Century Learning

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students expect a full glass of water to hold only a small number of paper clips before spilling, underestimating water's surface tension.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Water can support many paper clips because cohesive intermolecular forces create substantial surface tension at the water's surface.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should predict that the water surface behaves like a stretched film due to cohesion; therefore, careful addition of paper clips can be supported until the surface tension is overcome.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Most students will predict less than 30 paperclips, but the real answer is HUNDREDS of paperclips."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Most students
all_misconceptions.population: students in the lesson activity (9th-12th grade chemistry/physical science students)
all_misconceptions.source_file: K20 LEARN _ The Attraction Is REAL/K20 LEARN _ The Attraction Is REAL.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Authentic Lessons for 21st Century Learning

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think an electron literally orbits a nucleus in a simple planetary path, with a single electron moving around a single central particle like a person circling another person.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrons do not move in fixed planetary orbits around a nucleus; the Bohr picture is a simplification and real atoms have quantum electron distributions, with nuclei made of more than one particle and often multiple electrons.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should recognize that the atom picture used in the lesson is only an oversimplified model. They should reason that the nucleus contains protons and neutrons, and electrons occupy quantum orbitals or electron clouds rather than literal circular paths.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the instructor projected the simple Rutherford–Bohr atom picture on to the wall as an oversimplification and explained that nucleus is made up of more than one particle, atoms have mostly more than one electron revolving around a nucleus."
all_misconceptions.population: 60 freshmen prospective elementary teachers in an introductory chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: TEACHING INTERMOLECULAR FORCES WITH  LOVE ANALOGY: A CASE STUDY

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think London dispersion forces arise because electrons deliberately or persistently move toward one side in response to an attractive neighbor, as if the electron 'takes a look' and shifts like a person focusing attention.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces arise from instantaneous fluctuations in electron density that create temporary dipoles, which then induce dipoles in nearby particles and produce a brief attraction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason that electron density is constantly fluctuating; a momentary uneven distribution creates a temporary dipole, which induces an opposite dipole in a neighboring atom or molecule, leading to a fleeting electrostatic attraction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The instructor further explained that the induced dipole ... causes a brief electrostatic attraction between the two atoms"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 45/60 students received full grades on the final exam question about London dispersion force; 5/60 received 6/10; 4/60 received 5/10; 6/60 received 0
all_misconceptions.population: 60 freshmen prospective elementary teachers in an introductory chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: TEACHING INTERMOLECULAR FORCES WITH  LOVE ANALOGY: A CASE STUDY

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think the temporary dipole forms because a molecule is near an 'attractive' or 'positive charge' in a way that electrons consciously gather on one side and retreat from the other, like reacting emotionally to another person.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Temporary dipoles in London dispersion forces are caused by random, instantaneous fluctuations in electron density, not by conscious attraction or intentional movement; nearby particles become polarized by this uneven distribution.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should explain that electrons are always moving, so at any instant a molecule may have more electron density on one side. This temporary asymmetry can polarize a neighboring molecule, producing a weak, short-lived attraction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Electron density in a molecule may be redistributed by proximity to another multipole."
all_misconceptions.population: 60 freshmen prospective elementary teachers in an introductory chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: TEACHING INTERMOLECULAR FORCES WITH  LOVE ANALOGY: A CASE STUDY

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Strength and persistence of the force
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think London dispersion forces are complicated but comparable to human relationship drama, rather than recognizing them as weak and transient electrostatic attractions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces are weak intermolecular attractions because the induced dipoles are small and the attractions are very short-lived.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect the temporary nature of the induced dipole to the weakness of the force: the attraction appears only briefly and disappears as electron density shifts again.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "London dispersion forces are typically very weak because the attractions are so quickly broken"
all_misconceptions.population: 60 freshmen prospective elementary teachers in an introductory chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: TEACHING INTERMOLECULAR FORCES WITH  LOVE ANALOGY: A CASE STUDY

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think a dipole-dipole interaction is caused by a 'permanent problem in the relationship' or by one molecule being personally attracted to another, rather than by unequal electron sharing from electronegativity differences.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interactions occur between molecules with permanent dipoles created by differences in electronegativity that produce partial positive and partial negative ends.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason that a polar covalent bond forms when one atom pulls bonding electrons more strongly, creating a δ- and δ+ end; opposite partial charges on neighboring molecules then attract each other.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "dipole-dipole interactions and explained that they are caused by permanent dipoles in molecules"
all_misconceptions.population: 60 freshmen prospective elementary teachers in an introductory chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: TEACHING INTERMOLECULAR FORCES WITH  LOVE ANALOGY: A CASE STUDY

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think the more electronegative atom simply 'draws' the other partner closer like a more attractive person, instead of understanding that electronegativity differences polarize a bond by pulling shared electrons unevenly.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A more electronegative atom attracts the shared bonding electrons more strongly, creating partial charges across the bond and allowing electrostatic attraction between molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify which atom is more electronegative, infer that bonding electrons are displaced toward it, and then conclude that the molecule has a permanent dipole that can align with other dipoles.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the electronegative atom draws the electrons in the bond nearer to itself"
all_misconceptions.population: 60 freshmen prospective elementary teachers in an introductory chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: TEACHING INTERMOLECULAR FORCES WITH  LOVE ANALOGY: A CASE STUDY

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think hydrogen bonding is a special 'cheating' or relationship-based attraction between people, rather than a specific strong dipole-dipole interaction involving H bonded to F, O, or N and a lone pair on a neighboring molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is an especially strong form of dipole-dipole interaction that occurs when hydrogen is covalently bonded to F, O, or N and is attracted to a lone pair on F, O, or N in a nearby molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should check the structure: H must be attached to F, O, or N, creating a highly polar bond; then an intermolecular attraction forms between the Hδ+ and a lone pair on F/O/N of another molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "hydrogen bonds are form of dipole-dipole interactions"
all_misconceptions.population: 60 freshmen prospective elementary teachers in an introductory chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: TEACHING INTERMOLECULAR FORCES WITH  LOVE ANALOGY: A CASE STUDY

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think hydrogen bonding can occur with any strongly desired partner, rather than only with highly electronegative atoms F, O, and N and hydrogen attached to them.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires hydrogen bonded to fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen, and attraction to a lone pair on F, O, or N of a neighboring molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should recognize the narrow set of atoms capable of hydrogen bonding because of their high electronegativity and small size, which create very strong bond polarity and strong intermolecular attraction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "They occur between hydrogen ... and oxygen ... fluorine ... or nitrogen"
all_misconceptions.population: 60 freshmen prospective elementary teachers in an introductory chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: TEACHING INTERMOLECULAR FORCES WITH  LOVE ANALOGY: A CASE STUDY

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not clearly distinguish or correctly conceptualize intermolecular forces at the submicroscopic level, leading to scientifically flawed explanations of IMF strength.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are attractive interactions between particles that can be explained using molecular structure and polarity, and they must be interpreted at the particle level rather than as macroscopic properties.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the type of intermolecular interaction present from the molecular features involved, then justify relative strength using particle-level reasoning rather than relying on everyday appearances or vague descriptions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: students often struggle to conceptualize and depict IMFs because of challenges with abstract thinking and visualizing submicroscopic interactions
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 15.09% provided scientifically flawed justifications
all_misconceptions.population: 53 first-year undergraduate chemistry majors at a teacher training university in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Representing the Invisible: A Study of Students' Visual and Conceptual Conceptions of Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students produce inaccurate drawings of hydrogen bonding interactions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding should be represented as a specific attractive interaction between a hydrogen atom bonded to N, O, or F and a lone pair on another electronegative atom in a neighboring molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should draw the molecules with correct partial charges and indicate the hydrogen bond between the appropriate atoms, showing the interaction between molecules rather than within a molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: fewer produced accurate drawings (47.2%, 41.5%, and 28.3% respectively)
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 47.2% accurate drawings for hydrogen bonding; therefore 52.8% inaccurate/other responses
all_misconceptions.population: 53 first-year undergraduate chemistry majors at a teacher training university in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Representing the Invisible: A Study of Students' Visual and Conceptual Conceptions of Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students produce inaccurate drawings of dipole-dipole interactions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interactions should be depicted as attractions between the partial positive end of one polar molecule and the partial negative end of another polar molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first identify the molecular dipoles, then show the correct orientation of neighboring molecules so opposite partial charges attract.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: fewer produced accurate drawings (47.2%, 41.5%, and 28.3% respectively)
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 41.5% accurate drawings for dipole-dipole interactions; therefore 58.5% inaccurate/other responses
all_misconceptions.population: 53 first-year undergraduate chemistry majors at a teacher training university in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Representing the Invisible: A Study of Students' Visual and Conceptual Conceptions of Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.subtopic: visual representation of London dispersion forces
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students produce inaccurate drawings of London dispersion forces.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces should be represented as temporary induced dipole interactions arising from momentary electron density fluctuations between particles.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should show brief, induced dipoles on neighboring atoms or molecules and indicate that the attraction is temporary and present in all particles, especially more polarizable ones.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: fewer produced accurate drawings (47.2%, 41.5%, and 28.3% respectively)
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 28.3% accurate drawings for London dispersion forces; therefore 71.7% inaccurate/other responses
all_misconceptions.population: 53 first-year undergraduate chemistry majors at a teacher training university in Ghana
all_misconceptions.source_title: Representing the Invisible: A Study of Students' Visual and Conceptual Conceptions of Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think intermolecular forces occur only within a single molecule, for example only between atoms inside H2O rather than between separate water molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces act between molecules or particles, not within a single molecule's covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular bonding from intermolecular attraction: the H–O bond holds atoms together inside one water molecule, while IMFs are attractions between different H2O molecules that help explain phase behavior.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students' misconception about IMFs occur in molecules"
all_misconceptions.population: students (as reported from teacher interviews and cited prior studies)
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analyses of multiple representation about intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe intermolecular forces are stronger than chemical bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Chemical bonds are stronger than intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the energy needed to break a covalent bond with the energy needed to overcome intermolecular attractions; breaking H–O bonds requires more energy than evaporating water, showing bonds are stronger than IMFs.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "IMFs are stronger than chemical bonds"
all_misconceptions.population: students (cited from prior studies)
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analyses of multiple representation about intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think intermolecular forces cause chemical reactions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces do not cause chemical reactions; reactions involve breaking and forming chemical bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that IMFs influence physical properties like boiling point or solubility, whereas chemical reactions require changes in bonding and composition.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "IMFs is causes a chemical reaction"
all_misconceptions.population: students (cited from prior studies)
all_misconceptions.concept_category: role in reactions versus physical properties
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analyses of multiple representation about intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think ion-dipole forces are not part of intermolecular forces because IMFs are only between molecules, not ions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ion-dipole interactions are intermolecular attractions between ions and polar molecules and can be included when discussing IMFs depending on the definition used.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that a charged ion can attract the partial charges on a polar molecule, so Na+ or Cl- interacting with H2O is an ion-dipole interaction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "some books assume that the concept of IMFs is a force between molecules not ions so that the concept of iondipole force, ions-induced dipole forces not include the IMFs."
all_misconceptions.population: textbook frameworks discussed for students
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analyses of multiple representation about intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may focus only on Na+ and omit the role of Cl- when imagining ion-dipole interactions in salt water.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Both cations and anions interact with water molecules; cations orient water's negative end toward them, while anions orient water's positive end toward them.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should apply electrostatic attraction to both ions in NaCl: Na+ attracts the oxygen end of water and Cl- attracts the hydrogen end of water.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the symbolic representation shown in textbooks I and II only describes the Na+ ions but not the Cl ions."
all_misconceptions.population: students as implied by the representation analysis
all_misconceptions.source_title: An analyses of multiple representation about intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot explain paper chromatography in terms of intermolecular forces and instead give explanations that do not use intermolecular attractions between the solute, mobile phase, and stationary phase.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Paper chromatography should be explained by differences in intermolecular attractions between the components and the mobile and stationary phases.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should relate how strongly each substance interacts with the stationary phase versus the mobile phase; substances that are more strongly attracted to the mobile phase travel farther, while those more strongly attracted to the stationary phase move less.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students had diWculty in explaining paper chromatography experiments by means of intermolecular forces”
all_misconceptions.population: Students interviewed for the study and students taking the MACI; the MACI was administered to 407 high school students and 253 general chemistry students across the United States.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' misconceptions about intermolecular forces as investigated through paper chromatography experiments and the Molecular Attractions Concept Inventory

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students hold misconceptions about intermolecular forces in general, as shown by multiple incorrect ideas on the Molecular Attractions Concept Inventory.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are attractions between molecules that help explain properties such as boiling point and separation behavior.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use particle-level reasoning: identify the molecules present, determine the relevant intermolecular attractions, and connect the strength of those attractions to observable outcomes such as boiling point or chromatographic movement.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “Twenty-two misconceptions were found from the administration of MACI, consisting of nine misconceptions related to chromatography and thirteen misconceptions related to intermolecular forces.”
all_misconceptions.population: 407 high school students and 253 general chemistry students across the United States.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' misconceptions about intermolecular forces as investigated through paper chromatography experiments and the Molecular Attractions Concept Inventory

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Hydrogen bonding vs van der Waals / dispersion forces in cellulose
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the attractive bonds between cellulose fibers are van der Waals bonds or dipole-dipole bonds rather than hydrogen bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The fibers are held together by hydrogen bonds (with covalent/polar covalent bonds within each cellulose chain), not by van der Waals or dipole-dipole bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify the intermolecular attraction shown between cellulose fibers, distinguish it from the intramolecular bonds within each fiber, and recognize that hydrogen bonding is the relevant force between fibers in the teacher's representation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Student 1: "Dipole–dipole bond…" / Student 2: "van der Waals…" / Teacher: "Hydrogen bonds, hydrogen bonds between there."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: At least 2 students in the discussion
all_misconceptions.population: Students in one observed upper-secondary chemistry class
all_misconceptions.source_file: Science Education - 2021 - Patron - Qualitatively different ways of unpacking visual representations when teaching/Science Education - 2021 - Patron - Qualitatively different ways of unpacking visual representations when teaching.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Qualitatively different ways of unpacking visual representations when teaching intermolecular forces in upper secondary school

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not know that dipoles must be oriented with opposite partial charges facing each other for attraction; they initially orient the dipole the wrong way round.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole attraction arises when the positive end of one dipole is near the negative end of another dipole.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use the partial charges on each dipole to infer the attractive orientation: opposite ends attract, so the plus side of one dipole should face the minus side of the other.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "many of the students reacted and pointed out that the eraser should be turned around, so that the side with the plus drawn on it was closest to the drawn dipole's minus-side."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Many students reacted
all_misconceptions.population: Students in one observed upper-secondary chemistry class
all_misconceptions.source_file: Science Education - 2021 - Patron - Qualitatively different ways of unpacking visual representations when teaching/Science Education - 2021 - Patron - Qualitatively different ways of unpacking visual representations when teaching.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Qualitatively different ways of unpacking visual representations when teaching intermolecular forces in upper secondary school

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Recognizing dispersion forces in an animation
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not understand what the visual elements in the dispersion-force animation represent, including that the objects are uncharged overall and only temporarily polarized.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dispersion forces arise from temporary, momentary polarization in otherwise uncharged molecules; the animation's cloudlike objects and plus/minus signs represent this transient polarization and resulting attraction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect the visual symbols in the animation to temporary electron redistribution in uncharged particles and infer that the attraction is caused by a fleeting induced dipole, not a permanent charge.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the animation shows dispersion forces, that the substances are uncharged, but it is plus-minus charged during a fraction of a second"
all_misconceptions.population: Students viewing the dispersion-force animation in the observed lesson
all_misconceptions.source_file: Science Education - 2021 - Patron - Qualitatively different ways of unpacking visual representations when teaching/Science Education - 2021 - Patron - Qualitatively different ways of unpacking visual representations when teaching.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Qualitatively different ways of unpacking visual representations when teaching intermolecular forces in upper secondary school

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Distinguishing representations of the same concept
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not recognize that different visual representations can depict the same phenomenon, and may fail to relate the teacher-drawn dipole-dipole diagram to the animation's representation.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Different representations can depict the same intermolecular phenomenon using different visual modes and conventions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should compare the modes, identify the same underlying concept across representations, and translate the meaning from one representation to another rather than treating them as unrelated pictures.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The different ways in which hydrogen bonding between water molecules were illustrated in the movie and by the teacher, respectively, is shown in Figure 7."
all_misconceptions.population: Students in one observed upper-secondary chemistry class
all_misconceptions.source_file: Science Education - 2021 - Patron - Qualitatively different ways of unpacking visual representations when teaching/Science Education - 2021 - Patron - Qualitatively different ways of unpacking visual representations when teaching.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Qualitatively different ways of unpacking visual representations when teaching intermolecular forces in upper secondary school

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe they can make correct meaning from a chemistry visual representation without teacher unpacking or support.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Chemical visual representations often require explicit interpretative, inferential, or explanatory unpacking to make critical aspects discernible.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify which features are shown, infer what is appresent or implicit, and connect the representation to the intended chemical concept with teacher guidance when needed.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "assuming that a representation 'speaks for itself'"
all_misconceptions.population: Upper secondary school chemistry students interviewed in three schools (24 students total; 12 pairs).
all_misconceptions.source_file: Science Education - 2026 - Patron - Students  Experiences of Teachers  Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the/Science Education - 2026 - Patron - Students  Experiences of Teachers  Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Experiences of Teachers' Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the Context of Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a new visual representation of the same chemical idea will automatically be connected to earlier representations and thus be understandable without explicit explanation.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students need explicit links between representations to recognize that different visual forms can represent the same chemical phenomenon.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should compare the new representation with previous ones, look for common critical aspects, and use teacher explanation to map correspondences across representations.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "you don't connect them to the same things as you usually do. Then it becomes a bit strange."
all_misconceptions.population: Interviewed upper secondary chemistry students; reported by Sam and Jonny.
all_misconceptions.source_file: Science Education - 2026 - Patron - Students  Experiences of Teachers  Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the/Science Education - 2026 - Patron - Students  Experiences of Teachers  Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Experiences of Teachers' Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the Context of Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe they should be able to determine a molecule's structure directly from a molecular formula without unpacking.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A molecular formula does not on its own show the molecule's structure; students need additional representation or explanation to infer connectivity and spatial arrangement.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should recognize that a formula gives composition, then use structural models or teacher explanation to infer how atoms are connected and arranged.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "a molecule's structure when only given its molecular formula (in which the structure is an appresent feature)"
all_misconceptions.population: Upper secondary chemistry students interviewed; exemplified by Moa and Ella.
all_misconceptions.source_file: Science Education - 2026 - Patron - Students  Experiences of Teachers  Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the/Science Education - 2026 - Patron - Students  Experiences of Teachers  Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Experiences of Teachers' Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the Context of Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Identifying hydrogen-bond donors from a structural representation
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot infer that hydrogen bonding is impossible unless the hydrogen atom is directly bonded to fluorine, and they need the teacher to tell them this explicitly.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom such as F, O, or N; if H is bonded to carbon instead, hydrogen bonding of that type does not occur.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should inspect the structure, identify which atom H is attached to, and apply the rule for hydrogen-bond donor requirements to decide whether hydrogen bonding is possible.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "you wouldn't understand anything. But when he [verbally] explained, it was very clear."
all_misconceptions.population: Upper secondary chemistry students in a lesson on hydrogen bonding; reported in the interview with Loke and others.
all_misconceptions.source_file: Science Education - 2026 - Patron - Students  Experiences of Teachers  Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the/Science Education - 2026 - Patron - Students  Experiences of Teachers  Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Experiences of Teachers' Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the Context of Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Connecting macroscopic observations to submicroscopic explanations
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think they cannot explain a precipitate or other laboratory observation unless the teacher explicitly connects the experiment to particle-level causes.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Macroscopic observations should be explained by linking them to symbolic/submicroscopic representations of the particles and interactions involved.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should observe the experimental outcome, then use the underlying particle model to reason about why the observed macroscopic change occurs.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I do not know why a precipitate is formed."
all_misconceptions.population: Upper secondary chemistry students interviewed about a hydrogen-bonding lesson; reported by Ella.
all_misconceptions.source_file: Science Education - 2026 - Patron - Students  Experiences of Teachers  Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the/Science Education - 2026 - Patron - Students  Experiences of Teachers  Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Experiences of Teachers' Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the Context of Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Electron distribution in a polar bond
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may initially think the shared electrons are equally distributed between the bonded atoms in a polar covalent bond, and need the teacher to show the bond line moved toward chlorine to correct this.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In a polar covalent bond, the shared electrons are unevenly distributed toward the more electronegative atom.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should compare electronegativities, infer unequal electron sharing, and represent the bond polarity by shifting electron density toward the atom that attracts electrons more strongly.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the electrons were unequally shared between the two atoms"
all_misconceptions.population: Upper secondary chemistry students interviewed during discussion of polar covalent bonding; exemplified by Emmy and Linnea.
all_misconceptions.source_file: Science Education - 2026 - Patron - Students  Experiences of Teachers  Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the/Science Education - 2026 - Patron - Students  Experiences of Teachers  Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Experiences of Teachers' Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the Context of Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Need for more explicit visual detail
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think an underspecified atomic drawing is hard to interpret because it lacks critical features such as electrons and other structural details.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A representation should include the critical features needed to make the atomic structure discernible and meaningful to novices.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should look for which structural features are present, compare with a more explicit drawing, and use the added features to infer the intended atomic structure.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "you can do it, like, that you draw an atom, roughly how it's structured, but then you can make a drawing next to it, to make it even clearer, with electrons and stuff"
all_misconceptions.population: Upper secondary chemistry students interviewed; reported by Anna.
all_misconceptions.source_file: Science Education - 2026 - Patron - Students  Experiences of Teachers  Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the/Science Education - 2026 - Patron - Students  Experiences of Teachers  Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Experiences of Teachers' Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the Context of Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe a spoken explanation alone is enough to learn from a visual representation even when they later cannot retain or revisit the meaning.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Persistent visual support in addition to speech helps students revisit meanings and stabilize understanding over time.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use the spoken explanation to interpret the image, then rely on an additional stable representation or notes to consolidate and revisit the meaning later.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "when you have to look back [at the representations], then it's like, you forget a little bit."
all_misconceptions.population: Upper secondary chemistry students interviewed; reported by Anna.
all_misconceptions.source_file: Science Education - 2026 - Patron - Students  Experiences of Teachers  Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the/Science Education - 2026 - Patron - Students  Experiences of Teachers  Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' Experiences of Teachers' Ways of Unpacking Visual Representations in the Context of Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think electrons are stationary.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrons are not stationary; atomic models should represent electrons as moving in orbitals/electron clouds rather than fixed in place.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that atomic structure involves electrons in motion, and that a scientifically acceptable model must account for electron behavior as dynamic rather than fixed.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Student believes electrons are stationary
all_misconceptions.population: Students interviewed in the study
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students adhere to a solar system/Bohr model for electron orbitals.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The atom is not accurately represented by a simple planetary/solar-system model; electron behavior is better described by a quantum model/electron cloud.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between a historical planetary model and a modern quantum model, recognizing that electrons are not on fixed circular orbits around the nucleus.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Student adheres to a solar system model for electron orbitals.; (Bohr model)
all_misconceptions.population: Students interviewed in the study
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe the solar system model is wrong but replace it with an unspecified 'cloud' idea without a probabilistic understanding.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The modern atomic model uses electron clouds/probability to represent electron locations and behavior.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain that electrons occupy regions of probability rather than fixed paths, and that the cloud model is grounded in electron motion and probability.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Student understands that solar system model is wrong; uses some kind of "cloud" explanation
all_misconceptions.population: Students interviewed in the study
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat the atom as a simple sphere and do not know that atoms contain electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms have internal structure, including electrons, protons, and neutrons; a scientifically correct atomic model must include this composition.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect symbolic and visual representations of atoms to their internal subatomic particles and explain what those particles do and where they are located.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: student 0089 was unaware that atoms contain electrons. In his model, an atom is just a sphere
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 1 student case described (student 0089)
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry student 0089
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe atoms on the edge of metal are different from atoms in the bulk.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms in the edge and bulk of a solid are the same type of particles; the smoothness of a cut metal edge is not because edge atoms are fundamentally different in shape.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that surface appearance is a macroscopic effect and does not require different kinds of atoms at the edge versus the interior.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Student believes that atoms on the edge of metal are different than those in the bulk.
all_misconceptions.population: Students interviewed in the study
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a smooth edge is smooth because particles are too small to feel.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The smooth edge of a solid results from the arrangement and truncation of particles at the surface, not from particles being too small to feel.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from the particle arrangement at the cut surface and recognize that the macroscopic smoothness comes from the physical structure, not from sensory limitations alone.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Student believes that the edge is smooth because the particles are too small to feel.
all_misconceptions.population: Students interviewed in the study
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students rely only on extensive properties to identify substances.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Substances should be identified using intensive properties and, at a deeper level, by linking bulk properties to atomic/molecular structure.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish extensive from intensive properties and explain that intensive properties are characteristic of a substance because they do not depend on sample amount.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Relies only on extensive properties
all_misconceptions.population: Students interviewed in the study
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students mix extensive and intensive properties but do not understand the difference between them.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Extensive properties depend on amount; intensive properties do not and are more useful for identifying a substance.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should classify properties by whether they vary with amount and use that classification to decide which properties can identify a substance.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Extensive + intensive properties, but does not specify any meaning to the difference
all_misconceptions.population: Students interviewed in the study
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students can name intensive properties but do not understand why they are valuable for characterizing a substance.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intensive properties are characteristic because they remain the same regardless of sample size and thus help identify substances.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain that intensive properties are diagnostic of substance identity precisely because they do not change with amount.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Extensive + intensive properties; understands the value of intensive properties
all_misconceptions.population: Students interviewed in the study
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not separate bulk properties from atomic/molecular properties.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bulk observable properties should be distinguished from atomic/molecular-level properties, and both levels can be used to explain substance identity and behavior.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect macroscopic properties to microscopic structure and explain which properties are observed directly and which emerge from particle-level structure.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Separates the bulk properties (intensive + extensive) from the atomic/molecular properties
all_misconceptions.population: Students interviewed in the study
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not recognize that intensive properties likely change with changes at the atomic/molecular level.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Changes at the atomic or molecular level can alter intensive properties because those properties arise from microscopic structure and interactions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that if composition or structure changes, the characteristic properties of a substance can change as well, even if sample size does not.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Intensive properties likely change at the
all_misconceptions.population: Students interviewed in the study
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not know what forces keep atoms together in a solid.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Particles in solids are held together by interparticle/electrical forces that act at the atomic and molecular scale.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect solid structure to attractive forces between particles and explain that these forces maintain the solid arrangement.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: students cannot explain the forces that keep the atoms together in a solid (inter-particle forces).
all_misconceptions.population: Students interviewed in the study
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not spontaneously think that the arrangement of atoms gives a substance its properties.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The arrangement of atoms/molecules is a key determinant of a substance's properties and identity.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that different arrangements of the same particles can produce different properties and even different substances.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Nor do they volunteer that the arrangement of atoms gives a substance its properties
all_misconceptions.population: Students interviewed in the study
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students often believe bonding can only be intramolecular.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrical interactions also occur between molecules and particles; bonding/attraction is not limited to intramolecular bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize both intramolecular bonding and intermolecular attractions, and use the appropriate type of force to explain a phenomenon.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: students often believe that bonding can only be intramolecular
all_misconceptions.population: Students in the literature cited by the paper; used to interpret the interview findings
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students rely only on the octet model to explain inter-atomic interactions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Interatomic and intermolecular interactions are governed by electrical forces and cannot be reduced only to octet-rule reasoning.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain bonding and interactions using electron distribution, electronegativity, and electrical forces rather than only octet completion.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Often, they rely only the octet model to explain inter-atomic interactions
all_misconceptions.population: Students in the literature cited by the paper; used to interpret the interview findings
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students define bonding in terms of atoms 'needing' or 'wanting' to give away electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bonding should be explained in terms of electron interactions and electrical forces, not anthropomorphic 'need' or 'want' language.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use particle-level and electrostatic reasoning to explain why atoms form bonds rather than attributing intent to atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: students learn to apply the octet model and begin to define bonding in terms of atoms *needing* or *wanting to give away* electrons
all_misconceptions.population: Students in the literature cited by the paper; used to interpret the interview findings
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Substance identity and physical vs chemical change
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think grinding granulated sugar into powdered sugar changes the substance at the molecular level.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Grinding sugar is a physical change; the substance remains sugar even though particle size and surface behavior change.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish changes in size or form from changes in composition and reason that no new substance is formed by grinding.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: four of the six believed that grinding the granulated sugar to make powdered sugar resulted in a change on the molecular level.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 4 of 6 high school chemistry students in the described subgroup
all_misconceptions.population: Six high school students who had completed a year of chemistry
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Substance identity and physical vs chemical change
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think powdered and granulated sugar are different substances, or they are not the same substance.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Powdered and granulated sugar are the same substance, differing mainly in particle size and resulting behavior, not composition.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use composition and structure to decide substance identity, recognizing that different forms of the same sugar can behave differently without becoming different substances.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: These six students in this study believed that granulated and powdered sugar are the same substance.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 6 of 6 high school chemistry students in the described subgroup
all_misconceptions.population: Six high school students who had completed a year of chemistry
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Substance identity and physical vs chemical change
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Some students think powdered and granulated sugar are composed of different molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Different particle-size forms of sugar are built from the same molecules; particle size change does not change molecular identity.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that if a change is physical, the molecules remain the same even though their arrangement or size distribution changes.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Some even went as far to say that the two sugars were composed of the same molecules.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: some of the 6 students in the subgroup
all_misconceptions.population: Six high school students who had completed a year of chemistry
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think powdered sugar contains more particles because it is powder rather than crystal.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Powdered and granulated sugar samples contain the same substance; differences in sticking or packing are due to particle size, surface area, and intermolecular/electrostatic effects, not more particles of a different kind.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from structure and surface interactions rather than assuming one sample has more particles or a different molecular makeup.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: I'd think the powdered, I think there'd be a lot more particles in the powder than there would be in the crystal of the sugar.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: quoted from one student example; four of six showed the broader misconception about molecular-level change
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry student (quoted example)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the make-up is different on a molecular level and that there is less space between the particles in powdered sugar.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Differences in texture or flow do not mean the molecular makeup is different; sugar remains the same substance, and observed behavior can be explained by particle size and surface interactions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate macroscopic behavior from molecular identity and explain behavior using arrangement, size, and forces rather than a different molecular make-up.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: I like guess the, uh, make up is kinda' different, like on a molecular level…there's not as much space between them.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: quoted from one student example
all_misconceptions.population: High school physics student with one year of high school chemistry
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the intermolecular structure of crystallized sugar is stronger than powdered sugar's structure.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Strength of attraction should be explained in terms of particle interactions and structure, not by assuming the powdered form has a fundamentally weaker or different intermolecular structure.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the different behaviors of powdered and granulated sugar to surface area and intermolecular interactions, not infer a different substance structure.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: …the intermolecular structure isn't as strong …as crystallized sugar.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: quoted from one student example
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry student
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not realize that atoms contain electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms are composed of subatomic particles, including electrons, protons, and neutrons.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should interpret atomic diagrams and descriptions as having internal substructure, including electrons outside the nucleus.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: student 0089 was unaware that atoms contain electrons.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 1 student case described (student 0089)
all_misconceptions.population: High performing high school chemistry student
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think atoms are just spheres and cannot explain their composition.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms are not merely solid spheres; they have internal composition and structure.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should describe the nucleus and electrons rather than treating the atom as an undifferentiated ball.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: In his model, an atom is just a sphere
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 1 student case described (student 0089)
all_misconceptions.population: High performing high school chemistry student
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the color of atomic spheres is important.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The color in a textbook model is generally representational and not a property of actual atoms.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish features of a model from real properties of atoms and recognize which aspects are symbolic conventions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: He believed that the color of the spheres was important.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 1 student case described (student 0089)
all_misconceptions.population: High performing high school chemistry student
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think symbols like Na and Cl mean 'elements' only, while atoms are a totally separate entity.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Chemical symbols represent elements whose atoms participate in bonding; atoms are the entities that make up elements and compounds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect element symbols to atoms of those elements and use that link to explain how substances are formed.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: In his model, elements make up molecules and atoms are a totally separate entity.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 1 student case described (student 0089)
all_misconceptions.population: High performing high school chemistry student
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Learning Progressions to Inform Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment Design

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think interactions between oppositely charged species are ionic bonds rather than ion-dipole interactions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ion-dipole interactions are intermolecular attractions between an ion and the partial charges of a polar molecule; ionic bonds are intramolecular electrostatic attractions in an ionic lattice between full charges.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify whether the species involved are a charged ion and a polar molecule. If so, the attraction is an intermolecular ion-dipole force, not an ionic bond, because no new ionic lattice is formed and the attraction is between unlike charges across separate particles.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "interactions between oppositely charged species give ionic bonds"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 26% of the teacher trainees had alternative conceptions on Ion–dipole interaction
all_misconceptions.population: 82 firstyear chemistry major teacher trainees at the University of Education, Winneba
all_misconceptions.source_file: Teacher trainees' alternative conceptions about intermolecular forces _ University of Education, Winneba/Teacher trainees' alternative conceptions about intermolecular forces _ University of Education, Winneba.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teacher trainees' alternative conceptions about intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think London dispersion force occurs within a single molecule rather than between molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces are intermolecular forces arising from temporary induced dipoles between atoms or molecules, not forces within one molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first decide whether the interaction is inside a molecule or between separate molecules. Dispersion forces act between neighboring particles due to momentary electron fluctuations, so they cannot be located within a single molecule as a bond type.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "London dispersion force occurs within a single molecule rather than between molecules"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 37% of the teacher trainees had alternative conceptions on London dispersion forces
all_misconceptions.population: 82 firstyear chemistry major teacher trainees at the University of Education, Winneba
all_misconceptions.source_file: Teacher trainees' alternative conceptions about intermolecular forces _ University of Education, Winneba/Teacher trainees' alternative conceptions about intermolecular forces _ University of Education, Winneba.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teacher trainees' alternative conceptions about intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the major intermolecular force between I2 molecules is a covalent-ionic interaction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Between I2 molecules, the relevant intermolecular attraction is London dispersion force; covalent or ionic bonding does not occur between separate neutral I2 molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that I2 is a nonpolar diatomic molecule. Nonpolar molecules interact primarily through dispersion forces, so the force between distinct I2 molecules cannot be covalent or ionic.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Covalent –ionic interaction is the major intermolecular force that exists in different I2 molecules"
all_misconceptions.population: 82 firstyear chemistry major teacher trainees at the University of Education, Winneba
all_misconceptions.source_file: Teacher trainees' alternative conceptions about intermolecular forces _ University of Education, Winneba/Teacher trainees' alternative conceptions about intermolecular forces _ University of Education, Winneba.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teacher trainees' alternative conceptions about intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think any molecule containing O and H must form hydrogen bonding regardless of where those atoms appear in the structure.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to N, O, or F and an available lone pair on N, O, or F in another molecule or part of the same molecule, with molecular structure and proximity determining whether the interaction is possible.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should inspect the bonding context, not just the presence of O and H symbols. They must check whether H is directly attached to O, N, or F and whether a suitable acceptor atom is available for intermolecular donation/acceptance.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the perception that any molecule which contains 'O' and 'H' forms hydrogen bonding irrespective of their position in the molecule"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: more than 50% of the teacher trainees demonstrated alternative conceptions on hydrogen bonding
all_misconceptions.population: 82 firstyear chemistry major teacher trainees at the University of Education, Winneba
all_misconceptions.source_file: Teacher trainees' alternative conceptions about intermolecular forces _ University of Education, Winneba/Teacher trainees' alternative conceptions about intermolecular forces _ University of Education, Winneba.md
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teacher trainees' alternative conceptions about intermolecular forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonding only exists for O-H groups and not for N-H or F-H groups.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding can occur when hydrogen is bonded to N, O, or F, so N-H and F-H can also participate in hydrogen bonding.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should apply the general rule that H-bond donors are X-H where X is N, O, or F. They should not restrict hydrogen bonding to only hydroxyl groups.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonding only exists between 'O' and 'H' but not between N-H and F-H"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: more than 50% of the teacher trainees demonstrated alternative conceptions on hydrogen bonding
all_misconceptions.population: 82 firstyear chemistry major teacher trainees at the University of Education, Winneba
