all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that dispersion forces do not require a permanent dipole; they originate from momentary electron fluctuations that induce attraction between neighboring particles.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "London forces are forces that occur between nonpolar molecules and dipole permanent."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 4; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think London forces occur in ethanol specifically between the ethyl group and the OH group.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces can occur between all molecules and between regions of electron density; ethanol also exhibits dipole-dipole interactions and hydrogen bonding due to its polar O-H group.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate the different intermolecular forces present in ethanol and not assign dispersion only to named functional groups in a molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "London forces occur in ethanol i.e. between ethyl and OH"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 5; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think London forces in CH4 are caused by the tetrahedral shape of the molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces in CH4 are due to temporary induced dipoles; tetrahedral shape makes CH4 nonpolar overall, but shape itself is not the cause of dispersion forces.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should understand that molecular shape affects overall polarity, while dispersion forces come from instantaneous electron fluctuations present in all molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "London forces occur in CH4 due to the tetrahedral shape of the CH4 molecule"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 6; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think London force is simply a nonpolar force.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces are not defined as a 'nonpolar force'; they are attractive forces arising from temporary dipoles and can occur in all species, though they dominate in nonpolar substances.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain the source of the force, not label it only by the polarity class of the molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "London force is a nonpolar force"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 7; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think London forces occur between positive and negative ions on a molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces are attractions between instantaneous and induced dipoles, not ion-ion attractions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the interacting particles correctly: dispersion involves electron cloud fluctuations, not ionic charges.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "London force occurs between positive and negative ions on a molecule"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 8; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think London force is simply a force of attraction that occurs between atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces are intermolecular attractions arising from induced dipoles; saying 'between atoms' is too vague and can incorrectly imply ordinary atomic bonding.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should specify that these are transient dipole-based attractions between neighboring atoms or molecules, not generic attraction or covalent bonding.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The London force is a force of attraction that occurs between atoms"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 9; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think nonpolar molecules can undergo permanent dipoles.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nonpolar molecules do not have permanent dipoles; they can only have temporary, induced dipoles that give rise to London dispersion forces.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that permanent dipoles require an uneven, persistent charge distribution, which nonpolar molecules lack.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Nonpolar molecules can undergo permanent dipoles"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 10; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the bonds in CH4 and O2 are weak bonds in the context of London forces.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: CH4 and O2 are molecular substances held together within molecules by covalent bonds; London forces are the weak intermolecular attractions between molecules, not the covalent bonds inside them.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular covalent bonding from intermolecular attraction and recognize that London forces explain physical properties of the molecular substance.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The bond in the compounds CH4 and O2 is a weak bond"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 11; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a low boiling point is due to London forces being very weak and unrelated to the number of electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion strength generally increases with the number of electrons and polarizability; larger electron clouds usually lead to stronger dispersion and higher boiling points.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should relate dispersion strength to electron count and polarizability, then connect stronger dispersion to greater energy needed to separate molecules and thus higher boiling point.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students think that the low boiling point is due to the London force which is indeed very weak and is not related to the number of electrons"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 12; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think any polar molecule such as HCl is automatically described only as having 'polar intermolecular force' rather than as having specific dipole-dipole interactions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole forces are specific attractions between the positive end of one polar molecule and the negative end of another polar molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the partial charges on polar molecules and explain the attraction between opposite ends of neighboring molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "HCl molecules are polar molecules, so the interaction between HCl molecules is a polar intermolecular force"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 13; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the attractive force in HCl is simply because H is positive and Cl is negative as whole atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole attraction is due to partial charges within polar molecules, not full ionic charges on atoms.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the idea of partial positive and partial negative ends arising from electronegativity differences and molecular polarity.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "H atoms as positive atoms and Cl as negative atoms produce attractive forces"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 14; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think polar molecules have a positive dipole and a negative dipole in the polar region as if dipoles were objects or regions rather than a charge separation vector.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A dipole is a separation of partial positive and partial negative charge within a molecule; dipole-dipole attraction is the interaction between those molecular dipoles.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should describe the polarity of the molecule and the alignment of partial charges, rather than treating the dipole as a separate substance or region.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "This polar molecule has a positive dipole and negative dipole in the polar region"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 15; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think dipole-dipole attraction is just positive dipoles binding to negative dipoles without explaining the molecular polarity and partial charge distribution.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole forces are electrostatic attractions between the partially positive end of one polar molecule and the partially negative end of another polar molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify polar molecules, partial charges, and how orientation of molecules leads to attraction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Polar molecules have permanent dipoles so that positive dipoles will bind to negative dipoles."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 16; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonds are formed because electrons are shared in a covalent bond.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction involving H bonded to N, O, or F interacting with a lone pair on another electronegative atom; it is not formed by shared electron use in a covalent bond.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish covalent electron sharing within a molecule from hydrogen bonding between molecules based on H attached to N/O/F and attraction to a lone pair.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonds are formed due to shared electron usage"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 17; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonds occur between N and H atoms specifically.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding occurs when hydrogen covalently bonded to N, O, or F interacts with a lone pair on another N, O, or F atom in a neighboring molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the donor atom bonded to hydrogen and the acceptor lone pair on a nearby electronegative atom, not just any N-H pair.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonds occur between N and H atoms"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 18; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonding uses PEB for bonding.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is explained by electrostatic attraction involving a hydrogen donor and lone-pair acceptor; it is not a use of 'PEB' as a bonding mechanism.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should apply the accepted model of hydrogen bonding: H attached to N/O/F and attraction to a lone pair on a neighboring molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonds uses PEB fot bonding"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 19; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonds occur between atoms within a molecule rather than between molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular force; it occurs between molecules or molecular regions, not as an intramolecular atom-to-atom bond within one molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish internal covalent bonds from external intermolecular attractions and place hydrogen bonding between molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students define that hydrogen bonds occur between atoms in a molecule, not intermolecular"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 20; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think differences in electronegativity of covalent compounds affect boiling point in the same way as hydrogen-bond strength.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point depends on the overall intermolecular forces present; hydrogen bonding strength depends on the specific H-bonding interactions involving H bonded to N, O, or F and the acceptor lone pair.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect electronegativity differences to polarity and then determine whether hydrogen bonding is possible, rather than directly equating covalent bond electronegativity difference with boiling point.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students assume that the difference in electronegativity of covalent compounds affects the boiling point."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 21; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bond strength is directly determined by the electronegativity difference between H and N/O/F.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bond strength depends on factors such as the polarity of the H-X bond, the identity and proximity of the acceptor atom, and the environment; it is not simply a direct function of electronegativity difference alone.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from molecular structure and intermolecular geometry, not from a single electronegativity-difference rule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The strength of the hydrogen bond is affected by the difference in electronegativity between H and the elements N, O, and F."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 22; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bond strength is affected by PEB.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bond strength is determined by the nature of the donor and acceptor atoms and the intermolecular electrostatic interaction, not by an undefined factor labeled PEB.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the accepted structural criteria for hydrogen bonding and evaluate donor-acceptor interactions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bond strength is affected by PEB"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 23; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bond strength is related to the acidity of the substance.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bond strength is not the same as acid strength; it depends on the intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen donor and acceptor, not on how acidic the substance is.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate acid-base behavior from intermolecular hydrogen bonding and identify the molecular features that allow hydrogen bonding.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The strength of hydrogen bonds is related to the acidity of the substance"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 24; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonding occurs whenever H is attached to one of F, O, or N atoms, without requiring interaction with a neighboring acceptor.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires a donor H bonded to F, O, or N and an acceptor lone pair on a neighboring electronegative atom; mere presence of H-F, H-O, or H-N is not sufficient.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check both donor and acceptor requirements and recognize that hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular interaction between molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students assume that hydrogen bonding occurs at the H atom with one of the F, O, and, N atoms."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 25; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think ether molecules form hydrogen bonds between O and H atoms within the ether molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ethers do not hydrogen bond with themselves in the same way alcohols do because they lack an O-H bond; hydrogen bonding requires a hydrogen donor and an acceptor on another molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should inspect functional groups and determine whether a molecule can donate hydrogen bonds; ethers can accept but not donate hydrogen bonds.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonding occurs between O and H atoms in ether molecules"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 26; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the O-H bond in an alcohol molecule is a hydrogen bond.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The O-H bond inside an alcohol is a covalent bond; hydrogen bonding is the intermolecular attraction between the alcohol molecule and another molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular covalent bonds from intermolecular hydrogen bonds and identify the latter between molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The bond between the elements H and O in the alcohol molecule is a hydrogen bond"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 27; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonding is present in the OH group of any polar molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires a hydrogen atom directly bonded to N, O, or F and an acceptor lone pair; not every OH-containing or polar molecule necessarily exhibits the same hydrogen-bonding behavior.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate the donor-acceptor pattern and not infer hydrogen bonding from polarity alone.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonding is present in the OH group of polar molecules"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 28; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonding occurs in methane between carbon and hydrogen atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Methane does not exhibit hydrogen bonding because C-H bonds do not create the highly polarized donor required for hydrogen bonding, and methane lacks the required electronegative atoms and lone-pair acceptors.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine whether the molecule contains H bonded to N/O/F and whether another molecule provides an acceptor lone pair; methane does not meet these criteria.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonding occurs in methane (C and H atoms)"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented as misconception 29; no item-level percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: 88 chemistry education students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Misconceptions of Intermolecular Forces in General Chemistry Courses

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that both bond formation and bond breaking require energy, rather than recognizing that bond formation releases energy and bond breaking requires energy input.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Forming a chemical bond releases energy, while breaking a chemical bond requires energy input.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish the two processes: when atoms come together to form a bond, the system moves to a lower potential energy state and energy is released; when a bond is broken, energy must be supplied to overcome the attraction between atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "many students created a mental model where both bond formation and bond breaking require energy"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Only about 20% chose both correct statements (B + C); 63% of the CH14 cohort chose combinations with D
all_misconceptions.population: Swedish upper secondary students, Swedish first-term university chemistry students (CH13/CH14), and University of Cape Town first-term chemistry students (UCT)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching of chemical bonding: a study of Swedish and South African students' conceptions of bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students blend individual bond formation with exothermic/endothermic reaction concepts and may think that endothermic reaction diagrams mean bond formation requires energy.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Individual bond formation/breaking should be separated from overall reaction enthalpy; bond formation releases energy even though some reactions may be endothermic overall.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should not infer bond energetics from the overall heat flow of a reaction. They should reason about bond formation as a local process at the level of individual bonds and interpret energy diagrams correctly in that context.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "many students choose the alternative D which is interpreted as an indication of a blending of the concepts of individual bond forming and the concept of reactions being exo- or endothermic"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 63% of the CH14 cohort chose combinations with D
all_misconceptions.population: CH14 Swedish first-year university chemistry students after studying bonding
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching of chemical bonding: a study of Swedish and South African students' conceptions of bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that macroscopic properties such as hardness and conductivity determine the type of bond in a substance.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond type determines many macroscopic properties of a substance, not the other way around.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from microscopic structure to macroscopic properties: the bonding arrangement leads to characteristic properties such as conductivity and hardness.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students are inclined to believe that the inherent (macroscopic) properties of the substance determine the bond type and not vice versa"
all_misconceptions.population: Secondary and tertiary chemistry students discussed in the literature review and survey design
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching of chemical bonding: a study of Swedish and South African students' conceptions of bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students select a two-dimensional or non-tetrahedral representation as the closest shape of methane, indicating difficulty relating molecules to three-dimensional structures.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Methane has a three-dimensional tetrahedral shape.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use VSEPR-style reasoning or space-filling/3D models to recognize that four bonding pairs around carbon arrange tetrahedrally in 3D space.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students choosing the wheel spanner and the ceramic tile may have problems relating atoms and molecules to threedimensional structures."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Almost none chose the ceramic tile; 47% of South African students chose the tetrahedron
all_misconceptions.population: Swedish upper secondary students, Swedish first-term university chemistry students, and University of Cape Town first-term chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching of chemical bonding: a study of Swedish and South African students' conceptions of bonding

all_misconceptions.subtopic: intermolecular vs covalent bonding in methane
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think methane atoms are held together by intermolecular forces rather than covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The carbon and hydrogen atoms in methane are held together by covalent bonds within the molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify electron sharing between carbon and hydrogen atoms as the intramolecular covalent bonding mechanism, not intermolecular attraction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Indication of the use of concepts and with evidence of that the view of the interaction is intermolecular."
all_misconceptions.population: Students responding to Q4 about bonding in methane
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching of chemical bonding: a study of Swedish and South African students' conceptions of bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students explain covalent bonding in methane as ionic attraction due to partial charges, rather than electron sharing.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Covalent bonding in methane is explained by shared electrons and orbital reasoning, not by ionic attraction between oppositely charged atoms.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that carbon and hydrogen share electrons to achieve stable valence configurations; the bond is not formed because like or unlike charges attract as if it were ionic.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Indication of the use of concepts with evidence of the view of the interaction is of an ionic nature and/ or due to charge attraction."
all_misconceptions.population: Students responding to Q4 about bonding in methane
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching of chemical bonding: a study of Swedish and South African students' conceptions of bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think potassium chloride exists as molecules rather than as an ionic lattice.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Potassium chloride is an ionic solid consisting of a lattice of potassium ions and chloride ions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that ionic compounds form extended lattices, not discrete molecules, and should distinguish formula units from molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Potassium chloride exists in the form of molecules!"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 55-60% of students from all educational levels or curricula
all_misconceptions.population: Swedish upper secondary students, Swedish first-term university chemistry students (CH13/CH14), and University of Cape Town first-term chemistry students (UCT)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching of chemical bonding: a study of Swedish and South African students' conceptions of bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that after electron transfer, the potassium ion and chloride ion form a molecule together.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: After ion formation, KCl is held together in a non-directional ionic lattice; it does not become a molecule of ion pairs.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that electron transfer creates ions, but the resulting attraction organizes them into a repeating lattice rather than discrete molecular units.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "After donating its valence electron to the chlorine atom, the potassium ion forms a molecule with the chloride ion!"
all_misconceptions.population: Students responding to Q6 on potassium chloride
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching of chemical bonding: a study of Swedish and South African students' conceptions of bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think potassium chloride is a lattice of covalently bonded potassium and chlorine atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Potassium chloride is an ionic lattice of potassium ions and chloride ions, not a covalent network of atoms.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the ionic model: electron transfer forms ions, and electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions holds the lattice together.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Potassium chloride exists as a lattice of covalently bonded potassium and chlorine atoms!"
all_misconceptions.population: Students responding to Q6 on potassium chloride
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching of chemical bonding: a study of Swedish and South African students' conceptions of bonding

all_misconceptions.subtopic: bonding only between an ion pair rather than a lattice
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students see ionic bonding as a bond only between two ions in a pair and fail to understand the extended, non-directional lattice.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ionic bonding is a non-directional electrostatic attraction operating throughout the crystal lattice.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from repeating ion arrangement and charge attraction across the whole solid, not from a single bond between one cation and one anion.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "they fail to see ionic bonding as being non-directional; instead it is strictly seen as a bond between the two ions."
all_misconceptions.population: Students discussing KCl lattice structure and ionic bonding
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching of chemical bonding: a study of Swedish and South African students' conceptions of bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat the formula unit of an ionic compound as if it were a molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A formula unit is a representation of the simplest ion ratio in an ionic solid; it is not a discrete molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish molecular compounds from ionic solids and interpret formulas like NaCl or KCl as repeating units in a lattice.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "we didn't differentiate between molecules and ionic compounds"
all_misconceptions.population: CH14 interview students and students discussing ionic compounds
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching of chemical bonding: a study of Swedish and South African students' conceptions of bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Intermolecular forces, including London dispersion forces, occur within atoms or molecules rather than between separate species.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces are interactions between separate atoms or molecules, not within a single atom or molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular structure from intermolecular interaction and recognize that the attractive force acts across the space between two separate helium atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: students ... indicated that IMFs (hydrogen bonding, dipole-dipole, or London dispersion forces [LDFs]) are interactions within (rather than between) atoms.
all_misconceptions.population: General chemistry students discussed in prior work cited by the paper; also reflected in the paper's framing of student misconceptions
all_misconceptions.source_title: Characterizing Students' Mechanistic Reasoning about London Dispersion Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: London dispersion forces are only present between molecules, not between atoms such as helium atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces can occur between neutral atoms as well as molecules; helium atoms can interact via LDFs.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that any neutral species with electron clouds can experience temporary charge fluctuations that lead to attraction, including atoms like helium.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: he believed that intermolecular forces take place between molecules only (and not atoms).
all_misconceptions.population: Devon, an interview participant
all_misconceptions.source_title: Characterizing Students' Mechanistic Reasoning about London Dispersion Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Helium atoms will overcome repulsion and form an He2 molecule/covalent bond when they interact.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Helium atoms do not form a covalent bond or stable He2 molecule in the context discussed; the key interaction is a weak intermolecular London dispersion attraction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that helium atoms remain separate neutral atoms and that any attraction is due to temporary induced dipoles, not electron sharing or molecule formation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: then once they get over those repulsive forces, then they're gonna form a molecule of helium.
all_misconceptions.population: Devon, an interview participant
all_misconceptions.source_title: Characterizing Students' Mechanistic Reasoning about London Dispersion Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Atoms are attracted because of generic stability, the octet rule, or because atoms 'want' to bond, rather than because of electrostatic interactions from electron-cloud fluctuations.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The attraction arises from electrostatic interactions caused by momentary electron density fluctuations that create an instantaneous dipole and an induced dipole.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain that random electron motion can create an uneven charge distribution, which induces a dipole in a neighboring atom and leads to attraction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: These included the notions of "stability" or the octet rule as driving atoms to share electrons.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in the interview study; E1 was the least sophisticated category and more common in the online assessment
all_misconceptions.population: Undergraduate general chemistry students; one interview participant and more students in the online assessment
all_misconceptions.source_title: Characterizing Students' Mechanistic Reasoning about London Dispersion Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Atoms attract because they have an overall positive and negative charge, or because protons and electrons simply attract without a dipole/charge separation concept.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Neutral helium atoms attract through temporary separation of charge within the atom, producing instantaneous and induced dipoles rather than overall atomic charge.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the arrangement of electrons and protons to a temporary dipole, not just say that positive and negative charges attract in a generic way.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: I believe that helium atoms move towards each other because of the positive and negative charges within the atom. Since the atoms both have opposite charges, they attract to one another
all_misconceptions.prevalence: This was the E2 type; 43% of the 250 online responses were E2 explanations
all_misconceptions.population: 250 undergraduate general chemistry online responses
all_misconceptions.source_title: Characterizing Students' Mechanistic Reasoning about London Dispersion Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A student can explain the interaction by saying electrons fluctuate or dipoles are temporary, without being able to explain how electron-density fluctuation produces the dipole.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should explain that electrons are in constant motion; random fluctuations can create an instantaneous uneven electron distribution, which makes one side of an atom partially negative and the other partially positive.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should trace the causal sequence from electron motion to uneven charge distribution to dipole formation and then to attraction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: She mentioned that electrons "fluctuate", but seemed unsure of what this term meant.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Three interview participants were E3; two additional participants used terms like temporary dipole/fluctuation superficially
all_misconceptions.population: Interview participants in Study 1
all_misconceptions.source_title: Characterizing Students' Mechanistic Reasoning about London Dispersion Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Both interacting atoms must simultaneously experience temporary dipoles for attraction to occur.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A temporary dipole in one atom can induce a dipole in a neighboring atom; simultaneous temporary dipoles are not required.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that one atom's momentary dipole polarizes the neighbor, creating an induced dipole and thus attraction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: She did not seem to recognize that a more likely scenario is that a temporary dipole in one atom would induce a dipole in a second.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: This idea was expressed by 2 of the 12 interview participants
all_misconceptions.population: 12 semi-structured interview participants
all_misconceptions.source_title: Characterizing Students' Mechanistic Reasoning about London Dispersion Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Atoms interact because their electron cloud is 'floppy' or overlaps, without a coherent explanation of dipole formation from electron density fluctuation.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The interaction comes from an uneven electron distribution creating a temporary dipole, which then induces a dipole in the neighboring atom.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the electrostatic origin of the force and explain how shifting electron density creates partial charges across the atom.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Umm, their electron cloud is...floppy. So then it moves one way for an instant.
all_misconceptions.population: Macayla, an interview participant
all_misconceptions.source_title: Characterizing Students' Mechanistic Reasoning about London Dispersion Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: The paper identifies a misconception of the interaction as simply 'holding on' or electrons linking atoms without recognizing the need for a dipole; however the student did correctly reason that closer distance strengthens attraction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrostatic attraction depends on distance, but the key mechanism is the presence of a dipole and induced dipole, not just generic holding together or linking of electrons.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect distance-dependent electrostatic force to a specific charge separation in the atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Um, it was kind of just a representation of a, some sort of...like a, not dipole—dipole. It's a London dispersion bond.
all_misconceptions.population: Ryan, an interview participant
all_misconceptions.source_title: Characterizing Students' Mechanistic Reasoning about London Dispersion Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Strength of electrical interaction is not understood as inversely related to distance between interacting particles.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrical attraction becomes weaker as distance increases and stronger as particles get closer together.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that the nearer electron and nucleus experience a stronger attraction than more distant ones.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: he correctly identified that the strength of an electrical interaction would be inversely related to the distance between particles
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Identified across levels; students with all levels used this idea
all_misconceptions.population: Students across explanation levels in both studies
all_misconceptions.source_title: Characterizing Students' Mechanistic Reasoning about London Dispersion Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students use visual estimation from an image to judge bond length, rather than inferring bond length from bond order and atomic identity.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: For SO2, both S–O bonds are the same length because they are equivalent bonds with the same bond order.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify that each bond is between the same pair of atoms (S and O) and that each S–O bond has bond order 2; equivalent bonds with the same bond order should have the same length.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students may attempt a visual estimation of the length and predict that the bonds are of different lengths based on what their visual estimation of length from the image provided"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Visual estimation was coded in 5.8% of bond-length responses (63/1080).
all_misconceptions.population: 1086 second-semester general chemistry students; bond-length open-ended responses analyzed N=1080
all_misconceptions.source_title: The impact of representations of chemical bonding on students' predictions of chemical properties

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat the space-filling model's apparent atom sizes as a basis for deciding that the S–O bonds are unequal or for misjudging bond length.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond length should be inferred from chemical structure, especially bond order and whether the bonds are equivalent, not from superficial visual size cues in the model.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that the model is a representation and that bond length depends on the underlying bonding pattern; because both S–O bonds are equivalent, their lengths should be the same.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students might make an inaccurate visual estimate of the representation given or may be cued to features that are unrelated to the chemical property"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Size of atom was coded in 6.7% of bond-length responses (72/1080); it was the notable deleterious feature for correctness.
all_misconceptions.population: 1086 second-semester general chemistry students; space-filling group especially cued to size of atom
all_misconceptions.source_title: The impact of representations of chemical bonding on students' predictions of chemical properties

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students rely on resonance or Lewis structure conventions they infer from a chemical formula, even though the formula itself does not show bonding details.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The chemical formula alone does not show bond order or resonance; to infer equal bond lengths, students need to use actual structural information and recognize the equivalent S–O bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should not infer bond length directly from formula symbols; instead they should use a structure that shows connectivity and bond order, or reason from known chemistry that the two S–O bonds are equivalent.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students with chemical formula were more often cued to Lewis dot structures and resonance"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Resonance was coded in 4.1% of bond-length responses (44/1080).
all_misconceptions.population: 1086 second-semester general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: The impact of representations of chemical bonding on students' predictions of chemical properties

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a linear shape means SO2 is nonpolar.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SO2 is bent, so its bond dipoles do not cancel and the molecule is polar.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine the molecular geometry from the structure, recognize SO2 is bent, then infer that the polar S–O bonds produce a net dipole that does not cancel.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "No students citing linear shape made a correct polarity prediction"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Linear shape was coded in 1.5% of polarity responses (16/1081).
all_misconceptions.population: 1086 second-semester general chemistry students; polarity open-ended responses analyzed N=1081
all_misconceptions.source_title: The impact of representations of chemical bonding on students' predictions of chemical properties

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assume a Lewis dot structure explicitly shows molecular shape, and may therefore misread the geometry as linear.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lewis dot structures do not explicitly determine the molecular shape; the bent geometry of SO2 must be inferred using electron domains/VSEPR.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should count electron groups around sulfur, apply VSEPR, and conclude the molecule is bent rather than reading shape directly off the Lewis structure.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "a small proportion of students attribute molecular shape as an explicit property of Lewis dot structures"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 3.4% of students receiving Lewis dot structure described a linear shape, and all of those students were incorrect on polarity.
all_misconceptions.population: Students receiving Lewis dot structure in the polarity task
all_misconceptions.source_title: The impact of representations of chemical bonding on students' predictions of chemical properties

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe the bond dipoles in SO2 cancel out, making the molecule nonpolar.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In bent SO2, the bond dipoles do not cancel, so the molecule has a net dipole moment and is polar.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the S–O bonds as polar, then use the bent shape to conclude that the dipole vectors add rather than cancel.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the dipole forces cancel each other out making the structure of the molecule non-polar."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Net dipole moment zero was coded in 1.8% of polarity responses (19/1081).
all_misconceptions.population: 1086 second-semester general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: The impact of representations of chemical bonding on students' predictions of chemical properties

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the S–O bonds are nonpolar because electrons are shared equally or because the molecule has equal sharing of bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: S and O have different electronegativities, so each S–O bond is polar and contributes to the molecule's overall polarity.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare electronegativities of sulfur and oxygen, conclude the bond is polar, then combine that with bent geometry to infer the molecule is polar.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "This molecule is a nonpolar, because there is equal sharing of bonds in the electrons."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Nature of nonpolar bonds was coded in 1.1% of polarity responses (12/1081).
all_misconceptions.population: 1086 second-semester general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: The impact of representations of chemical bonding on students' predictions of chemical properties

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the bond dipoles or charges simply cancel because of symmetry-like reasoning without applying the actual bent geometry of SO2.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The bent molecular shape prevents cancellation of the bond dipoles, so the molecule remains polar.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from actual geometry and vector addition of bond dipoles, not from a vague idea that opposite charges always cancel.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the bond dipoles of the two s=o bonds do not cancel"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Net dipole moment nonzero was coded in 4.7% of polarity responses (51/1081).
all_misconceptions.population: 1086 second-semester general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: The impact of representations of chemical bonding on students' predictions of chemical properties

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students identify the strongest intermolecular force as occurring within H2O, confusing an intermolecular attraction with an intramolecular bond.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The strongest intermolecular force between SO2 and H2O occurs between H of water and O of SO2, not within one molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intermolecular attraction between two molecules from intramolecular bonding within a molecule, then locate the attraction between the partially positive H in water and partially negative O in SO2.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students mistake an intermolecular force for an intramolecular bond"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: The most common distractor for location was between O in H2O and H in H2O; exact percentage not given in text.
all_misconceptions.population: Students answering the intermolecular-force location prompt
all_misconceptions.source_title: The impact of representations of chemical bonding on students' predictions of chemical properties

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students select dipole-dipole interaction instead of hydrogen bonding as the strongest force between SO2 and H2O.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The strongest intermolecular force between SO2 and H2O is hydrogen bonding, because water hydrogen interacts with oxygen in SO2.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify that water has H bonded to O and that SO2 has a suitable electronegative O site, then apply the definition of hydrogen bonding rather than choosing the weaker generic dipole-dipole interaction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students receiving chemical formula were more likely to select dipole-dipole interaction"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Among incorrect responses, 41.4% of chemical-formula students selected dipole-dipole interaction.
all_misconceptions.population: Students receiving chemical formula in the intermolecular-force type prompt
all_misconceptions.source_title: The impact of representations of chemical bonding on students' predictions of chemical properties

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to O in the wrong molecule or otherwise misassign hydrogen bonding as an intramolecular feature.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding between SO2 and H2O occurs between the H of water and the O of sulfur dioxide.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should apply the hydrogen-bonding definition and identify the donor/acceptor sites across the two molecules, not within one molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bond is between hydrogen and oxygen"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Hydrogen bonding – intramolecular was coded in 16.7% of intermolecular-force responses (179/1070).
all_misconceptions.population: 1086 second-semester general chemistry students; intermolecular-force open-ended responses analyzed N=1070
all_misconceptions.source_title: The impact of representations of chemical bonding on students' predictions of chemical properties

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students state that hydrogen bonding is present without specifying the correct molecular location or applying it to the pair of molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding must be identified as an intermolecular interaction between specific atoms on two different molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should name hydrogen bonding and explicitly connect it to H in water and O in SO2 to justify the strongest interaction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Student mentions hydrogen bonding without specifying location"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Hydrogen bonding – ambiguous was coded in 16.6% of intermolecular-force responses (178/1070).
all_misconceptions.population: 1086 second-semester general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: The impact of representations of chemical bonding on students' predictions of chemical properties

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat hydrogen bonds as covalent bonds between water molecules, including hydrogen-to-hydrogen or oxygen-to-oxygen bonds between neighboring molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonds are intermolecular electrostatic attractions, not covalent bonds, and in water they form between a hydrogen atom on one molecule and a lone pair on the oxygen atom of another molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that covalent bonds hold atoms together within a water molecule, while hydrogen bonds are weaker attractions between separate molecules caused by polarity; therefore, the interaction is drawn between H of one molecule and O lone pairs of another, not as a shared covalent bond between molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "intermolecular interactions are represented as covalent bonds between molecules rather than as electrostatic interactions; hydrogen bonds are formed between hydrogen and hydrogen atoms, or oxygen and oxygen atoms."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 10/60 diagrams
all_misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Structure of water and bonding capacity
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a hydrogen atom in water can form more than one covalent bond, or that oxygen can make double bonds to hydrogen to complete an octet like carbon dioxide.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In water, each hydrogen forms only one covalent bond, and the water molecule has a bent structure with two O-H covalent bonds and two lone pairs on oxygen.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should apply valence and bonding rules: hydrogen can only have one bond, oxygen typically forms two covalent bonds in water, and lone pairs on oxygen influence molecular shape but do not create extra covalent bonds to hydrogen.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the oxygen atom formed double bonds with hydrogen atoms to complete an octet"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: part of 3/10 category A diagrams
all_misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students are unsure how lone pairs participate and may think lone pairs on oxygen collectively form one negatively charged region that attracts neighboring molecules without a clear directional lone-pair-to-hydrogen interaction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Each lone pair on oxygen can serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor site, and hydrogen bonds are directional interactions between a specific hydrogen atom and a specific lone pair on a neighboring molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify individual lone pairs as distinct electron-rich sites on oxygen and match them with hydrogen atoms on adjacent molecules, showing a directional interaction rather than a diffuse attraction from an undifferentiated negative region.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the role of lone pairs of electrons in forming a hydrogen bond is unclear. The lone pairs form an electron dense region around the oxygen atom to form one or numerous hydrogen bonds"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 20/60 diagrams
all_misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the two lone pairs on oxygen collectively form a single partially negative region that attracts multiple neighbors without directionality.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The lone pairs are separate electron domains on oxygen and hydrogen bonding involves specific donor-acceptor directions between particular sites on adjacent molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should represent each lone pair as a distinct accepting site and show how each site participates in a limited number of directional hydrogen bonds according to molecular geometry.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the two lone pairs of electrons collectively formed a single partially negative ( δ - ) region"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: about half of category B diagrams; 8/20 category B diagrams
all_misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a hydrogen atom in water can attract more than one neighboring oxygen, allowing one hydrogen to make multiple hydrogen bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Each hydrogen atom can donate only one hydrogen bond because it has only one covalently bonded hydrogen available as the donor site.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that a single hydrogen participates in one covalent O-H bond and can serve as one hydrogen-bond donor to one acceptor at a time, constrained by water's geometry.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "each hydrogen atom of a central molecule appeared to have enough positive charge to attract more than one oxygen atom from neighbouring water molecules"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: reported in category B; specific count not given
all_misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think each individual nonbonding electron on oxygen can independently form a hydrogen bond, as if each electron is a separate bonding site.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding involves the lone pair as the acceptor site on oxygen; it is not each electron individually that forms a bond.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason in terms of lone pairs/electron domains and molecular geometry, not individual electrons; the oxygen atom offers acceptor lone-pair sites for hydrogen bonding.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "each of the four nonbonding electrons on the oxygen atom in a water molecule can individually form a hydrogen bond with a hydrogen atom in a neighbouring water molecule"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 8/20 category B diagrams
all_misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonds are nondirectional attractions between broad positive and negative regions and can be represented in a flat 2D plane.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonds are directional intermolecular interactions between specific hydrogen atoms and lone pairs on neighboring molecules, and real water networks in snowflakes are three-dimensional.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should place molecules according to water's tetrahedral electron-domain geometry and show specific H-to-lone-pair interactions in 3D rather than a flat, undirected arrangement.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "hydrogen bonds were not covalent in nature – they are electrostatic interactions between molecules but the role of lone pairs of electrons in forming a hydrogen bond is unclear"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 25/60 diagrams for 2D space; 5/60 for 3D space
all_misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think water molecules in snowflakes interact only in a flat plane rather than in three dimensions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In snowflakes, water molecules form a 3D tetrahedral hydrogen-bond network with four hydrogen bonds per water molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should infer from water's molecular geometry that hydrogen bonding extends in three dimensions, with two donor and two acceptor sites arranged tetrahedrally.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the interactions among water molecules were represented in 2D space"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 25/60 diagrams
all_misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a water molecule can form only two hydrogen bonds because only the lone pairs on oxygen participate, or otherwise fail to recognize the four-bond maximum in snowflakes.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Each water molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds: two as donor through its hydrogens and two as acceptor through its lone pairs.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should count both donor and acceptor sites on water and use the tetrahedral arrangement to explain why the maximum number is four.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "one water molecule in a snowflake could form a maximum of two hydrogen bonds with neighbouring molecules in 2D"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: present in some category C diagrams; specific count not given
all_misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a water molecule can form more than four hydrogen bonds because molecules can approach too closely in a 2D representation.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A water molecule has only four hydrogen-bonding sites in total, so it cannot exceed four hydrogen bonds in the snowflake network.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the two hydrogens and two lone pairs as the limit on hydrogen-bond formation and recognize that geometry prevents more than four total hydrogen bonds per molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "water molecules could approach each other so closely that a hydrogen atom in one water molecule could form more than one hydrogen bond and a water molecule could form more than four hydrogen bonds with neighbouring molecules"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: in one category C example (Albert); not quantified for all students
all_misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think two oxygen atoms from different molecules can share a common hydrogen atom as part of hydrogen bonding.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A hydrogen bond is not a shared covalent hydrogen between two oxygens; it is an attraction between a hydrogen bonded to one oxygen and a lone pair on another oxygen.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish covalent O-H bonds within a molecule from hydrogen-bond attractions between molecules and avoid depicting a hydrogen atom as being jointly shared by two oxygens.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "two oxygen atoms of different molecules sharing a common hydrogen atom between them"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: listed among alternative conceptions in the conclusion; specific count not given
all_misconceptions.population: 60 first- and second-year undergraduate chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of students' diagrams of water molecules in snowflakes to reveal their conceptual understanding of hydrogen bonds

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think dipole-dipole interactions occur within a single molecule rather than between two molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interactions are intermolecular forces that occur between separate molecules, not within one molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the partial positive region of one polar molecule and the partial negative region of another polar molecule, then connect the interacting atoms across the two molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “a large portion of the students believed that intermolecular forces were within a single molecule rather than between”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: a large portion of the students (no exact count given)
all_misconceptions.population: students in a study of intermolecular forces cited in the paper
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat lone pairs as bonding sites that should be shared or filled by forming a new bond between molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lone pairs are nonbonding electron pairs; they do not become shared covalent bonds in a dipole-dipole interaction task.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use lone pairs to infer molecular polarity or geometry when appropriate, but should still locate dipole-dipole attraction between partial charges on separate molecules, not create a new covalent bond.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “participants carried a conception that these interactions could be thought of in a similar fashion to covalent bonding.”
all_misconceptions.population: participants in this study
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think lone pairs are ‘available’ or ‘free to bond’ with other atoms, so they identify the lone pair itself as the interaction site.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lone pairs are electron pairs on an atom; they can influence polarity and geometry, but the intermolecular attraction is between molecular dipoles, not a lone pair bonding with another atom.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that lone pairs contribute to electron density and molecular shape, then use the resulting dipole orientation to determine where the attraction between molecules occurs.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the lone pairs represent sites that are free to bond with other atoms”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 5 students in Version 1 (Sawyer, Sasha, Sadie, Sabrina, Sebastian)
all_misconceptions.population: Version 1 students working with the Lewis dot representation
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a molecule has an ‘open spot’ or incomplete octet that must be filled, and use that as the dipole-dipole interaction site.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interactions are not determined by filling an octet; they depend on the alignment of partial charges in polar molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate electronegativity and molecular geometry to locate partial positive and negative ends, rather than searching for empty bonding sites.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students considered the space around each atom as the location where dipole-dipole interactions could occur”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: observed in Version 1 and discussed as recurring across participants; exact count not given
all_misconceptions.population: students in Version 1 and in the discussion of the study overall
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assume molecular geometry is explicit in Lewis dot structures and can be read directly without considering lone pairs.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lewis dot structures do not explicitly show 3D geometry; geometry must be inferred from electron domains and lone pairs.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should count bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central atom to infer shape, then use that shape to determine polarity and the dipole-dipole interaction site.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “three students carried the assumption that molecular geometry was explicit in Lewis dot structures”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 3 students in Version 2 (Regan, Rachel, Rebecca)
all_misconceptions.population: Version 2 students working with the Lewis dot representation
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think selenium dioxide is linear and nonpolar when lone pairs are ignored.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SeO2 has lone pairs on selenium that create a bent molecular geometry, making the molecule polar.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should include selenium’s lone pairs in the electron-domain arrangement, infer a bent shape, and then recognize that the dipoles do not cancel.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “designated the molecule as linear and non-polar, without taking into account the influence of lone pairs”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 3 students in Version 2 initially (Regan, Rachel, Rebecca)
all_misconceptions.population: Version 2 students in the Lewis dot structure task for selenium dioxide
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think bigger atoms produce stronger dipole-dipole interactions, or that size itself determines the interaction site.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atom size in these models is not the basis for dipole-dipole attraction; the interaction depends on molecular polarity and partial charges.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use electronegativity and molecular geometry to determine the dipole direction, and treat size as a representational feature not directly tied to interaction strength.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “The bigger the two atoms that are bonding are, the weaker the forces are.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 3 students in Version 1 (Sandeep, Sebastian, Spencer) used size in the ball-and-stick task; Sandeep remained consistent with size in space-filling
all_misconceptions.population: Version 1 students working with ball-and-stick and space-filling representations
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the number of bonds indicates the strength of dipole-dipole interactions or that more bonds mean a stronger intermolecular force.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond order describes intramolecular bonding; dipole-dipole strength is determined by molecular polarity and the arrangement of partial charges between molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate intramolecular bond order from intermolecular force strength, then compare electronegativity differences and geometry to locate the dipole-dipole interaction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the number of bonds signifies the strength of dipole-dipole interactions in the molecule”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: observed in Version 2 ball-and-stick task; exact count not given
all_misconceptions.population: Version 2 students in the ball-and-stick representation
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assign ionic or valence charges to atoms and use opposite charges as the basis for dipole-dipole attraction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interactions arise from partial charges in polar covalent molecules, not from assigning full ionic charges to atoms.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should infer partial positive and partial negative regions from electronegativity and molecular geometry, rather than treating atoms as ions with fixed charges.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students began assigning charges to each of the atoms in the molecules”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 4 students in Version 2 (Ria, Rachel, Rebecca, Richard)
all_misconceptions.population: Version 2 students working with the space-filling representation
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think dipole-dipole interaction could cause atoms to rearrange into new products, as if the molecules were undergoing a reaction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interaction is an intermolecular attraction in the present molecules; it does not imply atom rearrangement or product formation.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should locate the most positive and negative ends of the two molecules and draw an attraction between them without changing the molecules’ connectivity.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “I guess you could rearrange the atoms so that it would make each-- HCl would be a product.”
all_misconceptions.population: Richard in Version 2
