all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a central atom cannot participate in dipole-dipole interactions because it is central or less accessible.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The central atom can still contribute to molecular polarity and can be part of the dipole orientation; being central does not prevent intermolecular attraction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate the full molecular dipole from electronegativity and geometry, including the central atom’s role in bond polarity.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “chlorine is the central… and I don't really know how it's going to connect to the hydrogen”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: observed in Version 2 chemical formula task; exact count not given
all_misconceptions.population: Rachel and also Ranger/Richard with central carbon in Version 2
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think any bent geometry automatically means a molecule has dipole moments or that geometry alone determines polarity.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bent geometry can contribute to polarity, but polarity must be evaluated by considering bond polarity and whether dipoles cancel.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify molecular shape from lone pairs and then determine whether the vector sum of bond dipoles is nonzero.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “molecules with bent geometry always have dipole moments”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 1 student explicitly: Roger in Version 2
all_misconceptions.population: Version 2 ball-and-stick task
all_misconceptions.source_title: How ordering concrete and abstract representations in intermolecular force chemistry tasks influences students' thought processes on the location of dipole-dipole interactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Atoms form bonds because they "want" an octet.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms form bonds because the bonded system is more stable than the unbonded system, i.e. bonding lowers the system's energy.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that bonding occurs when atom-atom interactions decrease potential energy and produce a more stable arrangement; the octet rule is a guideline for drawing Lewis structures, not the causal explanation for bond formation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: One common misconception that students hold is that atoms form bonds because they "want" an octet, rather than because bonded atoms are more stable than unbonded ones.
all_misconceptions.population: students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Development and Assessment of a Molecular Structure and Properties Learning Progression

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Lewis structures are the same as the actual three-dimensional molecular structure, rather than simplified representations of it.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lewis structures are two-dimensional representations ("cartoons") that encode information about underlying three-dimensional molecular structure.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should understand that a Lewis structure is a symbolic, simplified model; they should translate between 2D drawings and 3D geometry rather than treating the drawing as the molecule itself.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: we stress the fact that Lewis structures are merely a convenient way to represent something more complex.
all_misconceptions.population: students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Development and Assessment of a Molecular Structure and Properties Learning Progression

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students can read only explicit structural information from Lewis structures and do not recognize that they also encode information needed to infer physical and chemical properties.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lewis structures can be used, together with molecular shape, electronegativity, and intermolecular forces, to infer properties such as boiling point, melting point, acidity/basicity, and reactivity.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the structural features in the Lewis structure, infer 3D shape and bond polarity, determine intermolecular forces, and then use those forces to predict macroscopic properties.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: the information that can be determined from a Lewis structure
all_misconceptions.prevalence: End of Fall: physical properties 13% control vs 38% treatment; reactivity 13% control vs 40% treatment; acidity/basicity 14% control vs 19% treatment. End of Spring: physical properties 27% control vs 54% treatment; reactivity 37% control vs 63% treatment; acidity/basicity 38% control vs 70% treatment.
all_misconceptions.population: general chemistry students in control and CLUE treatment cohorts
all_misconceptions.source_title: Development and Assessment of a Molecular Structure and Properties Learning Progression

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat boiling point and melting point as isolated facts to rank, but do not generalize to the broader category of physical properties.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: From molecular structure, students should infer broader physical properties, not only specific ranking tasks such as boiling point or melting point.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should move from structure to intermolecular forces and then to a wider class of physical properties, recognizing that boiling/melting point are examples rather than the whole category.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: some students from the control group chose melting and boiling points, but not physical properties.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: End of Fall: relative boiling points 20% control vs 56% treatment; relative melting points 18% control vs 50% treatment; physical properties 13% control vs 38% treatment. End of Spring: relative boiling points 46% control vs 54% treatment; relative melting points 38% control vs 48% treatment; physical properties 27% control vs 54% treatment.
all_misconceptions.population: general chemistry students in control and CLUE treatment cohorts
all_misconceptions.source_title: Development and Assessment of a Molecular Structure and Properties Learning Progression

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not recognize that a molecular structure can indicate acidic or basic behavior.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Functional groups and local structure can signal whether a substance may have acidic and/or basic properties.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should inspect the structure for proton-donating or proton-accepting sites and reason from those functional groups to acidity/basicity.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: CLUE students appear to have a better understanding of the uses of and information that is encoded into a Lewis structure.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: End of Fall: 14% control vs 19% treatment. End of Spring: 38% control vs 70% treatment; alanine prediction: 51% CLUE vs 23% control recognized acidic/basic properties.
all_misconceptions.population: general chemistry students in control and CLUE treatment cohorts
all_misconceptions.source_title: Development and Assessment of a Molecular Structure and Properties Learning Progression

all_misconceptions.topic: Dissolution of ionic and molecular compounds
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat gaseous HCl as an ionic compound made of H+ and Cl− ions, or think it breaks apart into ions like NaCl when dissolved in water.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: HCl(g) is a molecular compound; it first dissolves as HCl(aq), and only then reacts with water to form hydronium and chloride ions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish a molecular gas from an ionic solid: HCl has covalent bonding in the gas phase, so dissolution should be represented as HCl(g) -> HCl(aq), followed by the acid reaction with water if describing the aqueous acid equilibrium.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the most common representations displayed HCl gas as an ionic compound that breaks up into H+ and Cl- ions”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Teachers: 54% used HCl(g) -> H+(aq) + Cl−(aq); 46% used HCl(g) + H2O(l) -> H3O+(aq) + Cl−(aq). Students: 2/13 wrote HCl dissociating into ions initially; 3/13 drew ions forming.
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry teachers (N=13) and first-semester general chemistry students (N=13)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

all_misconceptions.topic: Dissolution of ionic and molecular compounds
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the dissolution of HCl is simply HCl -> H+ + Cl−, with no separate solvation step, as if HCl were an ionic solute.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The correct process is first solvation/dissolution of the molecular gas into aqueous HCl, then acid ionization in water; the molecular compound itself is not initially ionic.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that a molecular solute can dissolve without immediately producing ions; the equation should show HCl(g) -> HCl(aq) when the focus is dissolution, and only then show reaction with water if focusing on acid behavior.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the more pressing issue was the ‘simplification’ of the dissolution, resulting in H+ and Cl- ions, effectively portraying HCl as an ionic compound.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 13/13 teachers discussed this issue; among students, 6/13 continued to describe or depict HCl as ionic despite instruction.
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry teachers and first-semester general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

all_misconceptions.topic: Dissolution of ionic and molecular compounds
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students conflate dissolution and acid reaction, writing HCl(g) + H2O(l) -> H3O+(aq) + Cl−(aq) as if the dissolution and ionization happen as a single step.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dissolution of HCl gas and its acid reaction with water are distinct processes; the molecular gas first becomes HCl(aq), then can react with water to form ions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate the physical process of dissolving from the chemical reaction in water, and should not collapse both into one equation unless explicitly modeling the acid-base equilibrium in solution.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “reacting gaseous HCl as an acid without representing the solvation of HCl in addition to the acid-base reaction that occurs in solution”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 5/13 teachers and 3/13 students initially used a direct reaction with water for HCl(g)
all_misconceptions.population: High school chemistry teachers and first-semester general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

all_misconceptions.topic: Dissolution of ionic and molecular compounds
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe pure HCl(g) is already composed of H+ and F−/Cl− ions, or otherwise has ionic composition before dissolving.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Pure gaseous HCl is a molecular substance with covalent bonding, not an ionic assembly of ions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the state and bonding information: a gas-phase molecular compound consists of molecules held together by covalent bonds, not pre-existing ions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “more than a third of students answered that pure gaseous HF is in some way composed of H+ and F- ions despite being explicitly told in the prompt that HF is a molecular compound.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: HF question on summative assessment: 22% selected ‘is made up of H+ and F− ions’; 15% selected both that and ‘is held together by a sigma bond’; total >33% endorsed ionic composition.
all_misconceptions.population: First-semester general chemistry students (N=686)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

all_misconceptions.topic: Dissolution of ionic and molecular compounds
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think NaCl remains intact in water and should be written as NaCl(aq).
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: NaCl is an ionic compound that dissociates into hydrated Na+(aq) and Cl−(aq) ions in water.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that ionic lattices separate into ions upon dissolution, and the aqueous notation should represent separated hydrated ions rather than intact NaCl molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “students relied on inaccurate alternative conceptions of ionic compounds remaining intact upon dissolving—i.e., NaCl(aq).”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 4 students represented NaCl remaining intact in solution; 30% of students relied on NaCl(aq).
all_misconceptions.population: First-semester general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

all_misconceptions.topic: Dissolution of ionic and molecular compounds
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students interpret HCl as a strong acid that simply ‘splits’ or ‘breaks apart’ into H+ and Cl− because the bond breaks when it dissolves.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Acid behavior in solution must be distinguished from the molecular nature of HCl(g); dissolution and ion formation are not the same as an ionic compound simply breaking apart.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first identify that HCl is molecular, then distinguish dissolution into water from acid ionization; strong acid behavior does not mean the pure gas is ionic.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “Yes, it's a strong acid, so it will split, the bond will break, and it will go into H plus ions, and Cl minus.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Quoted student response; 6/13 students overall still described/drew HCl as ionic after instruction.
all_misconceptions.population: First-semester general chemistry student
all_misconceptions.source_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

all_misconceptions.topic: Dissolution of ionic and molecular compounds
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that once HCl is described as molecular, nothing further happens in solution; they stop at HCl(aq) and deny subsequent acidic reaction with water.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: HCl(aq) can further react with water to produce H3O+(aq) and Cl−(aq); being molecular does not mean it remains unchanged in aqueous solution.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that molecular identity and acidic behavior are compatible: after dissolution, an acid can ionize in water, so the process is not complete at HCl(aq).
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “they completely disregarded its acidic nature once dissolved”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Several students who wrote HCl(g) -> HCl(aq) paused; 5 students (N, U, V, X, Z) believed the process was complete, and 1 student (X) said nothing else would occur.
all_misconceptions.population: First-semester general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

all_misconceptions.topic: Intermolecular forces in molecular hydrogen chloride
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students classify pure HCl(g) as having ion-ion interactions, implying it is made of ions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Pure gaseous HCl has London dispersion forces and dipole-dipole interactions; it is molecular, not ionic.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the compound type from bonding and state of matter, then assign intermolecular forces appropriate to polar molecules rather than ion-ion attractions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the most common mistake was selecting ‘ion-ion’ interactions in their responses, which accounted for 27% of students describing HCl(g) as an ionic compound composed of ions.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 27% on second-semester general chemistry assessment (N=675)
all_misconceptions.population: Second-semester general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Disentangling the Dissolution of Ionic and Molecular Compounds: Alternative Conceptions and Teaching Considerations in Chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Type of atoms forming covalent bonds
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Covalent bonding is formed between a metal and a nonmetal atom.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Covalent bonding is typically formed between nonmetal atoms that share electrons.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the element types and compare their tendency to share rather than transfer electrons; two nonmetals form covalent bonds by sharing valence electrons, whereas metal–nonmetal pairs usually form ionic bonds by electron transfer.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "covalent bonding is formed between a metal and a nonmetal atom"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Held by multiple students; Appendix-2 lists S4 and S5, and the discussion says a "great deal of students" had this misconception.
all_misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58); also 10 interviewed students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Type of atoms forming covalent bonds
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think covalent bonding is formed only when atoms 'want' or 'need' to gain electrons to achieve noble-gas configuration, as if atoms have human-like intentions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms do not 'want' anything; bonding depends on electronic structure, electronegativity, and energetic stability, not intentional desire.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain bonding in terms of valence electrons, electronegativity, and attraction between nuclei and shared electron pairs rather than anthropomorphic 'wants' or 'needs'.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "They form covalent bonding, because they want to gain electrons to resemble stable noble gases configuration."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in interview responses (e.g., S1); Appendix-2 notes this idea for S1 and S9.
all_misconceptions.population: Interviewed 11th grade students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Type of atoms forming covalent bonds
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen is treated as a metal atom, so students classify H-containing covalent compounds as if they involved metal–nonmetal bonding.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen is not a metal in this context; whether a bond is covalent depends on the bonding partners and electron sharing/transfer, not on misclassifying hydrogen as a metal.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize hydrogen’s role in bonding and use periodic-table category plus electron behavior correctly; hydrogen in HCl, NH3, and H2O participates in covalent bonding with nonmetals by sharing electrons.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Because hydrogen is a metal atom and oxygen is a nonmetal atom, they bond to each other by the electron transfer"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Reported for H2O in Appendix-1; also linked to HCl and NH3 misconceptions in Appendix-2.
all_misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Covalent bonds are formed by electron transfer rather than electron sharing.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Covalent bonds are formed when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons; electron transfer is characteristic of ionic bonding.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should describe covalent bond formation as mutual sharing of valence electrons and identify electron transfer as producing ions and ionic bonds, not covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "covalent bonding is formed by the electron transfer within hydrogen chloride and ammonia"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented across several items and interviews; Appendix-1 and discussion indicate this was common.
all_misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58); also interviewed students
all_misconceptions.concept_category: bond formation / electron transfer vs sharing
all_misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Formation of covalent bonds in water
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Water contains ionic bonding because hydrogen is a metal and oxygen is a nonmetal, so electrons are transferred between them.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Within H2O, the O–H bonds are covalent; oxygen and hydrogen share electrons, with oxygen attracting the bonding electrons more strongly.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify H2O as a covalent molecule and reason from electron sharing and electronegativity, not from metal/nonmetal transfer logic.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Ionic bonding is formed between oxygen and hydrogen atom within a water molecule, because hydrogen is a metal and oxygen is a nonmetal atom. They bond with each other by the electron transfer."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Shown in item 3 and Appendix-1 (7% for this specific version; also 9% for ionic bonding in water).
all_misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Formation of covalent bonds in water
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonding is the bond within a water molecule, instead of covalent bonding.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The bonds within a water molecule are covalent O–H bonds; hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction between molecules, not the intramolecular bond in H2O.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular covalent bonds from intermolecular hydrogen bonds and apply the term hydrogen bonding only to attractions between molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Hydrogen bonding is formed between oxygen and hydrogen atoms in a water molecule."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Item 3 and Appendix-1 report this misconception (5%); Appendix-2 lists it for interview student S9.
all_misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Polar and nonpolar covalent bonds are reversed: identical atoms are said to form polar covalent bonds and different atoms nonpolar covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Identical atoms generally form nonpolar covalent bonds, while different atoms with different electronegativities generally form polar covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use electronegativity difference to determine bond polarity and keep the definitions of polar and nonpolar bonds consistent with electron distribution.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Nonpolar covalent bonding is formed between different nonmetal atoms, while polar covalent bonding is formed between identical nonmetal atoms."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Appeared in item 2 and interview 3; Appendix-1 lists several variants, e.g. 12% polar in H2 and 14% nonpolar in H2S.
all_misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58); also interviewed students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Bond polarity is the same as molecule polarity; students use 'polar/nonpolar molecule' instead of 'polar/nonpolar bond'.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond polarity refers to unequal or equal sharing of bonding electrons in a bond; molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and molecular shape.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish the polarity of a bond from the overall polarity of a molecule and reason from electronegativity and geometry separately.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students confused 'polar and nonpolar molecule' with 'polar and nonpolar covalent bonding'"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented in the discussion and Appendix-1 note (5).
all_misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Bonding electrons are equally distant from both atoms in all covalent molecules, regardless of electronegativity differences.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In polar covalent bonds, bonding electrons are drawn closer to the more electronegative atom; only in nonpolar bonds are electrons shared equally.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the electronegativities of the bonded atoms and place the electron pair closer to the atom that attracts electrons more strongly.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Bonding electrons place equidistantly to the bonded atoms in all covalent molecules"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Appendix-1 reports 7%.
all_misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Type of covalent bonding and bond formation
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: There is no distinction among covalent bonds; all covalent bonds are the same and are based on electron transfer.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Covalent bonds can differ, for example as polar and nonpolar covalent bonds, and they are formed by electron sharing, not transfer.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize bond types based on electronegativity differences and electron sharing patterns, not collapse all covalent bonds into one category or into ionic-like transfer.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "No, all covalent bonds are the same. Covalent bonding is formed between atoms by sharing of single electrons."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in interview question 3 for students S4 and S5.
all_misconceptions.population: Interviewed 11th grade students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Van der Waals forces, dipole-dipole forces, and hydrogen bonding are types of covalent bonding.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Van der Waals forces, dipole-dipole interactions, and hydrogen bonding are intermolecular forces, not types of covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate intramolecular covalent bonding from intermolecular forces and classify each interaction according to whether it holds atoms within a molecule or molecules together.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Van der Waals, dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonding are the types of covalent bonding"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in interview student S9.
all_misconceptions.population: Interviewed 11th grade students
all_misconceptions.concept_category: intermolecular forces vs covalent bond types
all_misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Graphite conducts electricity because it contains free carbon atoms that are not bonded to anything and can move through the structure.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Graphite conducts electricity because it has delocalized electrons that are free to move through its layers; carbon atoms are still covalently bonded in a network.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain conductivity in terms of mobile delocalized electrons in graphite’s structure, not free carbon atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "there is a free carbon atom which was not bonded to any carbon atom. These free carbon atoms move through the structure of graphite. Graphite conducts electricity due to these free carbon atoms."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Appendix-1 reports 26%.
all_misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Graphite conducts electricity because its carbon layers can slide over each other.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrical conductivity in graphite is due to delocalized electrons, not the sliding of layers.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the role of delocalized pi electrons and distinguish mechanical layering from electrical conduction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "graphite has the layers of carbon atoms which slide over each other, it conducts electricity due to these layers which could be able to move"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Appendix-1 reports 17%.
all_misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Diamond is viewed as a 'unitary' structure without layers, contrasted with graphite layers, rather than as a giant covalent network.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Diamond and graphite are both giant covalent structures, but diamond is a 3D tetrahedral network and graphite is layered with delocalized electrons between layers.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should describe each allotrope with the correct extended covalent structure and connect structure to properties like conductivity.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Diamond has a unitary structure. It has no layers."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Linked to item 4 responses; no exact percentage provided for this wording.
all_misconceptions.population: 11th grade students (n=58)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Secondary School Students' Misconceptions of Covalent Bonding

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that when water is heated, the molecules simply move faster without necessarily connecting that speed change to particle-level motion in the boiling process, or they describe motion only in macroscopic terms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Heating increases the kinetic energy of water molecules, so they move faster at the molecular level.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect added heat to increased molecular kinetic energy and infer that water molecules move faster as temperature rises and during boiling.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "most students understood that as the temperature rises, the particles/molecules move faster"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Mentioned as a common pattern; no exact percentage given.
all_misconceptions.population: 35 high school students in six Scientific Visualization classes
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Composition of bubbles in boiling water
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the bubbles are not steam, or that bubble composition is something like air, oxygen/hydrogen, or unspecified gas rather than water vapor.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The bubbles in boiling water are steam (water vapor).
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the idea that boiling converts liquid water to gaseous water and infer that the bubbles are water vapor/steam, not air or split elements.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "What are the bubbles made of?"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: The paper notes that there was no change on this item across groups, but gives no exact misconception count.
all_misconceptions.population: Students in the 35-student analysis sample; also the full pre/posttest population of 94 originally participated.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think water can keep getting hotter while it is boiling, or that temperature continues to rise during boiling.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: At the boiling point, added energy goes into the phase change and the temperature remains constant until boiling is complete.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that once water reaches its boiling point, additional energy is used to overcome intermolecular attractions rather than increase temperature, so temperature plateaus.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "you cannot get hotter than boiling water. Like I thought that there was boiling and then you could still get higher."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in student interview responses; no percentage given.
all_misconceptions.population: Student T3-2 and others in the interview sample
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students define boiling point only as a specific temperature value or as the moment water is very hot, without relating it to vapor pressure and atmospheric pressure.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid’s vapor pressure equals atmospheric pressure.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect boiling to pressure balance, recognizing that boiling occurs when vapor pressure matches external pressure and that the numerical temperature depends on pressure.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "When water reaches 212°F (100°C) –or just before it does (The temperature only)"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Appears in the rubric as a low-level response category; no exact count reported.
all_misconceptions.population: Students responding to WISE question 6
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think boiling bubbles rise simply because 'heat rises' or because they contain gas, rather than because of pressure differences between the vapor in the bubble and surrounding water.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Vapor bubbles rise because their internal vapor pressure is lower than the surrounding water pressure; density differences also matter.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from pressure and density: vapor bubbles form, and if internal pressure is less than surrounding pressure the bubbles rise to the surface.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I didn't know that the, um, the bubbles didn't have like as much pressure as the outside area did."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Reported as a student misconception in Table 4.10; no percentage given.
all_misconceptions.population: Student T3-7
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not distinguish particle spacing across phases, treating proximity as similar in solids, liquids, and gases, or failing to represent gas particles as far apart and liquid particles as close together.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Particles are closer together in liquids than in gases; gas particles have negligible interactions and are far apart.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use a particulate model in which particle arrangement changes with phase: tightly packed in condensed phases and much farther apart in gases.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "This may represent an incomplete knowledge of the actual positioning and configuration of molecules in each phase"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Discussed qualitatively; rubric data show Group 1 average PROXIMITY 0.67, Group 2 0.78, Group 3 1.42, but no direct misconception percentage given.
all_misconceptions.population: 35 students across Groups 1-3
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students rely on macroscopic images and do not include molecules/particles in their representations, or treat the animation as only a macroscopic boiling scene.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A scientifically accurate animation should include a particulate-level representation of water molecules and their motion during boiling, alongside macroscopic features.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the text to both macro and micro levels, adding molecular representations to show how boiling occurs at the particulate level.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "only 22.9% of students including molecules in their animations"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 22.9% included molecules in their animations.
all_misconceptions.population: 8 of 35 analyzed students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Movement of particles in a liquid vs. gas
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think particles in one phase move together or all at the same speed, instead of showing random motion and different speeds across phases.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Particles move randomly, and motion varies with phase; in general gas particles move faster than liquid particles.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that thermal energy increases random molecular motion and that gaseous particles move faster and more randomly than particles in the liquid state.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Shows particles in motion but they are all moving together (coordinated movement)"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Appears in the project rubric as a low-level motion category; no direct count reported.
all_misconceptions.population: Student animations from the 35-student sample
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe water molecules move at the same speed in the solid, liquid, and gaseous phases.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular speed differs by phase; molecules move fastest in the gaseous phase.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare kinetic energy across phases and infer that heating increases molecular speed and that gas particles move fastest.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Water molecules move at the same speed in the solid, liquid, and gaseous phases."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: This was a specific incorrect option on the pre/posttest; no percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: Pre/posttest respondents
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think matter is continuous or that there is matter between atoms/molecules in a substance.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: There is empty space between atoms and molecules, especially in liquids and gases.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that substances are particulate and that the spaces between particles are not filled with matter.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "matter is continuous and there is no vacuum or space between them"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Presented as a documented misconception from prior research cited in the paper; not tied to a new count in this study.
all_misconceptions.population: Prior literature cited in the paper
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think atoms are large enough to be seen under a microscope, or they confuse atom size with macroscopic objects.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms and molecules are too small to be seen directly with classroom microscopes.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize the nanoscopic scale of atoms and infer that they require indirect models and instruments rather than direct viewing.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "atoms are large enough to be seen under a microscope"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Listed as a common misconception in cited literature.
all_misconceptions.population: Grade-12 students in Griffiths & Preston, as cited by the paper
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Molecule and atom movement in solids
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think molecules in a solid do not move.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecules in solids do move; they vibrate in place.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should understand that solid particles have kinetic energy even though the solid maintains shape, so the particles vibrate rather than remain motionless.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Molecules in a rock are not moving"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: This item appears on the pre/posttest as a misconception probe; no percentage reported.
all_misconceptions.population: Pre/posttest respondents
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think molecules and atoms are all the same size.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms and molecules differ in size; molecules are composed of atoms and can vary in size.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from molecular structure that different substances have different particle sizes and that molecules are built from atoms.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Molecules and atoms are all the same size"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Listed as an assessment item targeting a known misconception.
all_misconceptions.population: Pre/posttest respondents
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think molecules in liquids are always further apart than in solids, with no distinction based on phase-specific packing.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecules in liquids are close together but can move past one another; gases are much farther apart.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare phase structures and recognize that liquids remain relatively dense while allowing flow, unlike gases.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Molecules in liquids are always further apart than in solids"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Included in the ParNoMA instrument; no study-specific percentage provided.
all_misconceptions.population: Pre/posttest respondents
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Matter made of visible objects only
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think only visible things are made of molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: All matter, visible or not, is made of molecules/atoms.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should infer that invisibility to the eye does not mean absence of molecules, because molecules make up all matter.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Only things you can see are made of molecules"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Included in the ParNoMA instrument; no study-specific percentage provided.
all_misconceptions.population: Pre/posttest respondents
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Composition of matter in a gas
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think something other than empty space exists between molecules in a gas, such as air or atmosphere.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: There is empty space between molecules in a gas.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that gas particles are widely separated and that the space between them is not filled with matter.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "In a pure sample of oxygen gas, what exists between the oxygen molecules?"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Included in the pre/posttest; no percentages reported.
all_misconceptions.population: Pre/posttest respondents
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think heat causes molecules to expand or makes molecules bigger.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Heat increases particle motion and, in phase changes, can separate particles; it does not make molecules themselves expand.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate molecular size from thermal motion and understand that heating changes motion and arrangement rather than molecule size.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Heat causes molecules to expand."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Included as a wrong option on the pre/posttest.
all_misconceptions.population: Pre/posttest respondents
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Student-Generated Animations about Water Boiling to Impact Student Understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe chemical bonds and intermolecular forces are the same force.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Chemical bonds are intramolecular forces that hold atoms together within a substance, whereas intermolecular forces are attractions between particles of different molecules or ions and are distinct interactions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish where each force acts: first identify bonding within a molecule or ionic lattice, then identify weaker attractions between separate molecules or particles. Because these act at different structural levels and have different roles, they cannot be treated as synonymous.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: they presented some conceptual errors about intermolecular forces, leaving to understand that for them the chemical bonds and the intermolecular forces were the same force.
all_misconceptions.population: high school students; 1st year class (22 students) and two 3rd year classes (47 students)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular forces: a methodological proposal of teaching based on experimentation

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe intermolecular forces act only in homogeneous mixtures and do not exist in heterogeneous mixtures.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces exist between particles in all पदार्थ/mixtures where particles are present; whether a mixture is homogeneous or heterogeneous depends on miscibility and interactions among components, not on the existence of intermolecular forces itself.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that all substances have intermolecular interactions, but the strength and type of interactions can lead to complete mixing or phase separation. Heterogeneous mixtures still involve intermolecular forces between the species present, even if they are not sufficient to produce one uniform phase.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: the students demonstrated to believe that intermolecular forces act only in homogeneous mixtures, thus not existing intermolecular forces in heterogeneous mixtures.
all_misconceptions.population: students in the experiment classes
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular forces: a methodological proposal of teaching based on experimentation

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think only homogeneous mixtures have interactions between components, and heterogeneous mixtures do not.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular interactions occur between components in both homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures; the difference is how completely the components mix or separate into phases.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify that particles of different substances can interact regardless of whether the final mixture looks uniform. The visible phase behavior does not mean interactions are absent; rather, the balance of attractions, polarity, and other properties determines the mixture type.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: only has interactions between compounds that form a homogeneous mixture, and in the heterogeneous mixture, there are no interactions between the components that compose it.
all_misconceptions.population: students discussed in the paper, as cited from classroom observations and literature context
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular forces: a methodological proposal of teaching based on experimentation

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Some students attributed the density difference as responsible for whether mixtures are homogeneous or heterogeneous.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Miscibility and mixture homogeneity are explained by intermolecular interactions, especially polarity and the relative strength of attractions between components, not simply by density differences.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the polarity and intermolecular attractions of the substances. If attractions between unlike particles are favorable, the substances mix to form a homogeneous mixture; if not, phase separation occurs. Density alone cannot explain why one pair mixes while another with different densities may still be homogeneous.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Some of them attributed the density difference as responsible for the heterogeneity of the mixtures. But when confronted with other mixtures with liquids of different densities that resulted in a homogeneous mixture, the students could not argue about the possible causes.
all_misconceptions.population: students in the observed classes
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular forces: a methodological proposal of teaching based on experimentation

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Most students thought surface tension is the factor responsible for the dye floating in milk.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The behavior of the dye in milk is explained by intermolecular interactions and the effect of detergent on the milk's fat and surface properties; surface tension alone is not the complete explanation for the observed phenomenon.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the dye movement to how detergent disrupts interactions in milk, especially between fat and water, changing the local balance of forces and allowing the dye to spread. The explanation should involve particle interactions rather than naming surface tension as the sole cause.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: On the surface tension, most of the students pointed out to be the same, the one responsible for the floating of the dye in the milk.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: most of the students
all_misconceptions.population: students in the Psychedelic Milk activity
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular forces: a methodological proposal of teaching based on experimentation

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think molecular structure and macroscopic properties are not explicitly connected.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular structure is directly connected to observable properties such as boiling point and melting point through intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use the molecular structure to infer the dominant intermolecular forces and then connect those forces to the observed property trend (e.g., stronger intermolecular forces generally correspond to higher boiling or melting points).
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "for many students structure and properties were not explicitly connected"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces and the Languages of Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students fail to represent an intermolecular force as an interaction between molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: An intermolecular force is an attraction between separate molecules, not a property of one molecule alone.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify two or more molecules and reason about the attractions between them, rather than treating the force as something within a single molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "only 10−30% of students represented each IMF as an interaction between molecules"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: only 10–30% of students represented each IMF as an interaction between molecules
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces and the Languages of Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think boiling involves breaking covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling is a phase change that overcomes intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds within molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should recognize that molecules remain intact during boiling; energy is used to separate molecules from each other, not to break the bonds within them.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "boiling involves breaking covalent bonds"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces and the Languages of Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think any molecule containing oxygen and hydrogen can form hydrogen bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires a hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom and an appropriate acceptor; not every O/H-containing molecule qualifies in the same way.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should examine the bonding arrangement and molecular structure, not just the presence of O and H atoms, to determine whether hydrogen bonding is possible.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "any molecule with O and H (even CH3OCH3 and CH3COH) can form hydrogen bonds"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces and the Languages of Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogenation must decrease molecular weight to explain the large drop in melting point.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogenation changes molecular shape and saturation, which alters packing and intermolecular forces; it does not need to decrease molecular weight to lower melting point.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should compare the structures before and after hydrogenation, note changes in unsaturation and packing, and then relate those structural changes to melting point rather than assuming mass decrease.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "because of the large decrease in melting point, hydrogenation must somehow decrease the molecular weight rather than change the molecular shape"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: a few students
all_misconceptions.population: students in the 2023–2024 general chemistry course (n = 63 for language identification; n = 70 for prediction assessments)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces and the Languages of Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a double bond directly makes intermolecular forces stronger and therefore requires a higher melting point.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Double bonds, especially cis double bonds, change molecular shape and packing, often lowering melting point by reducing intermolecular attractions between molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason that molecular geometry affects how well molecules pack together; poorer packing weakens intermolecular interactions and lowers melting point.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "making the forces stronger which requires a higher melting point"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: a number of students
all_misconceptions.population: students in a follow-up 3 weeks after the activity
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces and the Languages of Chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a C=C bond has higher energy than a C–C bond, so more heat is needed to break it during melting.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Melting does not involve breaking covalent C=C or C–C bonds; the change in melting point is due to intermolecular forces and molecular packing, not bond strength within the molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should distinguish covalent bond energies from intermolecular interactions and use structural packing arguments to explain melting point differences.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "a C=C bond has higher energy than a C–C bond, thus requiring more energy (heat) to break down and melt"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: a number of students
all_misconceptions.population: students in a follow-up 3 weeks after the activity
all_misconceptions.source_title: Intermolecular Forces and the Languages of Chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Relative strength of intermolecular vs intramolecular forces
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think intermolecular bonding is as strong as intramolecular bonding.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are much weaker than intramolecular bonds such as covalent or ionic bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between forces holding molecules together and bonds holding atoms together within a molecule. Boiling overcomes intermolecular attractions without breaking covalent bonds, so far less energy is needed for vaporization than for bond breaking.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The alternate conception that intermolecular bonding is as strong as intramolecular bonding was quite prevalent"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 26.3% of responses
all_misconceptions.population: control group students on the post-test (N=38)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Problem-Based Learning in 9th Grade Chemistry Class: 'Intermolecular Forces'

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Presence of hydrogen bonds in molecules containing hydrogen
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think there are hydrogen bonds between all molecules that contain hydrogen.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding only occurs when hydrogen is directly bonded to a highly electronegative atom such as N, O, or F and interacts with a lone pair on another electronegative atom.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check the bonding environment of hydrogen, not merely the presence of hydrogen. Hydrogen must be covalently attached to N, O, or F and the acceptor atom must have lone pairs; otherwise hydrogen bonding does not occur.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "There are hydrogen bonds between all molecules which contain hydrogen."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 34.2% of responses
all_misconceptions.population: control group students on the post-test (N=38)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Problem-Based Learning in 9th Grade Chemistry Class: 'Intermolecular Forces'

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think nonpolar molecules can become polar and therefore all molecules have dipole characteristics / dipole-dipole forces.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Only polar molecules have permanent dipoles and dipole-dipole forces; nonpolar molecules do not become polar just because they are liquid or because London dispersion forces are present.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine polarity from molecular structure and electronegativity differences, then decide whether permanent dipole-dipole interactions are possible. Nonpolar molecules can still have London dispersion forces, but they do not have permanent dipoles.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "nonpolar molecules can become polar, therefore all existing molecules have dipole characteristics"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 21.1% of responses
all_misconceptions.population: control group students on the post-test (N=38)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Problem-Based Learning in 9th Grade Chemistry Class: 'Intermolecular Forces'

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Intermolecular forces are forces within a molecule rather than attractions between molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are attractive forces between separate molecules or particles, not bonds within a molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular bonding from intermolecular attraction: covalent bonds hold atoms together inside a molecule, whereas intermolecular forces act between molecules and influence bulk properties like solubility.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: students maintain their initial misconceptions, such as that intermolecular forces are attractive forces within a molecule.
all_misconceptions.population: general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student Discovery of the Relationship between Molecular Structure, Solubility, and Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Any molecule containing hydrogen atoms can hydrogen-bond.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires hydrogen covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom such as N, O, or F, plus a suitable lone-pair acceptor.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check the bonding environment of hydrogen, not just its presence. If hydrogen is bonded to carbon only, the molecule does not serve as a hydrogen-bond donor in the usual chemistry sense.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: intuitive reasoning could cause students to incorrectly guess that all molecules containing hydrogen atoms are capable of hydrogen-bonding.
all_misconceptions.population: students taking the prelaboratory assessment
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student Discovery of the Relationship between Molecular Structure, Solubility, and Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think intermolecular forces are located within a single molecule rather than between separate molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces act between molecules, not inside one molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify two or more separate molecules and place the interaction in the space between them, because IMFs arise from attractions between molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "a majority of students draw representations showing that IMFs are located within a single molecule rather than between separate molecules"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Cohort 1 drawings: hydrogen bonding 72% (N=68) within; dipole-dipole 61% (N=57) within; LDFs 55% (N=52) within. Cohort 2 drawings: hydrogen bonding 56% (N=90) within; dipole-dipole 58% (N=93) within; LDFs 56% (N=89) within.
all_misconceptions.population: General chemistry college students; Cohort 1 N=94, Cohort 2 N=160
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonding is the covalent O-H bond within ethanol, or otherwise a bond inside one molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen attached to O, N, or F in one molecule and a lone pair on O, N, or F in another molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should locate hydrogen bonding between two molecules and recognize that the covalent O-H bond is not the hydrogen bond; the hydrogen donor must be bonded to O, N, or F and attract a heteroatom on a different molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "72% (N = 68) clearly represented hydrogen bonding as an O−H bond within a single molecule of ethanol."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 72% (N=68) within; only 15% (N=14) correctly indicated hydrogen bonding occurs between separate molecules
all_misconceptions.population: Cohort 1 general chemistry students, N=94
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a hydrogen-bonding representation can show only one molecule or no molecule at all.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: To represent hydrogen bonding, students should draw at least two molecules and show the interaction between them.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should include multiple molecules because hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular interaction; a single isolated molecule cannot show the between-molecule attraction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "54% (N = 51) of students drew only one molecule or none at all (even though they were explicitly asked to draw three molecules)."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 54% (N=51) drew only one molecule or none
all_misconceptions.population: Cohort 1 general chemistry students, N=94
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think dipole-dipole interactions occur within a single molecule, for example as bonds or interactions among parts of the same ethanol molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole interactions are attractions between the partial charges of different polar molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify two polar molecules and place the interaction between them, because dipole-dipole is an intermolecular force arising from charge separation across separate molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the majority of students (61%, N = 57) in Cohort 1 drew dipole−dipole interactions as occurring within the ethanol molecule"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Cohort 1: 61% (N=57) within; Cohort 2: 58% (N=93) within
all_misconceptions.population: General chemistry college students; Cohort 1 N=94, Cohort 2 N=160
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students describe dipole-dipole as a bond rather than an intermolecular interaction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dipole-dipole is an intermolecular attraction, not a covalent bond.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between a covalent bond that holds atoms together within a molecule and an intermolecular attraction that acts between molecules; the term bond should not be used for dipole-dipole.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Dipole−dipole is 'a pretty weak bond between polar molecules.'"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented in student written responses; no overall percentage given in the paper
all_misconceptions.population: Cohort 1 general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think London dispersion forces occur within a single molecule, or as bonds within the molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: London dispersion forces are intermolecular attractions between molecules caused by temporary induced dipoles.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify that dispersion forces arise from interactions between separate particles/molecules, not from bonds inside one molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "55% (N = 52) for LDFs"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Cohort 1: 55% (N=52) within; Cohort 2: 56% (N=89) within
all_misconceptions.population: General chemistry college students; Cohort 1 N=94, Cohort 2 N=160
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think London dispersion forces are simply a property that all substances have, rather than an interaction between particles.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: All molecules can experience London dispersion forces, but LDFs are still intermolecular forces arising from temporary dipoles between molecules or atoms.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should say that dispersion forces exist because of temporary electron fluctuations that create attractions between particles; universality does not mean they are an intrinsic property located within one molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "26% (N=24) of students who explicitly stated in their written responses that LDFs are present for all molecules or always present."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 26% (N=24) explicitly said LDFs are present for all molecules or always present
all_misconceptions.population: Cohort 1 general chemistry students, N=94
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students use atom and molecule interchangeably when describing IMFs, such as referring to an atom when they mean a molecule or vice versa.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Atoms and molecules are different entities; IMFs usually describe interactions between molecules (or particles), not confusion between the two terms.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should name the correct level of organization: an atom is a single atom, while a molecule is a bonded collection of atoms; the interaction should be described using the appropriate entity.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students often used atom to mean molecule (or vice versa)"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented qualitatively in student responses; no overall percentage given
all_misconceptions.population: Cohort 1 general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students use bond and interaction interchangeably, treating IMFs as bonds in the same sense as covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are attractions or interactions between molecules; covalent bonds are intramolecular bonds within a molecule, except that hydrogen bond is a special term for an IMF.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular covalent bonding from intermolecular attraction and reserve bond language for covalent bonds or clearly identified hydrogen bonds when appropriate.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "some students used the terms bond and interaction interchangeably."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented qualitatively in student responses; no overall percentage given
all_misconceptions.population: Cohort 1 general chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces: A Multimodal Study

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think intermolecular forces are bonds within molecules rather than attractions between molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are attractions between molecules, not within molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intramolecular bonding from intermolecular attraction by asking whether the interaction is holding atoms together inside one molecule or attracting separate molecules to each other.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "They are forces, often referred to as 'bonds', between (not within) molecules."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat intermolecular forces as comparable in strength to, or not clearly weaker than, ionic and covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are generally much weaker than intramolecular ionic and covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the type of interaction and recognize that IMFs are secondary attractions between molecules, so they are weaker than chemical bonds holding atoms together within a molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "these forces are ... almost always weaker than intramolecular bonds such as ionic and covalent"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe hydrogen bonding can only occur between hydrogen and nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, or carbon.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding involves hydrogen bonded to N, O, or F interacting with a lone pair on N, O, or F; carbon is not a hydrogen-bonding partner in the usual definition.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify that H-bond donors are H attached to N/O/F and acceptors are lone pairs on N/O/F, then verify whether both parts of the interaction are present.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "A hydrogen bond is a rather strong bond and - can only occur between hydrogen and nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, or carbon."
all_misconceptions.population: Student preactivity response
all_misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a hydrogen bond is simply a weak bond between hydrogen atoms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction involving hydrogen attached to an electronegative atom and a lone pair on another electronegative atom; it is not a bond between two hydrogen atoms.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check the donor-acceptor requirement for hydrogen bonding and recognize that hydrogen atoms do not hydrogen-bond to each other directly.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Weak bond between hydrogen atoms."
all_misconceptions.population: Student preactivity response
all_misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students can memorize textbook definitions of IMFs without understanding how molecules interact in three dimensions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should connect verbal definitions of IMFs to the 3D arrangement and interaction of molecules at the microscopic level.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use molecular geometry and intermolecular contact points to explain attraction rather than only reciting a definition.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students often can provide textbook level definitions but leave general chemistry and enter into organic chemistry without a thorough conceptual understanding of IMFs"
all_misconceptions.population: College chemistry students discussed in cited literature
all_misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may be able to give correct definitions from drawings but still lack a 2D-to-3D mental model of intermolecular interactions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should translate among symbolic, 2D, and 3D representations and use 3D structure to reason about intermolecular interactions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should interpret a structural drawing in terms of 3D molecular shape, electron distribution, and possible intermolecular contacts before deciding on IMF type or strength.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "These drawings reveal students' ability to provide definitions, but this does not necessarily translate to a 2D or 3D understanding."
all_misconceptions.population: Students in CLUE-related assessments cited by the paper
all_misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Incomplete or incorrect understanding from memorization
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students who memorize the term hydrogen bonding may have an incomplete or incorrect understanding of what it is.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding should be understood as a specific intermolecular attraction with defined structural and electronic requirements.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should move beyond memorized wording and determine whether the molecular structures satisfy the requirements for hydrogen bonding.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "when students solely memorize the terms, they have an incomplete or incorrect understanding of hydrogen bonding"
