all_misconceptions.population: Organic chemistry students cited in prior work
all_misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Physical properties and molecular level causes
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students fail to connect macroscopic properties such as boiling point to the molecular-level arrangement and interactions causing them.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point and similar properties should be explained by the strength and nature of intermolecular interactions among molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should relate a higher or lower boiling point to the energy required to overcome intermolecular attractions and to molecular structure and polarity.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students often fail to connect these concepts to what is occurring on the molecular level in terms of the consequential three-dimensional arrangements of the interacting molecules"
all_misconceptions.population: College chemistry students discussed in cited literature
all_misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students misconceive the factors that determine the strength of intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: IMF strength depends on molecular features such as polarity, shape, accessibility of lone pairs, and the type of intermolecular interaction present.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should examine molecular structure, polarity, and geometry to decide which intermolecular attractions are possible and how strong they are likely to be.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students may also misconceive the factors that affect the strength of IMFs"
all_misconceptions.population: College chemistry students discussed in cited literature
all_misconceptions.source_title: Tactile Models for the Visualization, Conceptualization, and Review of Intermolecular Forces in the College Chemistry Classroom

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe dispersion (London) forces are negligible compared with hydrogen bonding and dipole-dipole forces.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Dispersion forces are significant intermolecular forces and often increase with the number of electrons in a molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should recognize that electron-rich, more polarizable molecules experience stronger dispersion forces, which can strongly affect physical properties such as boiling point.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the widespread misconception that dispersion (London) forces are of negligible strength when compared with hydrogen-bonding and dipole—dipole (Keesom) forces."
all_misconceptions.population: Introductory chemistry students (implied by the paper's discussion of first-year instruction)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching Intermolecular Forces to First-Year Undergraduate Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that intermolecular forces have a simple, universal, one-to-one correlation with boiling points across all compounds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point is often correlated with intermolecular-force strength, but there are exceptions and anomalies, so boiling point is only a reasonably good measure rather than an exact universal proxy.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should compare structures, intermolecular interactions, and additional factors such as molecular polarity and surface charge effects before inferring IMF strength from boiling point alone.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it may be assumed that all of these physical properties necessarily have a similar, simple correspondence to IMFs as that which is generally shown by boiling points."
all_misconceptions.population: First-year undergraduate students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching Intermolecular Forces to First-Year Undergraduate Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe melting point should show the same neat trend with intermolecular forces as boiling point does.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Melting point is influenced by both enthalpy and entropy factors, so it may not correlate simply or consistently with intermolecular-force strength.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason that melting depends on $Delta_{fus}H$ and $Delta_{fus}S$ and that symmetry, crystal packing, and disorder can change melting points independently of IMF strength.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the correlation of IMFs with many physical properties is not necessarily as straightforward as is generally the case with boiling points and vapor pressures."
all_misconceptions.population: First-year undergraduate students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching Intermolecular Forces to First-Year Undergraduate Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assume viscosity should track intermolecular-force strength in the same straightforward way as boiling point.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Viscosity depends on both intermolecular forces and molecular shape/entanglement, so structural effects can dominate and invert the expected trend.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should consider how molecular shape affects surface contact and entanglement when comparing viscosities, not just the number or type of intermolecular forces present.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "their viscosities show a strong and unexpected trend in the opposite direction."
all_misconceptions.population: First-year undergraduate students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching Intermolecular Forces to First-Year Undergraduate Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assume surface tension should always increase in the same direction as intermolecular-force strength across a homologous series.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Surface tension can increase or decrease depending on whether enthalpy or entropy effects dominate; it is not guaranteed to follow a simple IMF trend.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should evaluate the balance of enthalpic and entropic contributions to surface tension rather than expecting a universal monotonic relationship with IMF strength.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the surface tension, in defiance of expectations, shows exactly the opposite trend."
all_misconceptions.population: First-year undergraduate students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching Intermolecular Forces to First-Year Undergraduate Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe intermolecular forces are the sole influence governing physical properties such as melting point, viscosity, or surface tension.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Physical properties are affected by intermolecular forces along with other factors such as molecular symmetry, shape, entropy, crystal structure, and bonding directionality.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify all relevant factors for the property in question and not attribute changes to IMFs alone.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "may mistakenly lead students to believe that IMFs are the sole influence that needs to be considered."
all_misconceptions.population: Students in introductory chemistry contexts
all_misconceptions.source_title: Teaching Intermolecular Forces to First-Year Undergraduate Students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Surface tension is a force, or force per unit area, rather than energy required to increase unit surface area.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Surface tension is work/energy required to increase the unit surface area (J/m^2).
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the macroscopic phenomenon to the definition of surface tension as energy needed to create more surface; the unit should be interpreted as energy per area, not force.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Most responses were "force (N)" or "force per unit area  (N/m^2)".
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 12/16 students gave incorrect unit responses; only 1/16 gave the correct answer.
all_misconceptions.population: 16 undergraduates majoring in chemistry education in Korea
all_misconceptions.source_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Surface tension can be predicted only from intermolecular interaction indicators such as boiling point, hydrogen bonding, or molecular weight; molecular area is not considered as a factor.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Surface tension depends on both intermolecular interaction and molecular area (or number of molecules per unit area).
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from the definition of surface tension as work per unit area and recognize that both the energy contribution from intermolecular interaction and the area occupied by molecules affect the value; therefore, liquids with similar or stronger interactions can still have lower surface tension if molecular area differs.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Students attempted to predict the degree of surface tension only by intermolecular interaction. No one described it in terms of molecular area or unit area.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 16/16 students used only intermolecular interaction in the preconception test for question 2.
all_misconceptions.population: 16 undergraduates majoring in chemistry education in Korea
all_misconceptions.source_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Surface tension acts inward on the liquid surface.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Surface tension acts parallel to the surface.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between fewer interactions at the surface and the actual direction of the tension force/work; the surface molecules are in force equilibrium, and the surface tension direction is parallel to the interface.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Most students expressed that an inward direction.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 12/16 students answered inward; 3/16 outward; 1/16 inward and outward; 0/16 correct.
all_misconceptions.population: 16 undergraduates majoring in chemistry education in Korea
all_misconceptions.source_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Explaining the water/ethylene glycol/diethylene glycol/ethanol counterexample
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: If surface tension data do not match the predicted order based on intermolecular forces, the data are likely invalid due to experimental error.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The measured anomaly should be accepted as valid and explained by a scientifically grounded model that includes both intermolecular interaction and molecular area.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate whether the measurements are trustworthy, then revise the explanation if the data are valid rather than dismissing them; the anomaly should trigger reconsideration of the model, not rejection of the results.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: I think intermolecular forces, that is, the number of hydrogen bonding and the boiling point have a great influence. In the experiment, between diethylene glycol and ethylene glycol, the surface tension of the latter was larger, which was contrary to my expectation. But the difference could be regarded as an experimental error, so my thought has not changed.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 1/16 students
all_misconceptions.population: 16 undergraduates majoring in chemistry education in Korea
all_misconceptions.source_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Anomalous surface tension measurements can be accepted as valid, but no explanation is needed or possible.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Valid anomalous data should be explained using a coherent scientific account, ideally integrating intermolecular interaction with molecular area.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the anomaly to test and refine their conception, producing an explanation that links the observed values to molecular structure and unit area rather than stopping at description.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: They believed anomalous data were valid, but there were not any attempts to explain the anomaly.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 2/16 students
all_misconceptions.population: 16 undergraduates majoring in chemistry education in Korea
all_misconceptions.source_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Surface tension is influenced more by hydrogen bonding than by dispersion force, without a basis in the definition of surface tension.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Surface tension should be explained from the work/energy per unit area, considering both intermolecular interaction and molecular area, not by an unsupported ranking of interaction types alone.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the strength/type of intermolecular interactions to surface tension through the surface-area definition and explain why those interactions matter in relation to molecular area.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Surface tension is influenced greater by hydrogen bonding than by dispersion force."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 2/16 students
all_misconceptions.population: 16 undergraduates majoring in chemistry education in Korea
all_misconceptions.concept_category: response to anomalous data / peripheral theory change
all_misconceptions.source_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Surface tension is determined by intermolecular interaction plus intermolecular accessibility, where molecular spacing/accessibility is treated as the causal factor instead of molecular area.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Surface tension is explained by intermolecular interaction together with molecular area (number of molecules per unit area), not by a vaguely defined accessibility factor.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should relate any structural factor to the surface-area definition and show how molecular area changes the number of molecules per unit area and thus the energy required to create surface.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: Student S12 thought that the difference in molecular area could affect intermolecular accessibility (the degree to which molecules approach each other), resulting in changes in intermolecular interaction and hence in surface tension.
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 1/16 students
all_misconceptions.population: 16 undergraduates majoring in chemistry education in Korea
all_misconceptions.concept_category: response to anomalous data / peripheral theory change
all_misconceptions.source_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Surface tension depends on molecular weight because heavier molecules cannot be pulled apart well during measurement, so gravity affects the measured surface tension directly.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Surface tension is a surface property arising from intermolecular interactions and molecular area; it is not directly explained by molecular weight or gravity in the way described.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should avoid attributing surface tension to gravitational weight of molecules and instead reason about surface energy, intermolecular interactions, and the surface-area term.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The reason why the surface tension of diethylene glycol is lower than that of ethylene glycol is that diethylene glycol is much heavier. Surface tension is a force that pulls molecules from each other, and if molecules are too heavy, it will be difficult to pull them from each other."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 1/16 students
all_misconceptions.population: 16 undergraduates majoring in chemistry education in Korea
all_misconceptions.concept_category: response to anomalous data / peripheral theory change
all_misconceptions.source_title: Undergraduate Students' Understanding of Surface Tension Considering Molecular Area

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe a molecule with polar bonds must be polar, even if the molecular geometry is symmetrical.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular polarity depends on the vector sum of bond dipoles; symmetrical molecules can be nonpolar when bond dipoles cancel.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine whether the molecule has polar bonds, then consider the 3D shape and whether the bond dipoles cancel. If the geometry is symmetrical, the molecule can have zero net dipole even with polar bonds.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "symmetrical molecules with polar bonds are non-polar because they have no positive or negative end."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Control group scored 0.9/2 vs experimental group 1.6/2 on classifying symmetric molecules with polar bonds as nonpolar.
all_misconceptions.population: Traditional students majoring in natural sciences in two sections of second-semester introductory chemistry (N=36 control, N=36 experimental).
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Computer-Based Visualization Strategies to Improve Students' Understanding of Molecular Polarity and Miscibility

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students explain that oil and water do not mix only by stating that one is polar and the other is nonpolar, treating 'like dissolves like' as a memorized rule rather than an explanation.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oil and water are immiscible because water molecules are more strongly attracted to each other than to nonpolar oil molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare intermolecular attractions: water-water attractions are stronger than water-oil attractions, so mixing is unfavorable and the liquids separate.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "More than 80% of the students in the control group responded with the idea that water is polar and oil is nonpolar or that 'like dissolves like' a mere statement of the rule with no real explanation of why it is valid."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: More than 80% of the control group; just over 30% of the experimental group gave the rule without explanation.
all_misconceptions.population: Introductory chemistry students in the control and experimental groups.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Computer-Based Visualization Strategies to Improve Students' Understanding of Molecular Polarity and Miscibility

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe there are no attractions between oil and water molecules.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: There are attractions between all molecules; oil and water simply have much weaker cross-attractions than water-water attractions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize intermolecular attractions are universal but differ in strength. Water molecules preferentially attract each other more strongly than they attract nonpolar oil molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "similar numbers of students in each group suggested that there are no attractions between oil and water molecules (18%)"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 18% in each group.
all_misconceptions.population: Students in both control and experimental groups.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Computer-Based Visualization Strategies to Improve Students' Understanding of Molecular Polarity and Miscibility

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe oil and water molecules repel each other.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Oil and water do not repel each other; they are immiscible because water-water attractions are stronger than water-oil attractions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish repulsion from weak attraction. Separation occurs because the system lowers energy by keeping stronger like-like interactions rather than because unlike molecules repel.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "similar numbers of students in each group suggested that there are no attractions between oil and water molecules (18%) or that oil and water molecules repel each other (7%)."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 7% in each group.
all_misconceptions.population: Students in both control and experimental groups.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Computer-Based Visualization Strategies to Improve Students' Understanding of Molecular Polarity and Miscibility

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen molecules attract water oxygen atoms, or more generally that all H and O atoms attract each other regardless of charge.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Water molecules attract each other through the H of one water to the O of another water, but hydrogen gas does not provide opposite charges for strong H-O attraction to water.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify partial charges first: attraction occurs between opposite charges. Water has polar O-H bonds and partial charges; H2 is nonpolar and should not be shown attracting water's O atoms in this context.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "This question was designed to determine whether students believed that all H and O atoms are attracted to each other or if they recognized that H and O atoms are attracted to each other only when they have opposite charges."
all_misconceptions.population: Students responding to the conceptual question on intermolecular attractions in immiscible mixtures.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Computer-Based Visualization Strategies to Improve Students' Understanding of Molecular Polarity and Miscibility

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students omit the attraction between sodium ions and chloride ions when describing an aqueous sodium chloride system, focusing only on ion-water attractions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A complete description includes water-water attractions, Na+ to water oxygen attractions, Cl- to water hydrogen attractions, and Na+ to Cl- attractions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should account for all relevant intermolecular/ion-ion attractions in the system, not only solvation interactions. Both ion-water and ion-ion attractions matter in the aqueous mixture.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "A majority of the responses from students in the control group recognized attractions between the water molecules and the ions in sodium chloride but ignored the attractions of the water molecules to each other and of the sodium ions to the chloride ions"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: A majority of the control group; experimental students also tended to ignore only the sodium ion-chloride ion attractions.
all_misconceptions.population: Students in the control group and experimental group answering the aqueous sodium chloride attraction question.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Computer-Based Visualization Strategies to Improve Students' Understanding of Molecular Polarity and Miscibility

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students give incomplete explanations of how soap removes grease, omitting the dual hydrophobic/hydrophilic nature of soap and its role as a molecular bridge.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Soap molecules have both hydrophobic and hydrophilic ends; the hydrophobic end interacts with grease, the hydrophilic end interacts with water, and soap helps emulsify grease so it can be washed away.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain that soap is amphiphilic, orient itself with the hydrophobic tail in grease and hydrophilic head in water, and thereby form micelles/emulsions that allow grease to disperse in water.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Both instructors agreed that a correct response should include four concepts: (i) soap is a special molecule in that it has a hydrophobic end and a hydrophilic end; (ii) soap is attracted to water by its hydrophilic end; (iii) soap is attracted to the grease by its hydrophobic end; and (iv) soap acts as a 'molecular bridge'"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Students who viewed the elpot maps gave more complete responses; 61% experimental vs 39% control provided completely correct responses.
all_misconceptions.population: Students in the control and experimental groups answering the soap/grease question.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Computer-Based Visualization Strategies to Improve Students' Understanding of Molecular Polarity and Miscibility

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think hydrogen bonds are fixed bonds rather than dynamic intermolecular interactions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonds are temporary intermolecular interactions that continually form and break as molecules move.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that intermolecular attractions depend on molecular positions and thermal motion, so hydrogen bonding is not permanent; as molecules move, bonds can form and dissociate repeatedly.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: students have a tendency to think of hydrogen bonds as fixed bonds rather than dynamic intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.population: students in the chemistry courses described in the article
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Molecular Dynamics Simulation To Reinforce Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Acid dissociation and molecular dynamics limitations
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think molecular dynamics simulations can model the dissociation of strong acids in water by breaking and forming covalent bonds.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: These simulations do not change covalent bonds; they are suitable for intermolecular interactions, not chemical dissociation reactions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish intermolecular forces from intramolecular covalent bonding and reason that a model based on fixed covalent structures cannot represent proton transfer or bond breaking/forming in acid dissociation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: trying to simulate the dissociation of a strong acid in water will fail, because in that case, intramolecular bonds are being broken and formed.
all_misconceptions.population: students using molecular dynamics simulations
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Molecular Dynamics Simulation To Reinforce Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may expect molecular dynamics simulations to give exact quantitative values, such as the exact boiling point of a substance.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: MDS is better for qualitative or relative predictions, such as comparing boiling points, not exact agreement with experiment.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the simulation to compare relative intermolecular strength and relative boiling behavior, but not infer an exact boiling point from the temperature at which aggregation ceases.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: trying to determine the exact boiling point of a substance by finding the temperature at which the molecules no longer associate with each other would be unwise.
all_misconceptions.population: students using molecular dynamics simulations
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Molecular Dynamics Simulation To Reinforce Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Periodic boundary conditions and empty space
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think the empty space in a low-density simulation cell is physically unrealistic and therefore invalidates the simulation.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In these simulations, empty space can be treated as a nonpolar environment, and low density can be used to improve efficiency without changing the final outcome.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should understand that the model is designed to represent intermolecular interactions efficiently; the low-density setup is an intentional simplification, not a claim that real condensed phases contain that much empty space.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: While the use of low densities may seem unrealistic, they need not be cause for concern. Empty space in a cell should be viewed as a nonpolar environment.
all_misconceptions.population: students constructing simulation cells
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Molecular Dynamics Simulation To Reinforce Student Understanding of Intermolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a state change breaks the covalent bonds within a molecule, so the molecule changes into different substances.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: During a physical change of state, intermolecular forces are overcome but intramolecular covalent bonds remain intact.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between forces between molecules and bonds within molecules, and reason that melting/boiling changes molecular arrangement and spacing, not molecular composition.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "when water changes in state, its chemical bond in the molecule does not be destroyed"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 2: 12.70% alternative conception; Question 4: 11.11% alternative conception
all_misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe water changes its composition when ice melts, so liquid water is not the same substance as ice.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ice, liquid water, and water vapor are the same substance; the molecular composition of water remains H2O across state changes.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that state changes alter physical arrangement and intermolecular attractions, while the molecule H2O itself stays the same.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "water will change to hydrogen gas"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 2: 12.70% alternative conception
all_misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that when water becomes gas, the oxygen and hydrogen atoms separate and become free atoms or separate gases.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: When water evaporates or boils, water molecules separate from each other, but each molecule remains H2O; atoms do not split apart.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that vaporization changes the spacing and motion of molecules, not the atoms within each molecule.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "oxygen atom and hydrogen atom will separate when it reaches the gas state"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 3: 46.03% alternative conceptions
all_misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Formation of hydrogen and oxygen gases
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that phase change produces hydrogen gas and/or oxygen gas from water.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Phase change does not decompose water; it remains H2O unless a chemical reaction occurs.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that boiling or melting is a physical change, so only the arrangement/state changes, not the chemical identity of the substance.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "water will change to hydrogen and oxygen gas when the state changed"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Described qualitatively in the discussion; included within Question 3 alternative conceptions (46.03%)
all_misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think intramolecular covalent bonds are the forces that break during a change of state.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermolecular forces are the attractions relevant to changes of state; intramolecular covalent bonds are not broken in ordinary phase changes.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify that the change of state depends on forces between molecules, so the correct force name is intermolecular force.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the bond between N and H atom is destroyed"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 4: 11.11% alternative conception
all_misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe ammonia is an ionic substance rather than a covalent molecular substance.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ammonia (NH3) is a covalent molecular compound; its phase behavior is governed by intermolecular forces such as hydrogen bonding.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify NH3 as molecular/covalent, then reason that phase change involves overcoming intermolecular attractions, not ionic bonding.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it was an ionic substance"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 4: included in the 11.11% alternative conception responses
all_misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Covalent bond treated as intermolecular force
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students classify a covalent bond as an intermolecular force.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Covalent bonds are intramolecular bonds within a molecule; intermolecular forces are separate attractions between molecules.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish bonds within NH3 from attractions between NH3 molecules and select an intermolecular force such as hydrogen bonding.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Covalence bond as an intermolecular force"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 5: 7.94% alternative conception
all_misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Wrong force named for boiling point difference
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the boiling point difference between ammonia and methane is explained by covalent bonding or by the number of hydrogen atoms, rather than by intermolecular forces.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ammonia has hydrogen bonding, while methane has only London dispersion forces; these intermolecular forces explain the boiling point difference.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the intermolecular forces present in each substance and link stronger intermolecular attraction to a higher boiling point.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the difference of boiling point depending on the number of hydrogen atom in a molecule"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 6: 23.81% alternative conception
all_misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that any substance containing hydrogen must have hydrogen bonding, including methane.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Hydrogen bonding requires hydrogen bonded to N, O, or F; mere presence of hydrogen is not sufficient.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check which atom hydrogen is bonded to and whether the molecule has an appropriate electronegative partner before naming hydrogen bonding.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "methane and ammonia have hydrogen bond because both of them have hydrogen in their molecules"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 6: included in the 23.81% alternative conception responses
all_misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Covalent substances have highest boiling points
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe substances with covalent bonds always have the highest boiling points compared with other substances.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Boiling point depends on the strength of intermolecular forces and particle interactions, not simply on whether a substance is covalent.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the actual intermolecular forces present and recognize that covalent bonding within molecules does not determine ordinary boiling point by itself.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "substance with covalent will have the highest boiling point"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Question 6: included in the 23.81% alternative conception responses
all_misconceptions.population: 64 Grade 10 Thai students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Using Open-Ended Questions to Diagnose Students' Understanding of Inter- and Intramolecular Forces
